handouts.title: High blood pressure
handouts.text:
High blood pressure

Your blood pressure goal is below 130 over 80.

High blood pressure can hurt your heart, brain, and kidneys. Most people do not feel it.

What you can do:

- Take your medicine every day, even if you feel fine.
- Eat more fruits, vegetables, beans, and whole grains.
- Use less salt. Aim for less than 2,300 mg of sodium a day. Less than 1,500 mg is even better.
- Read food labels. Canned, frozen, and restaurant foods have a lot of salt.
- Be active for 30 minutes on most days.
- Limit alcohol. Do not smoke.
- Check your blood pressure at home and write it down. Bring your log to every visit.

Call the clinic if your blood pressure is over 160 over 100 more than once.

Call 911 or go to the ER if your blood pressure is over 180 over 120 and you have:

- Chest pain
- Trouble breathing
- A bad headache
- Weakness or trouble speaking
- Vision changes

handouts.title: Diabetes
handouts.text:
Diabetes

Your blood sugar goal before meals is 80 to 130. Your A1c goal is ***.

At each meal:

- Fill half your plate with vegetables.
- Fill one quarter with lean protein like chicken, fish, beans, or eggs.
- Fill one quarter with starch like brown rice, potatoes, or whole grain bread.
- Drink water instead of soda or juice.

Be active for 30 minutes on 5 days each week.

Low blood sugar is below 70. Signs are shaking, sweating, fast heartbeat, hunger, confusion, or feeling dizzy. If this happens, eat or drink 15 grams of sugar, like 4 ounces of juice or 4 glucose tablets. Check again in 15 minutes. Repeat if still below 70.

Foot care:

- Look at your feet every day for cuts, blisters, or color changes.
- Wear shoes and socks. Do not walk barefoot.
- Keep your feet clean and dry.

Get a diabetes eye exam every year.

Call the clinic if your sugar is often over 250 or under 70. Go to the ER if you are confused, vomiting and cannot keep fluids down, or very short of breath.

handouts.title: Home blood pressure
handouts.text:
How to check your blood pressure at home

- Use an arm cuff that fits your upper arm.
- Do not smoke, exercise, or drink coffee for 30 minutes before.
- Empty your bladder.
- Sit in a chair with your back supported and feet flat on the floor. Do not cross your legs.
- Rest quietly for 5 minutes.
- Put your arm on a table at the level of your heart.
- Put the cuff on bare skin.
- Do not talk during the reading.
- Take 2 readings 1 minute apart. Write both down.
- Check in the morning and in the evening for 7 days before your next visit.

Bring your log and your cuff to your next visit.

Call 911 if your blood pressure is over 180 over 120 and you have:

- Chest pain
- Trouble breathing
- A bad headache
- Weakness
- Vision changes

handouts.title: Low back pain
handouts.text:
Low back pain

Most back pain gets better in 4 to 6 weeks. X-rays and scans are usually not needed.

What helps:

- Keep moving. Walk a little more each day.
- Avoid bed rest. It can make pain last longer.
- Use heat for 15 to 20 minutes at a time.
- Take your pain medicine as directed.
- Do the stretches you were shown.

Go to the ER right away if you have:

- New weakness or numbness in your legs
- Trouble controlling your bladder or bowels
- Numbness in your groin or inner thighs
- Fever with back pain
- Back pain after a bad fall or accident

Call the clinic if your pain is not better in 4 weeks or gets worse.

handouts.title: Cold and upper respiratory infection
handouts.text:
Colds and upper respiratory infections

Colds are caused by viruses. Antibiotics do not help.

Most people feel better in about 1 week. A cough can last 2 to 3 weeks.

What helps:

- Rest and drink plenty of fluids.
- Warm drinks or soup, like chicken soup, can soothe a sore throat and may help loosen mucus.
- Use saline nose spray or a humidifier.
- Honey can help a cough. Do not give honey to babies under 1 year old.
- Use acetaminophen or ibuprofen for fever or pain as directed on the label. For children, use the dose based on weight.
- Wash your hands often. Cover your cough.

Acupressure you can try:

- For a stuffy nose, press the spot beside each nostril, in the crease where the nose meets the cheek.
- Also press the spot between the eyebrows. Use firm small circles for 2 to 3 minutes per spot.
- For a child, use light pressure and no more than 30 seconds per spot.
- This was studied in nose allergies more than colds. It may help a little.

Call the clinic if:

- Fever lasts more than 3 days
- Symptoms last more than 10 days or get better and then worse
- You have bad ear pain or sinus pain

Go to the ER if you have:

- Trouble breathing or chest pain
- Lips turning blue
- Confusion
- Signs of dehydration, like no urine in 8 hours

handouts.title: High cholesterol
handouts.text:
High cholesterol

Cholesterol is a fat in your blood. Too much can clog your blood vessels. This raises your risk of heart attack and stroke.

Your LDL, or bad cholesterol, is ***. Your goal is ***.

What you can do:

- Take *** every day, even if you feel fine.
- Eat more vegetables, fruit, beans, nuts, and whole grains.
- Eat fish 2 times a week.
- Eat less red meat, fried food, butter, and cheese.
- Be active for 30 minutes on most days.
- Do not smoke.

We will check your cholesterol again in ***.

Call the clinic if you have muscle pain or weakness that does not go away, or dark brown urine.

Call 911 if you have chest pain, trouble breathing, a drooping face, arm weakness, or trouble speaking.

handouts.title: Prediabetes
handouts.text:
Prediabetes

Prediabetes means your blood sugar is higher than normal. It is not diabetes yet. You can often stop it from turning into diabetes.

Your A1c is ***. Normal is below 5.7.

What you can do:

- Lose a small amount of weight. Losing 7 percent of your weight cuts your risk a lot. For you, that is about *** pounds.
- Be active for 30 minutes, 5 days a week. Walking counts.
- Drink water instead of soda, juice, or sweet tea.
- Eat less white bread, white rice, and sweets.
- Fill half your plate with vegetables.
- Join a diabetes prevention program: ***

We will check your A1c again in ***.

Call the clinic if you:

- Are very thirsty
- Pee a lot more than usual
- Have blurry vision
- Lose weight without trying

handouts.title: Weight management
handouts.text:
Weight management

Losing even 5 to 10 percent of your weight can lower your blood pressure, blood sugar, and joint pain.

Your goal: *** pounds by ***.

Food:

- Eat protein at every meal, like eggs, chicken, fish, beans, or yogurt.
- Fill half your plate with vegetables.
- Drink water instead of soda, juice, or alcohol.
- Eat fewer chips, sweets, fast food, and packaged snacks.
- Eat slowly. Stop when you feel full.

Activity:

- Work up to 150 minutes a week, like 30 minutes on 5 days.
- Do muscle exercises 2 days a week, like squats, push-ups, or bands.

Sleep 7 to 9 hours a night. Poor sleep makes weight loss harder.

Medicine: ***

If you take a weight loss shot, nausea and constipation are common at first. Eat small meals and stop eating when full.

Call the clinic if you cannot keep food or fluids down.

Go to the ER if you have:

- Bad belly pain that goes to your back
- Pain in the upper right belly with fever

handouts.title: Depression
handouts.text:
Depression

Depression is a common illness. It is not your fault. It can be treated, and most people get better.

Your plan:

- Medicine: ***
- Counseling: ***
- Next visit: ***

About your medicine:

- Take it every day.
- It takes 4 to 8 weeks to work fully. Keep taking it even if you do not feel better yet.
- Side effects like upset stomach or headache often go away in 1 to 2 weeks.
- Do not stop it suddenly. Talk to us first.

Things that help:

- Get outside and move your body every day, even a short walk.
- Keep a regular sleep time.
- Spend time with people you trust.
- Avoid alcohol and drugs. They make depression worse.

In the first few weeks of medicine, some people feel worse or have new thoughts of suicide. This is more common in people under 25. Call us right away if this happens.

Call the clinic if you feel worse or side effects bother you.

If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, call or text 988 any time, day or night.

Call 911 if you are in danger right now.

handouts.title: Anxiety
handouts.text:
Anxiety

Anxiety is a common illness. It can be treated, and most people get better.

Your plan:

- Medicine: ***
- Counseling: ***
- Next visit: ***

Things that help:

- Slow breathing. Breathe in for 4 seconds, hold for 4, and breathe out for 6. Repeat for 2 minutes.
- Move your body for 30 minutes on most days.
- Cut back on coffee, energy drinks, and soda.
- Avoid alcohol and marijuana. They make anxiety worse over time.
- Keep a regular sleep time.

About your medicine:

- Take it every day.
- It takes 4 to 8 weeks to work fully.
- Do not stop it suddenly. Talk to us first.

Call the clinic if you feel worse, have panic attacks often, or side effects bother you.

If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, call or text 988 any time, day or night.

Call 911 if you have chest pain or trouble breathing, or if you are in danger right now.

handouts.title: Thyroid medicine
handouts.text:
Thyroid medicine

Your thyroid gland does not make enough hormone. Your medicine replaces it.

Your dose: levothyroxine *** mcg by mouth every morning.

How to take it:

- Take it when you wake up, with a full glass of water.
- Wait 30 to 60 minutes before you eat or drink coffee.
- Take calcium, iron, and antacids at least 4 hours apart from it.
- Stay on the same brand or maker. Tell us if your pill looks different.
- Stop biotin (hair, skin, nail vitamins) 2 days before thyroid blood tests.
- Take it every day. You will likely need it for life.
- If you miss a dose, take it when you remember that day.

We will check your thyroid with a blood test in ***. It takes 6 to 8 weeks to see the full effect of a dose change.

Call the clinic if you become pregnant. Your dose will likely need to go up right away. Take 2 extra pills each week as soon as your test is positive.

Call the clinic if you have a racing heart, shaking, trouble sleeping, or weight loss. Also call if you feel very tired, cold, or constipated.

Call 911 if you have chest pain or trouble breathing.

Asthma action plan

Name: ***

Daily controller: ***
Use your spacer with every inhaler.

Green zone: doing well

- No cough, wheeze, or chest tightness, day or night.
- You can do your usual activities.

What to do:

- Take ***, *** puffs, *** times a day, every day.
- Before exercise, take ***, *** puffs, if needed.

Yellow zone: getting worse

- Cough, wheeze, chest tightness, or short of breath.
- Waking up at night with asthma.

What to do:

- Take ***, *** puffs, every *** hours as needed.
- Also take: ***
- Call the clinic if you are not back in the green zone in 24 hours.
- Also call if you need your rescue inhaler more than ***.

Red zone: medical alert

- Very short of breath, or rescue inhaler is not helping.
- Trouble walking or talking because of breathing.
- Lips or fingernails are blue or gray.

What to do:

- Take ***, *** puffs, now.
- Call 911 or go to the ER now.

Avoid smoke and your triggers: ***. Get a flu shot every year.

handouts.title: COPD
handouts.text:
COPD

COPD makes it hard to move air in and out of your lungs. Treatment can help you breathe easier and stay out of the hospital.

Your inhalers:

- Every day: ***
- Rescue, as needed: ***

What you can do:

- Use your daily inhaler every day, even when you feel well.
- Quitting smoking is the best thing you can do for your lungs.
- Stay active. Ask about pulmonary rehab, an exercise class for your lungs.
- Get your flu, pneumonia, COVID, and RSV shots.
- Never smoke or use a flame near oxygen.

A flare means more shortness of breath, more mucus, or mucus that changes color.

If you have a flare:

- Use your rescue inhaler.
- Start ***, if we gave it to you.
- Call the clinic the same day.

Call 911 if you:

- Are too short of breath to talk
- Have blue lips
- Are confused or very sleepy
- Have chest pain

handouts.title: Chronic kidney disease
handouts.text:
Kidney disease

Your kidneys clean your blood. Your kidneys work at about *** percent. Good care can slow kidney damage.

What you can do:

- Keep your blood pressure below ***.
- Keep your blood sugar in your goal range, if you have diabetes.
- Use less salt.
- Do not smoke.
- Do not take ibuprofen, naproxen, or other NSAID pain pills. Acetaminophen is safer for your kidneys.
- Ask us before you take any new medicine, herbal product, or supplement.
- Tell every doctor and dentist that you have kidney disease.

Sick days:
If you are vomiting, have diarrhea, or cannot drink fluids, stop taking *** and call us. Start again when you are eating and drinking normally.

Next blood and urine tests: ***

Call the clinic if you:

- Have new swelling
- Are peeing much less
- Feel very tired or sick to your stomach

Go to the ER if you have not peed in 12 hours, or have chest pain, trouble breathing, or confusion.

handouts.title: Heartburn and reflux
handouts.text:
Heartburn and reflux

Reflux happens when stomach acid comes up into your throat. It causes burning in your chest or a sour taste. It happens when the valve at the bottom of your food pipe opens at the wrong time.

What you can do:

- Eat smaller meals.
- Stop eating 3 hours before you lie down.
- Raise the head of your bed 6 to 8 inches with blocks.
- You can also use a foam wedge under your upper body.
- Sleep on your left side. Lying on your right side brings on more reflux.
- Lose weight if you are overweight. The more you lose, the more it helps. Your goal: *** pounds.
- Cut back on foods that cause your symptoms, like spicy or fatty food, coffee, alcohol, or chocolate.
- Only cut out the foods that bother you. You do not need to give up all of them.
- Do not smoke.

Belly breathing to train the valve:

- Your breathing muscle, the diaphragm, wraps around the valve. It helps squeeze the valve shut.
- Training this muscle may ease reflux.
- Lie on your back with your knees bent and a pillow under your head.
- Put one hand on your chest. Put the other hand on your belly, just below your ribs.
- Breathe in slowly through your nose. Your belly hand should rise. Your chest hand should stay still.
- Breathe out slowly through pursed lips. Let your belly fall.
- Go slow, about 6 to 8 breaths each minute.
- Do this for 20 minutes, 2 times a day, for 8 weeks.
- A session after a meal can cut reflux after eating.
- Keep doing it after 8 weeks if it helps.
- If you feel dizzy, stop and breathe normally. Start again when it passes.

Medicines:

- Alginate, for heartburn after meals: take *** after meals and at bedtime as needed. Look for sodium alginate on the label.
- Antacid, for heartburn now and then: chew *** as needed. Do not take more than *** a day.
- For heartburn at night: take famotidine *** mg by mouth at bedtime as needed.
- Acid pill: take *** by mouth every day, 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast, for *** weeks. Then we will try to lower or stop it.
- Take the acid pill before a meal, not at bedtime. It works best that way.

Coming off your acid pill:

- Plan: ***
- You can lower the dose step by step or stop all at once. Both are OK.
- Heartburn may come back for a short time after you stop. This is called rebound. It fades.
- Use an alginate or antacid as needed while it settles.
- Some people need to stay on the pill, such as people with Barrett's esophagus. Ask us before you stop.

Call the clinic if you have trouble or pain when swallowing, keep vomiting, or lose weight without trying. Also call if you are not better in 8 weeks.

Go to the ER if you:

- Vomit blood
- Have black stools

Call 911 if you have chest pain with activity, sweating, or shortness of breath. It could be your heart.

handouts.title: Arthritis
handouts.text:
Arthritis

Arthritis is wear and tear of the cushion in your joints. It causes pain and stiffness. Moving more helps it.

What you can do:

- Stay active. Walking, biking, and swimming are good for your joints.
- Do the strength exercises you were shown. Strong muscles protect your joints.
- Lose weight if you need to. Each pound you lose takes about 4 pounds of pressure off your knees.
- Use heat for stiffness and ice for swelling, 15 to 20 minutes at a time.
- Rub *** gel on the joint up to 4 times a day.
- If you take pain pills like ***, take them with food.
- A cane or brace may help: ***

Call the clinic if:

- Pain keeps you from sleeping or doing daily tasks
- You have stomach pain from pain pills

Go to the ER or come in the same day if:

- A joint becomes red, hot, and swollen
- You have a fever
- You have black stools

handouts.title: Sleep
handouts.text:
Better sleep

This plan is called CBT-I. It retrains your body and brain to sleep. Over time it works better than sleeping pills.

Most people sleep better within 6 weeks. You may feel more tired during the day in the first weeks. This gets better as you keep going.

Step 1: Keep a sleep diary for 1 to 2 weeks

Each morning, write down:

- What time you went to bed
- About how long it took to fall asleep
- How many times you woke up, and for how long
- What time you woke up for good, and what time you got out of bed
- Any naps, caffeine, alcohol, or sleep medicine the day before
- How well you slept, from 1 (very poor) to 5 (very good)

Guess the times. Do not check the clock at night. Bring your diary to every visit.

Step 2: Set your sleep window

Your wake time: *** every day, even on weekends.
Your bedtime: ***
Your time in bed: *** hours

We set your time in bed from your diary. It is close to the time you actually sleep, but never less than *** hours.

- Get up at your wake time every day, even after a bad night.
- Do not go to bed before your bedtime, even if you are tired.
- Go to bed only when you feel sleepy.
- Try not to nap.

Each week, divide the hours you slept by the hours you spent in bed. Example: 6.5 hours asleep in 7 hours in bed is 0.93.

- If the answer is 0.9 or more and you still feel tired, go to bed 15 minutes earlier.
- If the answer is less than 0.85, keep the same window and call us.
- Always keep the same wake time.

Be safe:

- You may feel sleepy during the day in the first weeks.
- Do not drive or use machines if you feel drowsy.
- Ask us before shortening your time in bed if you have seizures, bipolar disorder, or untreated sleep apnea.
- Also ask us first if sleepiness would be dangerous at your job, like driving or running machines.

Step 3: Use your bed only for sleep

- Use your bed only for sleep and sex. No TV, phone, eating, or work in bed.
- If you are awake for about 20 minutes, get up and go to another room.
- Do something calm in dim light. Go back to bed only when you feel sleepy.
- Do this as many times as needed, including in the middle of the night.
- Turn your clock away so you cannot see it.

Step 4: Set up your day and evening

- Get outside in daylight every day.
- Be active for at least 30 minutes on most days. Avoid hard exercise in the 2 hours before bed.
- Caffeine can last up to 8 hours. No coffee, tea, soda, energy drinks, or chocolate after ***.
- Alcohol may help you fall asleep, but it wakes you up later in the night. Avoid it in the evening.
- Nicotine from cigarettes or vapes can keep you awake. Ask us for help quitting.
- Cannabis has not been shown to help long-term sleep problems. Stopping after regular use can cause poor sleep for a while.
- Avoid heavy meals in the 2 hours before bed. A light snack is fine.
- Use the last hour before bed to wind down. Dim the lights and turn off screens.

Step 5: Calm a racing mind

- Early in the evening, set aside a short worry time.
- Write down each worry and one possible next step. Then put the list away.
- Slow breathing: breathe in slowly through your nose so your belly rises. Breathe out slowly. Repeat for a few minutes.
- Muscle relaxation: tighten one muscle group for a few seconds, then let go. Work from your feet up to your face.

Acupressure you can try

This is optional. Do it along with this plan, not instead of it. In one study, people who pressed spots like these each night slept better.

- Each night, spend 10 to 15 minutes in total pressing these spots.
- Press firmly with your thumb or finger. It should feel good, not painful. Do both sides.
- The hollow on the pinky side of your inner wrist crease.
- About 3 finger widths above your inner wrist crease, between the 2 tendons.
- The 2 hollows at the base of your skull, one on each side of your neck.
- The top of your head, in line with the tops of your ears.

Mild soreness or bruising can happen. Stop if you feel dizzy. Skip any spot with a wound, numbness, or swelling. If you are pregnant, ask us first.

Sleep medicines

- Store-bought sleep aids contain diphenhydramine or doxylamine. They are only for occasional sleepless nights, not long-term use.
- They can cause confusion, dry mouth, constipation, and trouble peeing. People 65 and older should avoid them.
- Melatonin is not recommended for long-term insomnia. The amount in pills and gummies often does not match the label.
- Prescription sleep pills are short-term helpers. Use them only as prescribed, along with this plan.
- If you have taken a sleep pill for a long time, do not stop it suddenly. We can help you lower it slowly.

Free programs that teach this plan

- Path to Better Sleep: a free online course from the VA. Anyone can use it: https://www.veterantraining.va.gov/insomnia/
- Insomnia Coach: a free VA app you can use on your own. More at https://mobile.va.gov/app/insomnia-coach
- Insomnia Coach for iPhone: https://apps.apple.com/us/app/insomnia-coach/id1341944736
- Insomnia Coach for Android: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=gov.va.mobilehealth.ncptsd.insomniacoach
- CBT-i Coach: a free VA app to use with a sleep therapist. More at https://mobile.va.gov/app/cbt-i-coach
- CBT-i Coach for iPhone: https://apps.apple.com/us/app/cbt-i-coach/id655918660
- CBT-i Coach for Android: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=gov.va.mobilehealth.ncptsd.cbti
- Local sleep therapy referral: ***

Call the clinic if:

- You snore loudly, or someone sees you stop breathing, gasp, or choke in your sleep.
- You get drowsy or fall asleep while driving. Do not drive until we talk.
- You have an urge to move your legs at night that keeps you awake.
- Your mood is low, or you feel worried or on edge most days.
- Your sleep is not better after *** weeks on this plan.

If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, call or text 988 any time, day or night. Call 911 if you are in danger right now.

handouts.title: Quitting smoking
handouts.text:
Quitting smoking

Quitting is the best thing you can do for your health. Medicine and support double your chances of quitting.

Your quit date: ***

Your medicine:

- ***
- If you use varenicline, start it 1 week before your quit date. Take it with food and a full glass of water.
- If you use the patch, put on a new one every morning. Use gum or lozenges for cravings too.

Tips:

- Get rid of cigarettes, lighters, and ashtrays.
- Know your triggers, like coffee, alcohol, or stress. Plan what you will do instead.
- Cravings pass in a few minutes. Drink water, take a walk, or chew gum.
- If you slip, do not give up. Start again the next day.

Free help: call 1-800-QUIT-NOW.

Call the clinic if you have bad nausea or trouble sleeping on your medicine, or if your mood changes.

If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, call or text 988.

handouts.title: Birth control
handouts.text:
Birth control

Your method: ***
How to use it: ***

Backup: use condoms for *** days. Birth control does not protect against STIs, so condoms are a good idea.

If you miss a pill:

- Take it as soon as you remember, even if that means 2 pills in 1 day.
- If you miss 2 or more pills, use condoms for 7 days and call us.

Emergency birth control can prevent pregnancy if taken within 5 days after sex. The sooner you take it, the better it works. Ask us or your pharmacy.

Call the clinic if you think you might be pregnant, have bleeding that bothers you, or want to change methods.

If your method has estrogen, like the pill, patch, or ring, go to the ER right away for:

- Chest pain or trouble breathing
- Bad headache or vision changes
- Pain or swelling in one leg
- Bad belly pain

handouts.title: Bladder infection
handouts.text:
Bladder infection

A bladder infection is caused by germs in your bladder. It causes burning when you pee and a need to pee often.

What to do:

- Take your antibiotic *** as prescribed until it is gone, even if you feel better.
- Drink plenty of water.
- If we gave you a medicine for burning, it can turn your urine orange. This is normal.
- Pee after sex. It can help prevent new infections.

Call the clinic if you are not better in 48 hours or your symptoms come back.

Go to the ER if you have fever, chills, back or side pain, or vomiting. Also go if you cannot keep your antibiotic down.

handouts.title: Sore throat
handouts.text:
Sore throat

Most sore throats are caused by viruses. Antibiotics do not help viruses. Your strep test was ***.

If you have strep:

- Take your antibiotic *** until it is gone, even if you feel better.
- You can go back to work or school after 12 hours of antibiotics if you have no fever.

What helps:

- Drink warm or cold liquids.
- Gargle with warm salt water.
- Honey, lozenges, or popsicles can soothe the throat. Do not give honey to babies under 1 year old.
- Use acetaminophen or ibuprofen as directed on the label. For children, use the dose based on weight.

Call the clinic if:

- You are not better in 3 to 5 days
- Fever lasts more than 3 days
- You get a rash

Go to the ER if you have:

- Trouble breathing
- Drooling, or you cannot swallow your spit
- Trouble opening your mouth
- A muffled voice
- A stiff neck
- Swelling on one side of your throat

handouts.title: Sinus infection
handouts.text:
Sinus infection

Most sinus infections are caused by viruses. They get better on their own in 7 to 10 days. Antibiotics usually do not help.

What helps:

- Rinse your nose with salt water 1 to 2 times a day. Use distilled or boiled water that has cooled.
- Use your steroid nose spray *** every day.
- A decongestant spray can help, but do not use it for more than 3 days.
- Use acetaminophen or ibuprofen as directed on the label.
- Drink plenty of fluids and rest.

Your plan: ***

Call the clinic if you are not better in 10 days, or you get better and then worse. Also call for a fever over 102 F for 3 days.

Go to the ER if you have:

- Swelling or redness around your eye
- Vision changes
- A bad headache
- A stiff neck
- Confusion

handouts.title: Chest cold and cough
handouts.text:
Chest cold

A chest cold is caused by a virus. Antibiotics do not help. The cough often lasts 2 to 3 weeks, even after you feel better.

What helps:

- Rest and drink plenty of fluids.
- Honey in warm tea can calm a cough. Do not give honey to babies under 1 year old.
- Use a humidifier or breathe steam from a shower.
- Do not smoke, and stay away from smoke.
- Use your inhaler ***, if we gave you one.

Call the clinic if:

- Your cough lasts more than 3 weeks
- Fever lasts more than 3 days
- You cough up blood

Go to the ER if you have trouble breathing, chest pain, or blue lips.

handouts.title: Stomach bug
handouts.text:
Stomach bug

A stomach bug is usually caused by a virus. Vomiting often stops in 1 to 2 days. Diarrhea can last up to a week.

Drink fluids:

- Take small sips often. Start with 1 to 2 tablespoons every 5 minutes.
- Slowly drink more as you keep it down.
- Good choices are water, broth, and oral rehydration drinks from the store.
- Avoid alcohol and drinks with a lot of sugar.

Eat simple foods when you feel ready, like rice, toast, bananas, crackers, and soup.

Medicine for nausea: ***

Do not use anti-diarrhea medicine if you have a fever or blood in your stool.

Wash your hands often. Do not cook for others until 2 days after you feel better.

Acupressure you can try:

- Find the spot 3 finger widths above your wrist crease, on the palm side, between the 2 tendons.
- Press firmly with your thumb in small circles for 2 to 3 minutes. It should not hurt. Then do the other wrist.
- Repeat a few times a day. Acupressure wristbands from the store press on the same spot.
- It may ease nausea a little. Keep sipping fluids too.

Call the clinic if you are not better in 3 days.

Go to the ER if you have blood in your vomit or stool, black stool, or bad belly pain. Also go if you have not peed in 8 hours, feel dizzy when you stand, or cannot keep fluids down.

handouts.title: Hives and allergic reaction
handouts.text:
Hives

Hives are itchy, raised welts on the skin. Each spot usually fades within a day, but new ones can appear for days or weeks. Often the cause is never found.

What helps:

- Take cetirizine 10 mg by mouth once a day until the hives have been gone for a few days.
- Use cool cloths on itchy skin.
- Wear loose cotton clothes.
- Avoid hot showers, alcohol, and anything you think caused the hives: ***

If you were given an epinephrine pen, keep it with you at all times.

Call the clinic if the hives last more than 6 weeks or keep coming back.

Call 911 if you have any of these signs. If you have an epinephrine pen, use it first.

- Trouble breathing or wheezing
- Swelling of your lips, tongue, or throat
- A tight throat or trouble swallowing
- Feeling faint
- Vomiting along with hives

handouts.title: Headache
handouts.text:
Headache

Your headache is most likely ***. These headaches are painful but not dangerous.

During a headache:

- Take your medicine *** as soon as the headache starts.
- Rest in a dark, quiet room.
- Use a cool cloth on your forehead or neck.

Acupressure you can try:

- Squeeze your thumb and first finger together. Press the top of the bump between them. Skip this spot if you are pregnant.
- Press the 2 hollows at the base of your skull, 1 finger width out from the spine.
- Press the spot between your eyebrows.
- Use firm small circles for 1 to 3 minutes per spot, on both sides. It may ease pain a little.

To prevent headaches:

- Sleep and eat meals at regular times.
- Drink plenty of water.
- Have the same amount of caffeine each day.
- Get regular exercise, like walking, biking, or yoga.
- If your doctor suggests it, take *** each day to help prevent migraines.
- Keep a headache diary. Write down the time, what you ate, and what you were doing.
- Do not use pain medicine more than 2 to 3 days a week. Using it more can cause more headaches.

Call the clinic if your headaches come more often or change.

Call 911 if you have:

- The worst headache of your life that starts suddenly
- Headache with fever and a stiff neck
- Weakness, numbness, trouble speaking, or vision loss
- Confusion or fainting
- A headache after a head injury

handouts.title: Vertigo
handouts.text:
Vertigo

Vertigo feels like the room is spinning. Your kind of vertigo happens when tiny crystals in your inner ear move out of place. It is not dangerous and often goes away in a few weeks.

What helps:

- Do the exercises you were shown, *** times a day.
- Move your head slowly. Get up slowly.
- Sit down right away when you feel dizzy.
- Remove rugs and clutter to prevent falls.
- Do not drive while you feel dizzy.
- If we prescribed medicine for dizziness, use it only for bad spells. It can make you sleepy.

Call the clinic if you are not better in *** weeks or it keeps coming back.

Call 911 if dizziness comes with double vision, trouble speaking, a drooping face, or weakness or numbness. Also call for trouble walking, a sudden bad headache, chest pain, fainting, or new hearing loss.

handouts.title: Sprain
handouts.text:
Sprain

A sprain is a stretched or torn ligament. Most sprains heal in 2 to 6 weeks.

First 2 to 3 days:

- Rest the injured area.
- Ice it for 15 to 20 minutes every 2 to 3 hours. Put a cloth between the ice and your skin.
- Wrap it with an elastic bandage. Loosen it if your toes or fingers tingle or turn cold.
- Raise it above the level of your heart.

After 2 to 3 days:

- Start moving it gently.
- Slowly return to normal activity as pain allows.
- Brace or crutches: ***

Use acetaminophen or ibuprofen as directed on the label.

Call the clinic if you cannot put weight on it after 1 week or it is not getting better.

Go to the ER if:

- Your fingers or toes are numb, cold, pale, or blue
- You have very bad pain

handouts.title: Wound and stitch care
handouts.text:
Wound care

Your wound was closed with ***.

First 24 hours:

- Keep it clean and dry.

After 24 hours:

- Gently wash it with soap and water once or twice a day. Pat it dry.
- Put on a thin layer of petroleum jelly and a clean bandage.
- Do not soak it in a bath, pool, or hot tub until it is healed.

If you have skin glue, do not put ointment on it. Do not pick at it. It falls off in 5 to 10 days.

Stitches out in *** days at ***.

Your tetanus shot is ***.

Protect the scar from the sun for 1 year to help it fade.

Call the clinic or come back if you have spreading redness, red streaks, pus, warmth, or fever. Also call if the wound opens or pain gets worse after 2 days.

Go to the ER if bleeding does not stop after 10 minutes of firm pressure.

handouts.title: Concussion
handouts.text:
Concussion

A concussion is a mild brain injury. Common symptoms are headache, dizziness, feeling tired, and trouble focusing. Most people feel better in 2 to 4 weeks.

First 1 to 2 days:

- Rest, but you do not need to stay in a dark room.
- Limit screens, reading, and loud places if they make symptoms worse.
- Do not drink alcohol.
- Use acetaminophen for headache.

After that:

- Slowly add light activity like walking, as long as symptoms do not get worse.
- Go back to school or work with breaks as needed. School or work note: ***
- Do not drive until ***.
- Sleep at regular times.

No sports, contact activities, or anything that could cause another head injury until a doctor clears you. Return to sports step by step.

Call the clinic if you are not getting better in 2 weeks or symptoms get worse.

Go to the ER right away if you have:

- A headache that gets worse and worse
- Vomiting more than once
- A seizure
- Trouble waking up, or being very sleepy
- Confusion, slurred speech, or acting strange
- Weakness or numbness
- One pupil larger than the other

handouts.title: Vaginal infection
handouts.text:
Vaginal infection

You have ***. This is not a sexually transmitted infection.

Your medicine: ***. Use all of it, even if you feel better.

If you take metronidazole, do not drink alcohol while taking it and for 3 days after.

To help prevent it from coming back:

- Do not douche.
- Wash the outside only, with water or plain unscented soap.
- Wear cotton underwear. Change out of wet clothes soon.
- Use condoms.

Call the clinic if you are not better after treatment or it comes back often. Also call if you have sores, pelvic pain, or are pregnant.

Go to the ER if you have bad belly pain with fever.

handouts.title: Constipation
handouts.text:
Constipation

Constipation means hard stools or not going often. It is common and usually gets better with simple changes.

What helps:

- Eat more fiber, like fruit, vegetables, beans, and whole grains. Add it slowly.
- Drink 8 to 10 cups of fluid a day, mostly water.
- Warm soups and broth count as fluid. Soups with beans, lentils, or vegetables add fiber too.
- A warm drink with breakfast can help you go.
- Move your body every day.
- Sit on the toilet at the same time each day, like after breakfast.
- Put your feet on a small stool when you sit on the toilet.
- Do not ignore the urge to go.

Foods that help (try them for 4 weeks):

- Eat 2 green kiwis a day.
- Or eat about 10 prunes a day (100 grams).
- Eat whole-grain rye bread instead of white bread. It can cause gas.
- Drink about 4 cups (1 liter) a day of mineral water high in magnesium.
- Ask us first about magnesium water if you have kidney disease or must limit salt.
- Psyllium fiber powder works best at more than 10 grams a day. Build up slowly.

Belly massage and acupressure you can try:

- Lie on your back. With a flat hand, rub slow circles up the right side, across, and down the left side.
- Do this for 10 to 20 minutes. Try it after a meal or at bedtime. It should not hurt.
- Skip belly massage if you are pregnant, had recent belly surgery, or have a hernia, Crohn's disease, or colitis.
- Press the back of your forearm, 4 finger widths above the wrist crease, between the 2 bones. Press for 1 minute, then rub small circles for 1 minute. Do both arms twice a day.

Medicine: polyethylene glycol 17 grams mixed in 8 ounces of liquid by mouth once a day. Use less if stools get too loose.

Call the clinic if:

- You have not had a stool in 3 days, even with medicine
- You see blood in your stool
- You lose weight without trying

Go to the ER if you have bad belly pain, a swollen belly with vomiting, or cannot pass gas.

handouts.title: After abscess drainage
handouts.text:
After abscess drainage

What to do:

- Keep the area covered with a clean bandage.
- Change the bandage once a day, or when it gets wet or dirty.
- Some drainage is normal for a few days.
- Packing: ***
- Antibiotic: ***
- Take the antibiotic exactly as prescribed. Tell us if you get diarrhea.
- Use acetaminophen or ibuprofen as directed on the label for pain.

To prevent spread:

- Wash your hands before and after touching the area.
- Do not share towels, razors, or clothes.
- Do not pick at or squeeze the area.
- Put used bandages in the trash.

If boils keep coming back:

- Ask us about a 5-day plan with a nose ointment and a daily skin wash.
- During those 5 days, wash towels, sheets, and clothes every day.

Come back on *** for a wound check.

Call the clinic or come back if you have:

- Spreading redness or red streaks
- Fever
- More pain
- Pus building up again

handouts.title: After skin biopsy
handouts.text:
After skin biopsy

What to do:

- Keep the bandage on and dry for 24 hours.
- Then wash the area gently with soap and water once a day.
- Put on a thin layer of petroleum jelly and a clean bandage until it heals.
- Avoid heavy exercise that stretches the area for *** days.
- Stitches out in *** days.

Your results should be back in *** days. We will contact you. Call us if you have not heard in 2 weeks.

If it bleeds, press firmly on it for 20 minutes without peeking.

Call the clinic if bleeding does not stop after 20 minutes of pressure. Also call for spreading redness, warmth, pus, or fever.

handouts.title: After freezing treatment
handouts.text:
After freezing treatment

What to expect:

- The area will be red and swollen.
- A blister may form within 1 day. It may fill with clear fluid or blood. This is normal.
- It heals in 1 to 3 weeks.
- The skin may be lighter or darker afterward.

What to do:

- Keep the area clean.
- Do not pop the blister.
- If the blister breaks, wash it gently, put on petroleum jelly, and cover it.
- Use acetaminophen or ibuprofen as directed on the label for pain.

You may need another treatment in *** weeks.

Call the clinic if you have spreading redness, pus, or fever, or the spot does not go away.

handouts.title: After IUD placement
handouts.text:
After IUD placement

Your IUD: ***
It works until: ***

What to expect:

- Cramping and spotting are common for a few days. Spotting can last a few months.
- With a hormone IUD, periods often get lighter or stop.
- With a copper IUD, periods may be heavier with more cramps for the first few months.
- Use ibuprofen or acetaminophen as directed on the label for cramps.

Backup: use condoms for *** days.

The IUD does not protect against STIs. Condoms do.

You can feel for the strings once a month after your period. Do not pull on them.

Call the clinic if you cannot feel the strings, feel the hard plastic, or miss a period. Also call for new pain with sex.

Go to the ER if you have bad belly pain, fever, chills, or bad-smelling discharge. Also go if you soak a pad every hour for 2 hours.

handouts.title: After birth control implant
handouts.text:
After birth control implant

Your implant works until: ***

What to do:

- Keep the pressure bandage on for 24 hours.
- Keep the small bandage on for 3 to 5 days.
- Keep the area dry for 24 hours.
- Bruising and soreness are normal for a few days.
- Feel for the implant under your skin. You should be able to feel it.

Backup: use condoms for *** days.

Irregular bleeding is common with the implant. It often gets better over time.

The implant does not protect against STIs. Condoms do.

Call the clinic if you cannot feel the implant, or it seems bent or broken. Also call for spreading redness, pus, fever, or numbness in your arm. Call if you think you might be pregnant.

handouts.title: After endometrial biopsy
handouts.text:
After endometrial biopsy

What to expect:

- Cramping for 1 to 2 days.
- Light spotting for a few days.

What to do:

- Use ibuprofen or acetaminophen as directed on the label for cramps.
- Use pads, not tampons, for *** days.
- No sex for *** days.

Your results should be back in *** days. We will contact you. Call us if you have not heard in 2 weeks.

Call the clinic if you:

- Soak a pad every hour for 2 hours
- Have a fever
- Have bad pain
- Have bad-smelling discharge

handouts.title: After joint injection
handouts.text:
After joint injection

Your *** was injected with a steroid and numbing medicine.

What to expect:

- The numbing medicine wears off in a few hours. Pain may come back.
- Some people have more pain for 1 to 2 days. This is called a flare.
- The steroid starts working in 2 to 7 days. The full effect can take 2 weeks.
- Your face may feel warm or flushed for a day.

What to do:

- Rest the joint for 1 to 2 days. Avoid heavy use.
- Ice it for 15 to 20 minutes at a time for pain.
- If you have diabetes, your blood sugar may be higher for a few days. Check it more often.

Call the clinic if you are not better in 2 weeks.

Come in the same day or go to the ER if:

- The joint gets red, hot, and more swollen after 2 days
- You have a fever

handouts.title: Fever in children
handouts.text:
Fever in children

A fever is a temperature of 100.4 F or higher. Fever helps the body fight infection. It is not dangerous by itself.

Treat your child's comfort, not the number. How your child acts matters more than the temperature.

Fever does not cause brain damage. It often comes back when medicine wears off. Fevers from viruses usually last 2 to 3 days.

What helps:

- Give plenty of fluids.
- Dress your child in light clothes.
- Let your child rest.

Fever medicine:

- Acetaminophen: 15 mg/kg by mouth every 4 to 6 hours as needed. No more than 5 doses in 24 hours. Max 75 mg/kg a day, and never more than 4,000 mg a day.
- Ibuprofen: only for age 6 months and older. 10 mg/kg by mouth every 6 to 8 hours as needed. Max 40 mg/kg a day, and never more than 400 mg per dose.
- Your child's weight: *** kg
- Your child's acetaminophen dose: *** mL of ***
- Your child's ibuprofen dose: *** mL of ***
- Never give aspirin to children.

If a baby under 3 months has a fever of 100.4 F or higher, go to the ER now. Do not give medicine first.

Call the clinic if:

- Fever lasts more than 24 hours in a child under 2 years
- Fever lasts more than 3 days in an older child
- Your child has ear pain, a sore throat, or pain when peeing
- Your child has fewer wet diapers or is peeing less

Go to the ER or call 911 if your child:

- Has trouble breathing
- Is hard to wake up or very floppy
- Cannot be calmed down
- Has a rash of purple spots that do not fade when pressed
- Has a stiff neck or a seizure
- Has not peed in 8 hours

handouts.title: Ear infection in children
handouts.text:
Ear infection

Ear infections are common in children. Many get better on their own in 2 to 3 days.

Your child's plan: ***

If we prescribed an antibiotic:

- Give *** mL by mouth *** times a day for *** days.
- Give all of it, even if your child feels better.

If we chose to wait and watch:

- Fill the antibiotic prescription only if your child is not better in 2 to 3 days, or gets worse.

For pain or fever:

- Acetaminophen: 15 mg/kg by mouth every 4 to 6 hours as needed. No more than 5 doses in 24 hours. Max 75 mg/kg a day, and never more than 4,000 mg a day.
- Ibuprofen: only for age 6 months and older. 10 mg/kg by mouth every 6 to 8 hours as needed. Max 40 mg/kg a day, and never more than 400 mg per dose.
- Your child's acetaminophen dose: *** mL of ***
- Your child's ibuprofen dose: *** mL of ***

Fluid behind the eardrum can last for weeks. This is normal and usually goes away.

Call the clinic if your child:

- Is not better in 2 to 3 days
- Has a fever over 102 F
- Has fluid draining from the ear

Go to the ER if your child:

- Has swelling or redness behind the ear
- Has a stiff neck or a weak face
- Is very sleepy

handouts.title: Vomiting and diarrhea in children
handouts.text:
Vomiting and diarrhea in children

Vomiting and diarrhea are usually caused by a virus. Vomiting often stops in 1 to 2 days. Loose stools can last 1 to 2 weeks. The most important thing is to keep your child from getting dried out.

Give fluids:

- Use oral rehydration solution from the store.
- Give 1 teaspoon, or 5 mL, every 5 minutes with a spoon or syringe.
- If your child vomits, wait 15 minutes and start again.
- Slowly give more as your child keeps it down.
- If you breastfeed, keep nursing. Feed more often for shorter times.
- Avoid juice, soda, and sports drinks. They can make diarrhea worse.

Go back to normal food once vomiting stops.

Nausea medicine: ***

Wash hands often, especially after diaper changes.

Signs your child is dried out:

- No pee or wet diaper in 8 hours
- Dry mouth or no tears when crying
- Sunken eyes
- Very sleepy or fussy

Call the clinic if vomiting lasts more than 24 hours or diarrhea lasts more than 1 week.

Go to the ER if your child has:

- Signs of being dried out
- Green or bloody vomit
- Blood in the stool
- Bad belly pain
- Trouble waking up

handouts.title: Croup
handouts.text:
Croup

Croup is caused by a virus. It swells the airway below the voice box. It causes a barky cough, a hoarse voice, and noisy breathing. It is often worse at night. It usually lasts 3 to 5 days.

Your child got a steroid medicine today: ***

What helps:

- Keep your child calm. Crying makes breathing harder.
- Hold and comfort your child.
- Cool night air may help some children.
- Give plenty of fluids.
- For fever, use acetaminophen or ibuprofen. See our fever handout for your child's dose.
- Do not smoke around your child.

Call the clinic if croup lasts more than 1 week or fever lasts more than 3 days.

Call 911 or go to the ER if your child:

- Is working hard to breathe, or the skin pulls in between the ribs
- Has noisy breathing when calm and resting
- Is drooling or cannot swallow
- Has blue or gray lips
- Is very sleepy or hard to wake

handouts.title: Bronchiolitis
handouts.text:
Bronchiolitis

Bronchiolitis is caused by a virus. It causes swelling in the small airways of the lungs. It is common in babies and children under 2. It causes a runny nose, cough, and wheezing.

It is usually worst on days 3 to 5. The cough can last 2 to 4 weeks. Antibiotics do not help.

What helps:

- Put salt water drops in the nose and use a bulb suction before feeding and sleep.
- Give smaller feedings more often.
- Keep your child away from smoke.
- Wash hands often. Keep your child away from young babies.

Call the clinic if:

- Your child is drinking less than half the usual amount
- Fever lasts more than 3 days
- Your child has ear pain

Call 911 or go to the ER if your child:

- Is breathing very fast or working hard to breathe
- Has skin pulling in between the ribs, grunting, or flaring nostrils
- Stops breathing for a few seconds
- Has blue or gray lips
- Has not had a wet diaper in 8 hours
- Is under 3 months old with a fever of 100.4 F or higher

handouts.title: Newborn care
handouts.text:
Caring for your newborn

Feeding:

- Breastfed babies eat 8 to 12 times a day.
- Formula: about *** ounces every 2 to 3 hours.
- Wake your baby to eat if it has been 3 hours during the day or 4 hours at night.
- Ask us about vitamin D drops: ***

Diapers:

- By day 5, expect at least 6 wet diapers a day.
- Stools turn yellow and seedy by day 5 for breastfed babies.

Sleep safety:

- Always put your baby to sleep on the back.
- Use a crib or bassinet with a firm, flat mattress.
- No blankets, pillows, bumpers, or toys in the crib.
- Share a room, but not a bed.

Other care:

- Keep the cord dry. It falls off in 1 to 3 weeks.
- Use a rear-facing car seat every ride.
- Keep your home and car smoke-free.
- Never shake a baby. If crying is too much, put your baby in the crib and step away for a few minutes.
- Parents can have depression after a baby. Tell us if you feel sad or hopeless.

If your baby has a temperature of 100.4 F or higher, go to the ER now. Do not give medicine first.

Call the clinic if your baby:

- Has yellow skin spreading to the belly or legs
- Is very sleepy or not feeding well
- Has fewer wet diapers than expected
- Has a red or bad-smelling cord
- Vomits green

Call 911 if your baby has trouble breathing, turns blue, is limp, or will not wake up.

Next visit: ***

handouts.title: Blank instruction template
handouts.text:
***

What this is:
***

What to do:

- ***
- ***

Your next visit: ***

Call the clinic if:

- ***

Go to the ER or call 911 if:

handouts.title: New medicine
handouts.text:
Your new medicine

Name: ***
Dose: *** by ***, *** times a day
What it is for: ***
How to take it: ***
Common side effects: ***. These often get better in 1 to 2 weeks.
Do not take with: ***
If you miss a dose: ***

Do not stop this medicine without talking to us first.

Call the clinic if side effects bother you, or you are not sure how to take it.

Call 911 if you have trouble breathing, swelling of your face, lips, or tongue, or a rash with blisters.

handouts.title: Iron pills
handouts.text:
Iron pills

Your iron is low. Iron helps your blood carry oxygen. Low iron can make you tired, short of breath, or dizzy.

How to take iron:

- Take *** by mouth ***.
- Taking it every other day works as well and causes less stomach upset.
- Take it with water or orange juice, 1 hour before a meal if you can.
- If it upsets your stomach, take it with a small snack.
- Take it 2 hours apart from antacids, calcium, dairy, tea, and coffee.

What to expect:

- Your stools will turn dark green or black. This is normal.
- Constipation is common. Drink water and eat fiber.
- You will need iron for about 3 months after your blood count is normal.

Keep iron pills away from children. Too much iron can be deadly for a child.

Blood test again on ***.

Call the clinic if you cannot take the pills because of side effects.

Go to the ER if you have:

- Black, sticky stools with dizziness
- Vomiting blood
- Chest pain or trouble breathing

handouts.title: Gout
handouts.text:
Gout

Gout happens when uric acid builds up and forms crystals in a joint. It causes sudden pain, redness, and swelling.

During a flare:

- Take *** as soon as the flare starts.
- Rest and raise the joint. Use ice for 20 minutes at a time.
- Drink plenty of water.

To prevent flares:

- Take *** every day, even when you feel fine.
- Flares can happen in the first few months on this medicine. Keep taking it.
- Limit beer, liquor, red meat, organ meats, and shellfish.
- Avoid soda and drinks with high fructose corn syrup.
- Lose weight slowly if you are overweight.

Uric acid blood test on ***.

Call the clinic if a flare does not improve in 3 days, or you get a rash on allopurinol.

Go to the ER if the joint is red and hot and you have a fever or chills.

handouts.title: Bone health
handouts.text:
Bone health

Osteoporosis means your bones are thin and break easily. Treatment lowers your risk of a broken bone.

What you can do:

- Get calcium from food, like milk, yogurt, cheese, and leafy greens.
- Take vitamin D every day: ***
- Walk most days. Do strength exercises 2 or 3 days a week and balance exercises 3 or more days.
- Do not smoke. Limit alcohol.
- Prevent falls. Remove rugs, add night lights, and use rails.

If you take alendronate:

- Take it once a week, first thing in the morning.
- Swallow it with a full glass of plain water.
- Stay sitting or standing for 30 minutes.
- Do not eat, drink, or take other pills for 30 minutes.
- See your dentist regularly.

Bone scan again in ***.

Call the clinic if you have heartburn or pain when swallowing on alendronate, or new thigh or groin pain.

Go to the ER if you fall and cannot stand, or have severe pain after a fall.

handouts.title: Allergies
handouts.text:
Nose allergies

Allergies cause a runny or stuffy nose, sneezing, and itchy eyes.

What helps:

- Use your steroid nose spray every day. It works best after you use it for 1 to 2 weeks.
- Point the spray toward the outside of your nose, away from the middle.
- Take an allergy pill like cetirizine or loratadine when needed.
- Rinse your nose with salt water. Use distilled or boiled water that has cooled.
- Keep windows closed on high pollen days.
- Shower and change clothes after being outside.
- Wash bedding in hot water each week.

Acupressure you can try:

- Press the spot beside each nostril, in the crease where the nose meets the cheek.
- Press the spot between your eyebrows, and the web between your thumb and first finger. Skip the hand spot if you are pregnant.
- Use firm small circles for 2 to 3 minutes per spot, each day. It may ease nose symptoms.
- For a child, use light pressure and no more than 30 seconds per spot.

Call the clinic if you have nosebleeds or wheezing, or your symptoms do not get better in 4 weeks.

handouts.title: Eczema
handouts.text:
Eczema

Eczema is dry, itchy skin that comes and goes. It is not contagious.

Daily skin care:

- Use a thick, fragrance-free cream or ointment at least 2 times a day.
- Put it on within 3 minutes after a bath.
- Take short baths or showers in lukewarm water.
- Use a gentle, fragrance-free soap.
- Pat skin dry. Do not rub.

During a flare:

- Use *** on red, itchy areas *** times a day for up to *** days.
- Then go back to moisturizer only.
- Keep nails short. Try not to scratch.

Avoid wool, scented products, and very hot or dry air.

Call the clinic if the skin is not better in 2 weeks, or you have yellow crusts, pus, or pain.

Go to the ER if you have painful blisters or sores with fever.

handouts.title: Acne
handouts.text:
Acne

Acne happens when pores get clogged. It can be treated.

Your plan:

- Morning: wash with benzoyl peroxide wash. It can bleach towels and clothes.
- Night: put a pea-sized amount of *** on your whole face, not just on pimples.
- Pill: ***

Tips:

- Wash your face 2 times a day with a gentle cleanser. Do not scrub.
- Use oil-free moisturizer and sunscreen.
- Do not pick or squeeze pimples. This causes scars.
- Your skin may be dry or red for the first few weeks. Use the night medicine every other night if needed.

It takes 8 to 12 weeks to see results. Do not give up early.

If you take doxycycline, take it with a full glass of water and stay upright for 30 minutes. Use sunscreen.

Call the clinic if your skin is very irritated or not better in 3 months.

handouts.title: Fall prevention
handouts.text:
Preventing falls

Falls are common but many can be prevented.

At home:

- Remove loose rugs and clutter from floors.
- Add night lights in halls, bedrooms, and bathrooms.
- Put grab bars in the shower and by the toilet.
- Use rails on both sides of stairs.
- Keep things you use often within easy reach.

Your body:

- Do your strength and balance exercises 3 or more days a week, for at least 12 weeks.
- Good programs are physical therapy, the Otago program, or Vivifrail, free at vivifrail.com: ***
- Stand up slowly. Sit on the edge of the bed for a minute first.
- Wear shoes with thin, non-slip soles inside and outside.
- Use your cane or walker every time: ***
- Get your eyes checked every year.

Medicines: we changed ***. Ask us before taking sleep aids or allergy pills.

Call the clinic if you fall, even if you are not hurt.

Call 911 if you:

- Fall and cannot get up
- Hit your head while on a blood thinner
- Have new weakness or confusion

handouts.title: STI treatment
handouts.text:
Sexually transmitted infections

You were tested or treated for ***.

What to do:

- Take all of your medicine: ***
- Do not have sex for 7 days after you and your partners finish treatment.
- Tell your partners from the past 60 days so they can be tested and treated.
- Medicine for your partner: ***
- Use condoms every time to lower your risk.

Your results will be ready in *** days. We will contact you.

Get tested again in 3 months, even if your partner was treated.

Ask us about PrEP, a daily pill or shot that prevents HIV.

Call the clinic if symptoms do not go away after treatment, or you have pelvic or testicle pain.

Go to the ER if you have fever with belly pain, or a new rash with joint pain.

handouts.title: HIV PrEP
handouts.text:
HIV PrEP

PrEP is medicine that prevents HIV. It works very well when you take it as directed.

Your PrEP: ***

How to use it:

- Pills: take 1 pill every day at the same time.
- Shots: come in for every shot on time.
- Use condoms to prevent other STIs.

Pills protect best after 7 days for anal sex and 21 days for vaginal sex.

We will see you every 3 months if you take pills, or at each shot visit. At these visits, you get:

- HIV and STI tests
- A kidney test every 6 to 12 months, if you take pills
- A refill of your medicine

If you miss pills or shots, call us. Do not stop PrEP without talking to us first.

Call the clinic if you have fever, rash, sore throat, or body aches. These can be early signs of HIV.

handouts.title: Before surgery
handouts.text:
Before your surgery

Your surgery: *** on ***

Medicines:

- Keep taking: ***
- Stop *** on ***
- Stop *** on ***
- Morning of surgery, take *** with a small sip of water.

Eating and drinking: follow the instructions from your surgery team.

Bring to the hospital:

- A list of your medicines
- Your CPAP machine, if you use one
- Your ID and insurance card

Arrange a ride home. You cannot drive yourself after anesthesia.

Do not smoke or vape before surgery. Quitting even a few days helps.

Call your surgery team if you get a fever, cough, or cold before surgery.

Call the clinic if you have questions about your medicines.

handouts.title: After toenail removal
handouts.text:
After toenail removal

First 24 hours:

- Keep the bandage on and dry.
- Raise your foot as much as you can.
- The toe will feel numb for a few hours.

After 24 hours:

- Soak your foot in warm, soapy water for 10 to 15 minutes, 2 to 3 times a day.
- Pat dry, put on petroleum jelly, and cover with a clean bandage.
- Wear open-toe or loose shoes.
- Drainage and some redness are normal for 2 to 4 weeks, especially if phenol medicine was used.

Pain: use acetaminophen or ibuprofen as directed on the label.

To prevent ingrown nails, cut nails straight across and wear shoes with room for your toes.

Wound check: ***

Call the clinic if you have spreading redness, red streaks, pus, worse pain after 3 days, or fever.

handouts.title: After colposcopy
handouts.text:
After colposcopy

What to expect:

- Mild cramping for 1 to 2 days.
- Spotting for a few days.
- Dark brown or black discharge that looks like coffee grounds. This is from the medicine used to stop bleeding.

What to do:

- Use pads, not tampons, for *** days.
- No sex for *** days.
- Use ibuprofen or acetaminophen as directed on the label for cramps.

Your results will be ready in *** days. We will contact you. Call us if you have not heard in 2 weeks.

Call the clinic if you:

- Soak a pad every hour for 2 hours
- Have a fever
- Have bad pain
- Have bad-smelling discharge

handouts.title: Constipation in children
handouts.text:
Constipation in children

Constipation is common in children. Hard stools hurt, so children hold them in. This makes it worse. Treatment breaks this cycle.

Medicine:

- Polyethylene glycol powder, mixed in 4 to 8 ounces of drink.
- Your child's dose: *** capfuls or *** grams, *** times a day.
- Goal: 1 to 2 soft stools every day.
- If stools are watery, use less. If stools are still hard, use more.
- Keep giving it for at least 2 months, even when things get better. Stopping too soon often brings it back.

Toilet time:

- Have your child sit on the toilet for 5 minutes after meals.
- Use a footstool so knees are higher than hips.
- Praise trying. Never punish accidents.

Food and drink:

- Offer fruit 3 or more times a day, like prunes, pears, peaches, apricots, or figs.
- Offer vegetables like peas, beans, and broccoli.
- Offer whole grains, like oatmeal, brown rice, or whole wheat bread.
- Give plenty of water.
- Offer warm soups with beans, lentils, or vegetables. They add water and fiber.
- Limit milk to 2 to 3 cups a day.

Belly massage you can try:

- Belly massage may help along with the medicine. Have your child lie on their back.
- Use a flat hand and gentle pressure. Rub slow circles up your child's right side, across, and down the left side.
- Try it after a meal. Stop if it hurts or your child does not like it.

Call the clinic if your child has:

- Belly pain that does not go away
- Blood in the stool
- No stool in 3 days on medicine

Go to the ER if your child has a swollen belly with vomiting, green vomit, or severe belly pain.

handouts.title: Starting buprenorphine at home
handouts.text:
Starting buprenorphine at home

Buprenorphine treats opioid use disorder. It stops withdrawal and cravings. Starting it too early can make you feel much worse, so timing matters.

Before your first dose:

- Wait until you feel clear withdrawal. Last use: ***
- With fentanyl, this often takes longer than with other opioids.
- Signs to wait for: yawning, runny nose, goosebumps, sweating, aches, stomach cramps, and diarrhea.

Your first day:

- Put *** mg under your tongue. Let it melt all the way. Do not chew or swallow it.
- Do not eat, drink, or talk until it is gone.
- Wait 1 to 2 hours. If you still feel withdrawal, take *** mg more.
- Do not take more than *** mg on day 1.

Day 2 and after: take *** mg once a day.

If you feel much worse right after a dose, call us right away. Taking more buprenorphine is often the fix.

Keep naloxone with you. Do not mix buprenorphine with alcohol or sleeping pills.

Call the clinic at *** with any questions during your start.

Call 911 if someone is very sleepy and hard to wake or has slow breathing. Give naloxone.

handouts.title: Low-dose buprenorphine schedule
handouts.text:
Your buprenorphine start schedule

This plan starts buprenorphine slowly. You keep taking your current opioid for the first 6 days. You do not need to go into withdrawal.

Your film is 2 mg. Cut it into 4 equal pieces. Each piece is 0.5 mg.

- Day 1: 1 piece, once.
- Day 2: 1 piece, 2 times.
- Day 3: 2 pieces, 2 times.
- Day 4: 1 whole film, 2 times.
- Day 5: 1 and a half films, 2 times.
- Day 6: 2 whole films, 2 times.
- Day 7: 6 whole films, once. Stop your other opioid today.
- Day 8 and on: *** films once a day.

Keep taking your other opioid on days 1 to 6: ***

How to take it:

- Put it under your tongue. Let it melt all the way.
- Do not eat, drink, or talk until it is gone.

If you start to feel withdrawal, stay on the same dose for 1 to 2 days and call us.

Keep naloxone with you. Do not mix with alcohol or sleeping pills.

Call the clinic at *** if you feel sick, have withdrawal, or have questions.

Call 911 if someone is very sleepy and hard to wake or has slow breathing. Give naloxone.

handouts.title: Long-term opioid safety
handouts.text:
Your opioid pain medicine

Your medicine: ***
Your dose: ***

Safety rules:

- Take only as prescribed. Do not take extra doses.
- Do not mix with alcohol, sleeping pills, or anxiety pills like benzodiazepines.
- Keep naloxone at home and tell family where it is.
- Store opioids locked up, away from children and visitors.
- Do not share your medicine.
- Do not drive if you feel sleepy.

Your body is used to this medicine. Stopping suddenly can cause withdrawal and worse pain. Do not stop or change your dose without talking to us.

At each visit, we will check how this medicine helps your pain and daily life.

Call the clinic if you have bad constipation, feel sleepy, or your pain gets worse.

Call 911 if someone is very sleepy, hard to wake, or breathing slowly. Give naloxone.

handouts.title: Opioid taper schedule
handouts.text:
Your opioid taper plan

We are lowering your opioid dose slowly, together. The goal is better safety and a dose that works for you.

Your schedule:

- Starting ***: take ***
- Starting ***: take ***
- Starting ***: take ***

What to expect:

- After each change, you may have more pain or trouble sleeping for a few days.
- You may also have a runny nose, yawning, aches, or diarrhea.
- These usually get better in 1 to 2 weeks.
- Some people find their pain is the same or better at a lower dose.
- We can pause the taper if you need to.

Medicine for withdrawal symptoms: ***

Your tolerance goes down as your dose goes down. Taking your old dose, or any street drugs, could cause an overdose. Keep naloxone at home.

Call the clinic if you feel very low, have cravings, or symptoms are hard to manage.

If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, call or text 988.

Call 911 if someone is very sleepy, hard to wake, or breathing slowly. Give naloxone.

handouts.title: Switching to buprenorphine for pain
handouts.text:
Switching to buprenorphine for pain

Buprenorphine is an opioid medicine that treats pain. It has a lower risk of slowed breathing and overdose than other opioids.

Your plan: ***

How to take it:

- Put the film or tablet under your tongue or against your cheek. Let it melt all the way.
- Do not chew or swallow it.
- For pain, it is often taken 2 to 3 times a day.

During the switch:

- You may keep taking your current opioid at first. Follow your schedule exactly.
- Some people feel mild withdrawal. Call us if this happens. Do not stop the plan on your own.

Keep naloxone at home. Do not mix with alcohol or sleeping pills.

Call the clinic if your pain is much worse, or you feel sick or have withdrawal.

Call 911 if someone is very sleepy, hard to wake, or breathing slowly. Give naloxone.

handouts.title: About benzodiazepines
handouts.text:
Your benzodiazepine medicine

Your medicine: ***

Benzodiazepines include alprazolam, clonazepam, lorazepam, diazepam, and temazepam. Sleep pills like zolpidem work in a similar way.

They can help for a short time. Used for months or years, they can cause:

- Falls and broken hips
- Memory and thinking problems
- Car crashes
- Daytime sleepiness
- Breathing problems, especially with opioids or alcohol

Over time, your body gets used to the medicine. It may not help your sleep or worry as much. Stopping suddenly can cause withdrawal, including seizures.

The good news:

- Most people can lower or stop their dose with a slow plan.
- We go slowly and can pause any time.
- Counseling and some daily medicines work well for worry and sleep.

Do not stop or change your dose on your own. Talk with us first.

Call the clinic if you have questions or want to start a plan.

Call 911 if someone has a seizure, severe confusion, or trouble breathing.

handouts.title: Benzodiazepine taper schedule
handouts.text:
Your benzodiazepine taper schedule

We will lower your dose slowly. You can pause if you need to.

Your schedule:

- Starting ***: take ***
- Starting ***: take ***
- Starting ***: take ***
- Starting ***: take ***

What to expect:

- You may have more trouble sleeping, worry, or restlessness for a few days after each change.
- These feelings usually settle within 1 to 2 weeks.
- Keep using the sleep and coping skills you learned.

Do not take extra doses. Do not drink alcohol.

If symptoms are hard to manage, call us before the next step. We can slow down.

Call the clinic if you have shaking, sweating, a racing heart, or feel very anxious.

Go to the ER or call 911 if you:

- Have a seizure
- See or hear things that are not there
- Feel very confused

handouts.title: Changing or stopping a medicine
handouts.text:
Changing or stopping a medicine

As we get older, the body handles medicines differently. Some medicines that were fine before can now cause falls, confusion, or other problems.

What we are changing:

- Stop: ***
- Lower: ***
- Switch: *** to ***

Why: ***

Some medicines must be lowered slowly. Follow your schedule exactly: ***

Bring all your pill bottles, vitamins, and over-the-counter medicines to each visit.

Ask us before starting sleep aids or allergy pills. Many have diphenhydramine, which can cause confusion and falls.

Call the clinic if you feel worse after a change, or old symptoms come back.

Call 911 if you have chest pain, trouble breathing, a seizure, or sudden confusion.

handouts.title: Healthy habits for kids
handouts.text:
Healthy habits for your family

Small changes the whole family makes together work best. Your child's body is growing, so the goal is healthy habits, not dieting.

Try 5-2-1-0 every day:

- 5 or more fruits and vegetables
- 2 hours or less of fun screen time
- 1 hour or more of active play
- 0 sugary drinks. Choose water or plain milk.

More tips:

- Eat meals together at the table, without screens.
- Serve smaller portions. Let your child stop when full.
- Keep fruit and vegetables easy to grab.
- Keep TVs and phones out of bedrooms.
- Aim for 9 to 12 hours of sleep for school-age kids, and 8 to 10 for teens.
- Praise effort, not weight or looks.

Your family's goals:

- ***
- ***

Program or referral: ***

Next visit: ***

Call the clinic if your child seems sad or worried about weight, skips meals, or makes themselves throw up.

handouts.title: Screen time for kids
handouts.text:
Screen time for kids

Under 18 months: avoid screens except video chats with family.
18 to 24 months: if you use screens, pick good shows or apps. Watch with your child.
Ages 2 to 5: limit screens to 1 hour a day of good shows. Watch together and talk about what you see.
Ages 6 and up: make a family media plan. Set limits on time and type of media.

Why limits matter:

- Eyes: lots of up-close screen time may raise the risk of nearsightedness (blurry far vision).
- Attention: kids who use screens a lot are more likely to have trouble paying attention later.
- Sleep: screen time can make it hard for kids to sleep at night.
- Speech: a TV that is on, even in the background, means less talking with your baby. That slows how fast your baby learns to talk.
- Weight: kids move less during screen time, and food ads lead to more snacking.
- Mood: heavy social media use is linked to sadness, worry, poor body image, and bullying.

Try instead:

- Play outside every day. Outdoor time helps protect your child's eyes.
- Read books, play games, and talk together.

Keep screens out of bedrooms.
Turn screens off 1 hour before bed.
Do not use screens during meals.

Call us if your child has trouble sleeping, gets very upset when screens end, or seems sad or withdrawn.

handouts.title: Summer safety for kids
handouts.text:
Summer safety for kids

Wear a helmet for bikes, scooters, skates, and skateboards.
Watch your child closely around any water, including bathtubs, pools, lakes, and splash pads.
Stay within arm's reach of young children in water.
Use sunscreen SPF 30 or higher. Put it on again every 2 hours and after swimming.
Keep babies under 6 months out of direct sun.
Use bug spray with DEET or picaridin to prevent tick and mosquito bites. Do not use it on babies under 2 months.
Check for ticks after time outside.
Give lots of water on hot days.
Never leave a child alone in a car.

Call us if your child has a rash or fever after a tick bite.

Call 911 if your child stops breathing, is pulled from the water, or is hot and confused.

handouts.title: Piriformis stretch
handouts.text:
Piriformis stretch

Lie on your back with both knees bent.
Cross one ankle over the other knee.
Hold the outside of the crossed leg's knee with the opposite hand.
Gently pull that knee toward the opposite shoulder until you feel a stretch in your buttock.
Breathe slowly and hold for 20 to 30 seconds.
Switch sides.
Do this 2 to 3 times on each side, 1 to 2 times a day.

Stop if the stretch causes sharp pain.

Call us if the pain lasts more than 6 weeks or spreads down your leg.

Go to the ER if you have new leg weakness, numbness between your legs, or trouble controlling urine or stool.

handouts.title: After your hospital stay
handouts.text:
After your hospital stay

A nurse care manager will call you within 2 business days. They will talk about your hospital stay and help set up your follow-up visit.

Please make sure we have the right phone number for you.

If no one calls within 2 business days, call our office at 918-710-4200. Ask to speak to a care manager. Have your medicine list ready when you call.

Call the clinic if you have new or worse symptoms or questions about your medicines.

Call 911 or go to the ER if you have chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, or feel very sick.

handouts.title: Where to get labs drawn
handouts.text:
You can get your labs drawn at any RML lab, which is now part of Labcorp.
To find a location near you, go to labcorp.com.
Bring your photo ID and insurance card.
Ask us if you need to fast before your test.
Call our office if the lab cannot find your order or you have questions.

handouts.title: Healthy lifestyle choices
handouts.text:
Healthy choices can lower your risk of heart attack, stroke, kidney disease and memory loss.
They can also help your weight and your mood.
Pick 2 or 3 of these to start before your next visit:

- Eat a breakfast with protein, like eggs, yogurt or nuts
- Eat smaller portions at meals
- Cut back on sugary drinks, sweets, white bread and white rice
- Drink water instead of soda or juice
- Eat vegetables and fruits of different colors every day
- Cook with olive oil or canola oil instead of butter
- Eat fish 2 times a week
- Walk or move your body for 30 minutes, 5 days a week
- If you drink alcohol, drink less. Less is better.
- If you smoke or vape, ask us for help to quit
- Use sunscreen when you are outside

Call us if you have questions or want help making a plan.
Call 911 for chest pain, trouble breathing, or signs of stroke like face drooping or weakness on one side.

handouts.title: Natural family planning
handouts.text:
Natural family planning

Natural family planning is also called fertility awareness. You learn to read signs from your body. These signs show the days each cycle when you can get pregnant.

Your method: ***
Your teacher: ***

Body signs you may track:

- Mucus: before you release an egg, the fluid in your vagina gets clear, slippery, and stretchy.
- Temperature: your morning temperature goes up a little after you release an egg. Take it as soon as you wake up, before you get out of bed.
- Cycle days: you count the days of each cycle on a chart or app.
- Urine hormone tests (Marquette): a home monitor checks hormones that rise before you release an egg.

How well it works:

It depends on the method and on following the rules every time. Perfect use means you follow the rules every cycle. With perfect use, most well-studied methods have fewer than 5 pregnancies per 100 women in a year. Typical use is how people really use it, with some mistakes. With typical use, about 2 to 23 of every 100 women get pregnant in a year.

What helps it work:

- Learn from a trained teacher.
- Chart your signs every day.
- Both partners agree on the plan for fertile days.
- To avoid pregnancy, do not have sex on fertile days, or use a condom.
- Bring your chart to your visits.

Times it is harder:

- After having a baby
- While breastfeeding
- After stopping birth control pills, shots, or other hormones
- When your periods are not regular, such as with PCOS
- In the years before menopause
- When you are sick with a fever
- When you take some medicines that change your cycle

Your teacher can show you extra rules for these times.

Breastfeeding can prevent pregnancy for a while. It only works if all 3 of these are true:

- Your baby is less than 6 months old.
- Your period has not come back.
- Your baby gets only or almost only breast milk. You breastfeed at least every 4 hours by day and every 6 hours at night.

If any of these changes, start another method.

Using it to get pregnant:

- Your fertile days are the 6 days that end on the day you release an egg.
- Clear, slippery mucus is a sign of your most fertile days.
- Have sex every 1 to 2 days during your fertile days.
- Take folic acid 400 to 800 mcg every day if you could get pregnant.

Natural family planning does not protect against STIs or HIV. Condoms lower your risk.

If you had sex on a fertile day and do not want to be pregnant, call us soon. Emergency birth control can work up to 5 days after sex. It works best the sooner you take it.

Call the clinic if:

- You think you might be pregnant.
- Your cycles are shorter than 24 days or longer than 38 days.
- Your period lasts more than 8 days.
- You bleed between periods or after sex.
- You have no period for 3 months and are not pregnant or breastfeeding.
- You are not pregnant after 1 year of trying, or after 6 months if you are 35 or older.
- Your chart is hard to read and you have questions.

handouts.title: Marijuana and your health
handouts.text:
Marijuana and your health

Marijuana is also called cannabis or weed. Legal does not mean risk-free. Here are the facts so you can make your own choices.

What is in marijuana:

- THC is the part that makes you feel high.
- CBD does not make you high.
- Marijuana today is much stronger than in the past. The THC in tested samples almost doubled from 2008 to 2017.
- Stronger products raise the risk of a bad reaction and of addiction.

Short-term effects:

- Feeling high or relaxed
- Slower reaction time and poor coordination
- Trouble with memory, attention, and decisions
- Anxiety or paranoia, which means feeling that others want to harm you
- Faster heartbeat and higher blood pressure

Risks of regular use:

- Addiction: About 3 in 10 people who use marijuana have cannabis use disorder. This means it is hard to cut back even when it causes problems.
- The risk of addiction is higher with daily use and when you start young.
- Mood: Marijuana is linked to anxiety, depression, and thoughts of suicide.
- Psychosis: This means losing touch with what is real. The risk is higher with daily use and strong products.
- Memory and attention: Problems may last a long time.
- Sleep: Trouble sleeping is common when you cut back. It can last longer than other withdrawal symptoms.
- Lungs: Smoking can cause cough, mucus, and bronchitis. These often get better after you quit.
- Vaping: THC vapes from friends or dealers have caused serious lung injury.
- Heart: Marijuana raises heart rate and blood pressure right after use. It may raise the risk of stroke and heart disease.
- Vomiting illness: Heavy long-term use can cause bouts of bad vomiting and belly pain. This is called cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome.
- Hot showers may ease the vomiting for a short time. Only stopping marijuana cures it.

Driving:

- Do not drive for at least 6 hours after smoking or vaping.
- Do not drive for at least 8 hours after edibles or drinks with THC.
- Mixing marijuana with alcohol makes driving even less safe.
