- Never ride with a driver who is high.

Edibles:

- Edibles take 30 minutes to 2 hours to kick in.
- Do not take more if you do not feel it yet.
- Taking more can make you very sick. The effects can last longer than you expect.

Other medicines:

- Marijuana and CBD can change how some medicines work.
- Examples are the blood thinner warfarin and some seizure medicines.
- Tell us about every product you use, including CBD.

Pregnancy and breastfeeding:

- THC reaches your baby during pregnancy. It is linked to smaller babies.
- THC can pass into breast milk.
- No amount has been proven safe. If you are pregnant or breastfeeding, it is best not to use.

Keep children and pets safe:

- Edibles can look like candy, cookies, or chips.
- Keep all products in a locked, childproof box, out of sight.
- Children who eat marijuana can get very sick.
- If a child eats marijuana, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222.
- If a pet eats it, call your vet.

Delta-8 THC:

- Delta-8 THC can make you high, like regular THC.
- The FDA has not checked these products for safety.
- Some are made with harsh chemicals. Many look like candy.

When you cut back:

- After heavy use, you may feel grumpy, anxious, or restless.
- You may have trouble sleeping, less appetite, or a low mood.
- These start in 1 to 2 days and are worst in the first week.
- They usually go away in 2 to 3 weeks. Sleep problems can last longer.

Tips to cut back:

- Set a goal and a start date. Your goal: ***.
- Use on fewer days each week.
- Choose lower-THC products. Avoid dabs and concentrates.
- Do not mix with alcohol or tobacco.
- Products from friends or dealers are not tested. You cannot know what is in them.
- Remove marijuana and supplies from your home.
- Stay away from people and places that make you want to use.
- Counseling works. We can refer you.
- Free, private help any time: SAMHSA National Helpline, 1-800-662-4357.

Call the clinic if:

- You want help cutting back or quitting
- You have vomiting that keeps coming back
- You feel anxious, depressed, or paranoid
- You have a cough or wheeze that does not go away

Call or text 988 if you have thoughts of hurting yourself.

Call 911 or go to the ER if you:

- Have chest pain or trouble breathing
- See or hear things that are not there
- Have vomiting that will not stop, or cannot keep fluids down
- Have sudden weakness on one side or trouble speaking

Call 911 if a child ate marijuana and is very sleepy, cannot sit up, or has trouble breathing.

handouts.title: Marijuana and teens
handouts.text:
Marijuana and teens

Marijuana is also called weed or cannabis. Some adults use it legally. That does not make it safe for you.

Your brain is still growing:

- Your brain keeps growing until about age 25.
- Marijuana can change how your brain builds connections.
- This can make it harder to pay attention, learn, and remember.
- Teens who use marijuana may not do as well in school.

Your mental health:

- Marijuana is linked to depression, anxiety, and thoughts of suicide.
- It can cause psychosis. This means seeing or hearing things, or not knowing what is real.
- The risk is higher if you start young, use often, or use strong products.

Addiction:

- About 3 in 10 people who use marijuana have trouble stopping. This is a kind of addiction.
- The risk is higher when you start as a teen.

Vaping:

- Vaping THC is still using marijuana.
- THC vapes from friends or dealers have caused serious lung injury.

Edibles:

- Edibles can look like candy or snacks.
- They take 30 minutes to 2 hours to kick in.
- People often eat more while they wait. Then they get very sick.

Fake and unknown products:

- Products from friends or dealers are not tested. You cannot know what is in them.
- Fake weed, called K2 or Spice, can be much stronger than marijuana. It can be deadly.
- Delta-8 THC products are not checked for safety by the FDA.

Driving:

- Marijuana slows your reaction time. Driving high is dangerous and illegal.
- Never ride with a driver who used marijuana, alcohol, or other drugs.
- Call a parent or trusted adult for a ride instead.

Ways to say no:

- "No thanks, I'm good."
- "I have a game tomorrow."
- "I don't want to mess up my grades."
- Suggest something else to do, or just walk away.
- Spend time with friends who do not use.

If you already use:

- It is never too late to stop or cut back.
- Talk with us. We will not judge you.
- When you stop, you may feel grumpy or have trouble sleeping. This gets better in a few weeks.

Where to get help:

- A parent, school counselor, coach, or other trusted adult
- SAMHSA National Helpline: 1-800-662-4357. It is free, private, and open all day, every day.
- Call or text 988 if you feel hopeless or think about hurting yourself.

Call the clinic if you want help cutting back or quitting.

Call 911 if someone:

- Has trouble breathing or chest pain
- Passes out or cannot wake up
- Has a seizure
- Sees or hears things that are not there and is not safe

handouts.title: Potty training
handouts.text:
Potty training

Most children start potty training between ages 2 and 3. Most are trained by age 4. Watch your child, not the calendar.

Signs your child may be ready:

- Stays dry for 2 hours or more, or wakes up dry from naps
- Grunts, squats, or freezes before peeing or pooping
- Can follow simple directions
- Can walk to the bathroom and help pull pants down
- Does not like wet or dirty diapers
- Asks to use the potty or to wear big-kid underwear

Steps to try:

- Get a small potty chair. Your child's feet should reach the floor.
- Use simple, positive words for pee, poop, and body parts.
- Let your child watch you use the toilet and wash your hands.
- Sit your child on the potty first thing in the morning. Make potty trips part of the daily routine.
- Switch to underwear once training starts.
- Teach girls to wipe from front to back.
- Wash hands with soap after every potty trip.
- Let your child flush. Some children are scared of the toilet at first.

Praise, not punishment:

- Praise each success. Say what you are proud of, like "You used the potty all by yourself!"
- Accidents are normal. Stay calm and say, "Next time you will get to the potty."
- Let your child help clean up. Do not scold, shame, or punish.
- Avoid power struggles. Your child controls when and where they pee and poop.

Staying dry at night usually comes later than staying dry in the day. Some children still wet the bed at age 5 or older. It is not your child's fault.

Setbacks are common. A new baby, a move, a new school, or an illness can cause them. If your child resists or gets upset, take a break for 1 to 3 months. Then try again.

Call the clinic if your child:

- Is not dry during the day by age 5
- Has pain or burning when peeing, or pink pee
- Has hard or painful poops, or holds in poop
- Starts having accidents again after being trained
- Starts wetting the bed after being dry at night for 6 months or more
- Still wets the bed after starting school

handouts.title: Sleep and naps for kids
handouts.text:
Sleep and naps for kids

Enough sleep helps children with attention, behavior, learning, mood, and health. Here is how much sleep children need in 24 hours, including naps.

How much sleep:

- Newborns to 4 months: sleep on and off around the clock
- 4 to 12 months: 12 to 16 hours
- 1 to 2 years: 11 to 14 hours
- 3 to 5 years: 10 to 13 hours
- 6 to 12 years: 9 to 12 hours
- 13 to 18 years: 8 to 10 hours

Naps:

- Babies often take 2 to 3 naps a day.
- Most toddlers move to 1 nap a day around 18 months to 2 years.
- Many children stop napping between ages 3 and 5.
- Children over 6 should get all their sleep at night.
- Your child may be ready to stop napping if falling asleep at nap time takes 30 minutes or more.
- If your child stops napping, try an earlier bedtime.

Bedtime routine:

- Wake up at the same time every day, even on weekends. Keep a regular bedtime too.
- Use a short, calm routine, like brush, book, bed.
- Do the same routine every night.
- Keep TVs, tablets, and phones out of the bedroom, especially at night.
- Turn off all screens at least 1 hour before bed.

Safe sleep for babies:

- Place your baby on their back for every nap and at night.
- Use a firm, flat crib or bassinet with only a fitted sheet.
- Keep pillows, blankets, bumpers, and toys out of the crib.
- Share a room, but not a bed, for at least the first 6 months.

Teens:

- Teens need 8 to 10 hours of sleep each day.
- At puberty, the body clock shifts up to 2 hours later. This makes it hard to fall asleep early.
- Plan homework, sports, and work so there is time for enough sleep.
- Charge phones outside the bedroom at night.

Call the clinic if your child:

- Snores often
- Has pauses in breathing, gasps, or struggles to breathe during sleep
- Is very sleepy during the day
- Has trouble paying attention or new behavior problems
- Has trouble falling asleep or staying asleep most nights

handouts.title: Discipline, routines, and respect
handouts.text:
Discipline, routines, and respect

Discipline means teaching. The goal is to help your child learn self-control and good behavior. Clear rules, calm words, and lots of praise work best.

Tools for every age:

- Catch your child being good. Praise good behavior and good tries.
- Give your child plenty of attention. It is your most powerful tool.
- Set clear, simple rules. Explain them in words your child understands.
- Be consistent. Use the same rules every day.
- Keep regular times for meals, play, chores, and bed.
- Plan ahead for hard times, like errands or long waits.
- Listen to your child before you help solve the problem.
- Ignore small misbehavior, like whining, if no one is in danger.
- Stay calm. Your child learns how to handle strong feelings by watching you.

Babies (birth to 1 year):

- Babies learn by watching you. Show the behavior you expect.
- Save "no" for safety.
- Move your baby away from danger and give them something safe to play with.

Toddlers (1 to 3 years):

- Redirect. Move your child away and give them something else to do.
- Teach your child not to hit or bite. Show calm ways to solve problems.
- Stay consistent with limits.
- Teach "please" and "thank you." Use these words yourself.
- Simple chores: pick up toys and books, help wipe up spills, put dirty clothes in the hamper.

Preschool (3 to 5 years):

- Use time-out for unsafe behavior, hurting others, or breaking a clear rule.
- Give one calm warning first. Then follow through.
- A good rule is 1 minute of time-out for each year of age.
- Use logical consequences. If children fight over a toy, put the toy away for a while.
- Simple chores: make the bed, set the table, match socks, help make food.
- Have a daily tidy-up time, like putting toys away before bed.

School age (6 to 12 years):

- Use natural consequences when it is safe. A child who skips a coat will feel cold.
- Take away a privilege when a rule is broken.
- Balance privileges with responsibility.
- Ages 5 to 7: make the bed, set and clear the table, put toys away.
- Ages 8 to 10: help make dinner, vacuum, put away their own laundry and groceries.
- Ages 11 to 12: change bedsheets, do laundry, clean the bathroom, cook a simple meal with an adult nearby.
- Do chores at the same time each day. Praise the effort, not just the result.

Teens (13 to 18 years):

- Keep showing love and attention.
- Set clear expectations for school, chores, curfew, and phone use.
- Tie privileges, like the phone or the car, to meeting those expectations.
- Get to know your teen's friends.
- Listen more than you lecture.

Respect at home:

- Use kind words with each other, like "please" and "thank you."
- Speak calmly, even when you are upset.
- Yelling, shaming, and put-downs do not work and can cause harm.

When not to spank:

- Never shake, throw, or hit a baby. Shaking can cause brain damage, blindness, or death.
- Never when you are angry. Take a break first. Breathe deeply and count to 10.
- If a baby's crying makes you angry, put the baby in the crib. Step away for 10 to 15 minutes.
- Never with an object, like a belt, cord, switch, or paddle.
- Never on the head, face, or ears.
- Never hard enough to leave a mark or cause an injury.
- Never as the first or only way to discipline. Use the tools above first.

Call the clinic if you feel you might lose control or hurt your child. Also call if your child's behavior is hard to manage at home or school. Call 911 if a child is hurt or in danger.

handouts.title: Healthy relationships for teens
handouts.text:
Healthy relationships

You deserve to feel safe and respected in every relationship. This includes friends, dating partners, and people you meet online.

A healthy relationship has:

- Respect for each other's values and limits
- Trust and honest talk
- Room for your own friends, family, and interests
- No fear. Feeling afraid of a partner is never OK.

Consent:

- Consent means a clear, freely given yes, every step of the way.
- Silence, "maybe," or not saying no is not a yes.
- A yes given because of pressure or fear is not consent.
- A person who is drunk or high cannot give consent.
- Anyone can change their mind and stop at any time, even partway through.
- Saying yes once does not mean yes next time. Ask every time.

Warning signs of an unhealthy or controlling partner:

- Checks your phone, email, or social media without asking
- Puts you down, especially in front of others
- Keeps you away from friends or family
- Gets very jealous or possessive
- Has explosive anger or big mood swings
- Pressures or forces you into sex
- Hurts you in any way

Phones and pictures:

- Once you send a picture, you cannot control where it goes.
- Under federal law, a nude or sexual picture of anyone under 18 can count as child pornography.
- Taking, sending, or keeping these pictures can be a crime, even between teens.
- If someone pressures you for pictures or threatens to share them, leave the chat. Tell a trusted adult right away.

Pornography:

- Many teens see porn online, sometimes by accident.
- Porn is not how real sex or real relationships work.
- It often shows sex without caring or without consent.
- It can give you wrong ideas about what sex is really like.
- For some teens, it becomes hard to stop watching.
- If you have questions or worries, talk with a parent or another trusted adult.

Where to get help:

- Love Is Respect: call 1-866-331-9474 or text LOVEIS to 22522. Help is there 24 hours a day.
- 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline: call or text 988 any time.
- A parent, school counselor, or your doctor.

Call the clinic if you feel unsafe, sad, or worried about a relationship. Call 911 if you are in danger right now.

handouts.title: Talking with your teen about relationships
handouts.text:
Talking with your teen about relationships

Your teen learns a lot about relationships from you. In one survey, teens said they learned more about sex from trusted adults than from porn.

Start early and keep talking:

- Start talking about online safety when your child first uses the internet alone.
- Break big topics into short talks.
- Use everyday moments, like a TV show or a news story, to start a talk.

Listen more than you lecture:

- Listen without judging or reacting right away.
- Ask what your teen thinks before you give your view.
- Stay calm. Teens are more likely to come back to a calm parent.

Share your values:

- Tell your teen what your family believes about dating and sex.
- Set clear rules, like curfews and where your teen can go.
- Get to know your teen's friends and dating partners.
- A good partner respects your teen's values and limits.

Teach consent:

- Consent means saying yes each time.
- It is OK to change your mind at any time.
- A person who is drunk or high cannot give consent.
- Teach your teen to ask first and to respect a no.

Phone and internet rules:

- Make a family media plan together.
- Keep phones and screens out of bedrooms at night.
- Set up filters on devices. They do not block everything, so keep talking.
- Explain that pictures sent online can stay there forever.
- Explain that nude or sexual pictures of anyone under 18 can count as child pornography under federal law.
- Warn your teen about people online who ask for pictures, then threaten to share them.

Talking about pornography:

- In a 2022 survey, 73% of teens ages 13 to 17 had seen porn online.
- On average, teens first saw it at age 12. More than half had seen it by accident.
- Stay calm. Do not blame, shame, or punish your teen for seeing it.
- Explain that porn often shows sex that is not caring or not consensual. It is not real life.
- Let your teen know they can come to you without getting in trouble.

Warning signs of dating abuse:

- A partner checks your teen's phone or social media.
- A partner puts your teen down or calls them names.
- A partner keeps your teen away from friends and family.
- A partner is very jealous or controlling.
- A partner threatens or hurts your teen.
- Your teen seems sad, anxious, or withdrawn, or starts using alcohol or drugs.

Where to get help:

- Love Is Respect: call 1-866-331-9474 or text LOVEIS to 22522. Help is there 24 hours a day.
- 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline: call or text 988 any time.

Call the clinic if you are worried about your teen's relationship, mood, or safety. Call 911 if your teen is in danger.

handouts.title: Everyday hygiene
handouts.text:
Everyday hygiene

Good hygiene keeps your skin healthy and helps prevent body odor and skin infections. These tips are for kids going through puberty and for adults.

Showering:

- Shower or bathe every day once puberty starts.
- Use mild soap and warm water.
- Wash your underarms, groin, and feet with soap.
- Wash your hair every day or every other day if it gets oily.
- Shower after sports or heavy sweating.

Shower before bed:

- A night shower washes sweat and oil off your skin.
- It also washes pollen out of your hair, so it does not end up on your pillow.
- A warm shower or bath 1 to 2 hours before bed can help you fall asleep faster.

Body odor:

- Use deodorant or antiperspirant under your arms. Antiperspirant also cuts down on sweat.
- Scented body sprays may not stop body odor.
- Wear cotton clothes, socks, and underwear. They soak up sweat.
- Put on clean socks and underwear every day.

Face and teeth:

- Gently wash your face up to twice a day and after sweating.
- Use a gentle cleanser and your fingertips. Do not scrub.
- Do not pick or squeeze pimples.
- Brush your teeth twice a day for 2 minutes with fluoride toothpaste.
- Floss once a day.

Hands and nails:

- Wash your hands with soap for at least 20 seconds.
- Always wash after using the toilet and before eating.
- Cut nails straight across and keep them clean and dry.
- Do not bite your nails.

Sheets and towels:

- Wash your sheets and pillowcases every week in hot water.
- Wash bath towels at least once a week.
- Hang towels spread out so they dry between uses.

Sharing and shaving:

- Do not share towels, washcloths, or razors. Sharing can spread skin infections.
- Use a new, sharp razor blade to prevent cuts.

Call the clinic if you have:

- A rash that does not go away or keeps coming back
- Acne that keeps coming back after following these tips
- Heavy sweating that does not stop or that upsets you
- Body odor that does not go away with daily washing
- A red, swollen, painful, or warm bump, especially with pus or fever
- Body odor or body hair in a child younger than 8

handouts.title: Eating with diabetes
handouts.text:
Eating with diabetes

What you eat changes your blood sugar. Carbs raise blood sugar the most. You do not have to give up carbs. Pick better ones, and watch how much.

Where carbs are found:

- Bread, tortillas, rice, pasta, cereal, oatmeal, and crackers
- Starchy vegetables like potatoes, corn, and peas
- Beans and lentils
- Fruit and fruit juice
- Milk and yogurt
- Sweets, soda, sweet tea, and sports drinks

Non-starchy vegetables like salad, green beans, and broccoli are low in carbs. Fiber is a carb that does not raise blood sugar.

One carb serving is about 15 grams of carbs. Each of these is about 1 serving:

- 1 slice of bread
- 1/3 cup cooked rice or pasta
- 1/2 cup cooked oatmeal or other hot cereal
- 3/4 cup dry cereal
- 1/2 cup cooked beans, corn, or mashed potatoes
- 1 small apple or orange
- 1/2 banana
- 1/2 cup fruit juice
- 1 cup milk
- 3/4 cup (6 ounces) plain yogurt

Try to eat about the same amount of carbs at each meal. Your carb goal is *** grams per meal.

Reading a food label:

- Look at the serving size first.
- If you eat 2 servings, double the carbs.
- Look at Total Carbohydrate. This counts sugar, starch, and fiber.
- Added sugars are already part of the total. Pick foods with less added sugar.

Better swaps:

- Brown rice or whole grain bread instead of white rice or white bread
- Whole fruit instead of juice. Juice raises blood sugar faster.
- Baked, grilled, or broiled food instead of fried
- Vegetables instead of fries or chips

Drinks:

- Water is the best drink.
- Unsweetened iced tea is a good choice too.
- Cut out soda, sweet tea, juice, sports drinks, and sweet coffee drinks.
- Diet drinks are OK in place of soda, in small amounts.

Alcohol:

- If you do not drink, do not start.
- If you drink, keep it small and have it with a meal.
- Alcohol can drop your blood sugar too low, even hours later.
- This risk is highest with insulin or a sulfonylurea like glipizide, glimepiride, or glyburide.
- Check your blood sugar after drinking.

Protein and fiber with every meal:

- Eating carbs with protein, fat, or fiber slows how fast blood sugar rises.
- Fill one quarter of your plate with lean protein like chicken, fish, beans, tofu, or eggs.
- Pick high-fiber carbs like beans, whole grains, and whole fruit.

Snacks:

- Pick snacks with fiber and protein.
- A small handful of nuts is a good choice.
- Try a string cheese with a piece of fruit, or plain Greek yogurt with berries.
- Measure out snacks. Do not eat straight from the bag.

A sample day:

- Breakfast: 1/2 cup oats with 1 cup low-fat milk, part of a banana, and walnuts. About 65 grams of carbs.
- Lunch: Turkey sandwich on 2 slices of whole wheat bread, baby carrots, plain Greek yogurt with blueberries. About 60 grams.
- Dinner: Baked chicken, 1 cup brown rice, and 1 cup broccoli. About 57 grams.
- Snack: 1 string cheese and 2 tangerines. About 19 grams.

Your own needs may be different. Ask us about seeing a dietitian.

Eating out:

- Decide what to order before you go.
- Drink a big glass of water when you sit down.
- Skip the bread or chips basket.
- Ask for sauces and dressing on the side.
- Limit dishes named BBQ, glazed, sticky, honey, or teriyaki.
- Share your main dish, or take half home.

Call the clinic if your blood sugar is often over *** or under 70. Call if you want to see a dietitian.

handouts.title: Low-potassium eating
handouts.text:
Low-potassium eating

Your potassium is too high, or your kidneys cannot remove extra potassium well. High potassium can cause muscle weakness and a dangerous heartbeat. What you eat can help lower it.

Your potassium goal is ***.

Foods higher in potassium to limit:

- Bananas, oranges, orange juice, cantaloupe, kiwi, and nectarines
- Dried fruit like raisins, prunes, and dates
- Potatoes, sweet potatoes, and winter squash
- Tomatoes, tomato sauce, and tomato juice
- Avocado and cooked spinach
- Beans, lentils, and split peas
- Milk, yogurt, nuts, seeds, and peanut butter
- Bran cereal, granola, chocolate, and molasses

Lower-potassium choices:

- Apples, applesauce, berries, grapes, pears, peaches, pineapple, and watermelon
- Apple, grape, and cranberry juice
- Green beans, cabbage, carrots, cauliflower, cucumber, lettuce, onions, and bell peppers
- White rice, white bread, and plain pasta
- Rice or wheat cereals instead of bran cereals

Portion size matters:

- Almost all foods have some potassium.
- A large amount of a low-potassium food turns into a high-potassium food.
- One serving of fruit is 1 small piece or 1/2 cup.
- One serving of vegetables is 1/2 cup cooked.
- Have only a little of high-potassium foods. Try 1 slice of tomato or half an orange.

Cooking tips:

- Drain canned fruits and vegetables. Do not drink or use the liquid.
- Peel and cut potatoes into small pieces.
- Boil them, drain the water, then boil again in fresh water.
- Throw out the cooking water. This lowers potassium but does not remove it all.

Salt substitutes and labels:

- Do not use salt substitutes. Many are made with potassium chloride.
- Season food with herbs and spices instead.
- Read ingredient lists. Limit foods with potassium chloride, like some canned soups and tomato products.
- Look for potassium on the Nutrition Facts label.

Some medicines can also raise potassium. Do not stop any medicine on your own. Ask us first.

A kidney dietitian can help you plan meals. Ask us for a referral.

Call the clinic if you have new muscle weakness or feel very tired. Go to the ER if your heart races, skips, or pounds, or you cannot move your arms or legs.

handouts.title: High-potassium foods
handouts.text:
High-potassium foods

Your potassium is low. Low potassium can cause tiredness, muscle weakness, and constipation. Water pills, vomiting, and diarrhea can lower it.

Foods high in potassium, with about how much each has:

- Dried apricots, 1/2 cup: 755 mg
- Lentils, cooked, 1 cup: 731 mg
- Acorn squash, mashed, 1 cup: 644 mg
- Prunes, 1/2 cup: 635 mg
- Raisins, 1/2 cup: 618 mg
- Baked potato, 1 medium: 610 mg
- Kidney beans, canned, 1 cup: 607 mg
- Orange juice, 1 cup: 496 mg
- Banana, 1 medium: 422 mg
- Milk, 1 cup: 366 mg
- Spinach, raw, 2 cups: 334 mg
- Salmon, 3 ounces: 326 mg
- Yogurt, 6 ounces: 330 mg
- Tomato, 1 medium: 292 mg
- Broccoli, cooked, 1/2 cup: 229 mg
- Cantaloupe, 1/2 cup: 214 mg

Most adult men need about 3,400 mg a day. Most adult women need about 2,600 mg a day.

Be careful:

- If you have kidney disease, do not add potassium without asking us first.
- Some blood pressure pills raise potassium. Examples are lisinopril, losartan, and spironolactone.
- If you take one of these, ask before eating more potassium.
- Ask us before using salt substitutes or potassium pills.

Your potassium plan is ***. We will check your blood again on ***.

Call the clinic if you feel weak or very tired. Go to the ER if your heart races or skips, or you cannot move your arms or legs.

handouts.title: Iron-rich foods
handouts.text:
Iron-rich foods

Iron helps your blood carry oxygen. Food can help you get more iron. Some foods and drinks help, and some get in the way.

Two kinds of iron:

- Meat, chicken, and seafood have iron your body takes in easily.
- Beans, nuts, vegetables, and iron-fortified cereal and bread have plant iron.
- Your body takes in less plant iron. Eating it the right way helps.

Good sources of iron:

- Breakfast cereal with 100 percent of the daily value for iron: 18 mg per serving
- Oysters, 3 ounces: 8 mg
- White beans, canned, 1 cup: 8 mg
- Beef liver, 3 ounces: 5 mg
- Lentils, cooked, 1/2 cup: 3 mg
- Tofu, firm, 1/2 cup: 3 mg
- Spinach, cooked, 1/2 cup: 3 mg
- Kidney beans or chickpeas, 1/2 cup: 2 mg
- Beef, 3 ounces: 2 mg
- Sardines, 3 ounces: 2 mg
- Baked potato with skin: 2 mg
- Cashews, 1 ounce: 2 mg

Most women 19 to 50 need 18 mg a day. Men need 8 mg. Women over 50 need 8 mg. Pregnant women need 27 mg.

Help your body take in more iron:

- Eat vitamin C foods with iron foods.
- Vitamin C foods include oranges, strawberries, tomatoes, and potatoes.
- Add a little meat, chicken, or fish to beans or greens. This helps you take in the plant iron.
- Cook in a cast-iron pan. It adds iron to your food.

Keep these away from your iron meals:

- Tea and coffee. Drink them between meals instead.
- Milk and yogurt. Have them at a different meal or snack.
- Calcium pills. Take them at a different time of day than iron.

If you do not eat meat:

- You need almost twice as much iron as people who eat meat.
- Eat beans, lentils, tofu, and fortified cereal often.
- Pair them with a vitamin C food every time.
- Spinach has iron, but your body takes in only a little of it.

Do not take iron pills unless we tell you to.

Call the clinic if you have questions about your diet or iron pills. Go to the ER if you have black, sticky stools or vomit blood.

handouts.title: Mediterranean-style whole-food eating
handouts.text:
Mediterranean-style eating

This is a way of eating, not a strict diet. It is built on plants and whole foods. It is good for your heart and blood sugar.

What to eat most:

- Vegetables and fruit at every meal
- Beans, lentils, and chickpeas
- Whole grains like oats, brown rice, and whole wheat bread
- Nuts and seeds
- Olive oil as your main cooking fat
- Fish and other seafood, 2 or more times a week

What to eat less:

- Red meat like beef and pork
- Processed meat like bacon, ham, hot dogs, and deli meat
- Butter
- Sweets and desserts
- Soda, sweet tea, and juice
- Packaged foods like chips, snack cakes, and frozen meals

Simple first steps:

- Make half your plate vegetables.
- Cook with olive oil instead of butter.
- Try a bean or lentil meal in place of meat.
- Swap white bread and white rice for whole grain.
- Snack on fruit or a small handful of nuts instead of chips or sweets.
- Drink water instead of soda or juice.
- Season food with herbs and spices instead of heavy sauces.

How it can help:

- A large study looked at people at high risk for heart disease.
- This way of eating lowered heart attacks, strokes, and heart deaths.
- People in that study added extra olive oil or nuts. This prevented about 3 in 10 of those events.
- It can help keep blood sugar more stable.
- It can lower cholesterol and triglycerides.

Good to know:

- Olive oil and nuts are high in calories. Use them in place of other fats, not on top of them.
- You do not need wine. If you do not drink alcohol, do not start.
- If you eat less dairy, ask us if you need calcium.

Call the clinic if you want help planning meals or want to see a dietitian.

handouts.title: Palpitations
handouts.text:
Palpitations

Palpitations feel like your heart is racing, pounding, fluttering, or skipping. Most are not dangerous. We are checking for a cause.

What to do:

- Cut back on coffee, tea, energy drinks, and soda.
- Do not smoke or vape nicotine.
- Limit alcohol.
- Avoid cocaine, meth, and other street drugs.
- Ask us before you take cold medicines with decongestants.
- Try slow, deep breathing, yoga, or meditation when stressed.
- Get regular exercise.

If you wear a heart monitor:

- Wear it for ***.
- Press the button or write down the time when you feel symptoms.
- Write down what you were doing and how you felt.

Your follow-up visit is on ***.

Call the clinic if:

- Palpitations are new, more frequent, or different.
- Your pulse is over 100 at rest and you are not anxious or sick.
- You feel more than 6 extra beats a minute, or 3 or more in a row.

Call 911 if you have:

- Fainting or passing out
- Chest pain
- Trouble breathing
- Sweating with a racing heart
- Dizziness or feeling about to faint

handouts.title: Leg swelling
handouts.text:
Leg swelling

Leg swelling happens when fluid builds up in your legs. It has many causes. Your swelling is most likely from ***.

What to do:

- Raise your legs above your heart when you lie down. Use pillows.
- Walk and move your legs often. Flex your ankles up and down.
- Do not stand or sit still for a long time.
- On long trips, stop often to stand up and walk.
- Eat less salt.
- Lose weight if you need to.
- Do not wear tight clothes or bands around your thighs.
- Wear compression stockings ***.
- Do not stop any medicine on your own. Ask us first.

Your follow-up visit is on ***.

Call the clinic if:

- The swelling gets worse or does not get better.
- You have heart, kidney, or liver disease and the swelling gets worse.
- You are pregnant and the swelling is sudden or more than mild.

Go to the ER if:

- One leg is newly swollen, painful, red, or warm.
- You have a fever with a red, swollen leg.

Call 911 if you have:

- Trouble breathing
- Chest pain or pressure

handouts.title: Breast lump or pain
handouts.text:
Breast lump or pain: what to expect

Most breast lumps are not cancer. Breast pain alone is rarely a sign of cancer. We still check every new lump.

Common causes:

- Lumpy, sore breasts that are often worse before your period
- A cyst, which is a small sac filled with fluid
- A fibroadenoma, which is a smooth, rubbery lump that moves easily

What happens next:

- Your test is a breast _ultrasound / mammogram / mammogram and ultrasound on ***.
- An ultrasound shows if a lump is solid or filled with fluid.
- A cyst can sometimes be drained with a small needle.
- If a lump looks unclear, a needle biopsy takes a tiny piece to test.
- We will call you with results by ***.
- If you have not heard from us by then, call the clinic.

For breast pain:

- Wear a well-fitting, supportive bra, like a sports bra.
- Take acetaminophen or ibuprofen as directed on the label.
- Try heat or ice on the sore area.
- Use the pain gel *** on the sore spot ***.
- Cutting out caffeine, fat, or chocolate has not been shown to help.

Call the clinic if you have:

- A new lump, or a lump that does not go away after your period
- Skin that is dimpled or looks like an orange peel
- A nipple that turns inward
- Bloody or clear fluid from the nipple
- A bruise you cannot explain
- Breast pain that does not go away

Call the clinic today if you have redness, pus, or fever.

handouts.title: Overactive thyroid
handouts.text:
Overactive thyroid

Your thyroid gland makes too much hormone. This can cause a racing heart, shaking, weight loss, and trouble sleeping.

Your medicines:

- Methimazole *** mg by mouth ***. This lowers your thyroid hormone.
- *** mg by mouth ***. This slows your heart and calms shaking. We will stop it when your thyroid is better.

Blood tests:

- We checked your blood count and liver tests before you started.
- Thyroid blood test in 4 weeks on ***, then every 1 to 2 months.
- We will change your dose based on these tests.
- Many people take methimazole for 12 to 18 months, and some take it longer.

Other treatments:

- Radioactive iodine or surgery can treat the thyroid for good.
- Do not get pregnant for 6 months after radioactive iodine.
- After either one, most people need thyroid hormone pills for life.

Stop methimazole and call the clinic right away if you have:

- Fever or sore throat
- Yellow skin or eyes
- Dark urine or pale stools
- Belly pain, nausea, or vomiting
- A new rash or joint pain

Call the clinic right away if you become pregnant or plan to. Your medicine may need to change.

Methimazole can rarely stop your body from making white blood cells. If you get a fever or sore throat, get a blood count that day.

Stop biotin (hair, skin, nail vitamins) 2 days before thyroid blood tests.

Graves disease can affect the eyes. Smoking makes eye problems more likely, so ask us for help to quit.

Call the clinic if your eyes change or bother you.

Call 911 if you have chest pain or trouble breathing.

handouts.title: Trying to conceive
handouts.text:
Trying to get pregnant

Most couples get pregnant within 6 months of trying. Some need more time or some help.

Best days to try:

- Your fertile days are the 5 days before you ovulate and the day you ovulate.
- Have sex every 1 to 2 days during this time.
- Ovulation test kits from the pharmacy can help you find these days.
- Sex position and lying down after sex do not change your chances.

Healthy habits for both partners:

- Do not smoke or use drugs.
- Keep alcohol and caffeine low.
- Being very thin or overweight can lower your chances. Ask us about a healthy weight.
- Men should not use testosterone or steroids. They can lower or stop sperm production.
- Men should avoid frequent high heat to the testicles.

When to see us for a fertility checkup:

- Under 35: after 12 months of trying
- 35 to 40: after 6 months of trying
- Over 40: see us now
- Right away if you have irregular periods, endometriosis, pelvic infection, or past miscarriages
- Right away if either partner had cancer treatment or a testicle injury

What tests to expect:

- Both partners are checked at the same time.
- The man gives a semen sample to check the sperm.
- The woman may have blood tests and an ultrasound.
- A special x-ray with dye checks if the tubes are open.

Call the clinic to set up a fertility visit when it is time. Call sooner with any questions.

handouts.title: Bipolar disorder
handouts.text:
Bipolar disorder

Bipolar disorder is a lifelong illness with mood highs and lows. Treatment helps most people stay well.

Your plan:

- Medicine: ***
- Blood tests: ***
- Counseling: ***
- Next visit: ***

Daily habits that help:

- Take your medicine every day, even when you feel well.
- Keep a regular routine for sleep, meals, and exercise.
- Avoid alcohol and drugs.
- Track your mood in a journal or app.
- Learn your early warning signs. Share them with someone you trust.

Signs of a high (mania):

- Feeling very up, wired, or very irritable
- Needing much less sleep
- Racing thoughts or talking fast
- Doing risky things, like spending too much money
- Feeling unusually important or powerful

Signs of a low (depression):

- Feeling very sad, hopeless, or worthless
- Losing interest in almost everything
- Sleeping too much or too little
- Thoughts of death or suicide

Antidepressants alone can trigger a high. Do not start one without talking to us.

If you take lithium:

- You need blood tests to check the lithium level, kidneys, thyroid, and calcium.
- Get the lithium level drawn about 12 hours after your last dose.
- Drink enough fluids. Eat a normal amount of salt.
- Ask us before you take ibuprofen, naproxen, or a water pill.
- If you miss a dose, do not double the next one.
- Stop lithium and call us if you have vomiting, diarrhea, shaking, unsteady walking, bad sleepiness, or weakness.

If you take valproate (divalproex):

- You need blood tests for your liver and blood counts.
- It can cause serious birth defects. Use reliable birth control.
- Call us right away if you might be pregnant.
- Call us if you have weakness, vomiting, loss of appetite, or a swollen face.

If you take lamotrigine:

- We raise the dose slowly over 6 weeks. This lowers the risk of a serious rash.
- Call us the same day for any rash, blisters, or mouth sores.
- If you miss several days in a row, call us before you restart.
- Birth control pills can change how it works. Tell us if you start or stop them.

If you take quetiapine or a similar medicine:

- It can cause weight gain and raise blood sugar and cholesterol.
- We will check your weight, blood pressure, sugar, and cholesterol.

Call the clinic if you notice signs of a high or a low, or side effects bother you.

If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, call or text 988 any time. In Tulsa County, COPES is 918-744-4800, 24/7.

Call 911 or go to the ER if you are confused, have a seizure, or are in danger right now.

handouts.title: PTSD
handouts.text:
PTSD

PTSD can happen after a scary or harmful event. It is not a weakness. It can be treated, and most people get better.

Common signs:

- Bad memories, flashbacks, or nightmares about the event
- Staying away from people or places that remind you of it
- Feeling on edge, jumpy, or angry
- Trouble sleeping or focusing
- Feeling guilt, shame, or numb

Your plan:

- Counseling: ***
- Medicine: ***
- Next visit: ***

Counseling works best:

- The best treatments are talk therapies that help you work through the trauma.
- Names include CPT, PE, and EMDR.
- Most people go once a week. You may notice change after 4 to 8 sessions.

About your medicine:

- Take it every day.
- It can take 8 to 12 weeks to see the full effect.
- Side effects can include upset stomach, headache, and sexual problems.
- Do not stop it suddenly. Talk to us first.

If you take prazosin for nightmares:

- Take it at bedtime.
- It can make you dizzy or faint, mostly after the first doses.
- Get up slowly from lying or sitting.
- Tell us if you take blood pressure pills or erection pills.

Things that help:

- Avoid marijuana and calming pills like benzodiazepines. They are not good treatments for PTSD.
- Limit alcohol and avoid drugs.
- Keep a regular sleep time.
- Stay in touch with people you trust.
- Try the free PTSD Coach app from the VA.

Call the clinic if you feel worse, sleep very poorly, or side effects bother you.

If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, call or text 988 any time. Veterans can dial 988, then press 1.

In Tulsa County, COPES is 918-744-4800, 24/7.

Call 911 if you are in danger right now.

handouts.title: Panic attacks
handouts.text:
Panic attacks

A panic attack is a sudden wave of strong fear. It can feel like a heart attack. Panic disorder can be treated, and most people get better.

During an attack you may have:

- A pounding or racing heart
- Sweating, chills, or shaking
- Trouble breathing
- Feeling dizzy
- Numb or tingly hands
- Chest pain or an upset stomach

An attack can last a few minutes to an hour.

Your plan:

- Counseling: ***
- Medicine: ***
- Next visit: ***

What to do during an attack:

- Slow your breathing. Breathe in for 4 seconds, hold for 4, and breathe out for 6.
- Remind yourself the feeling will pass.

Things that help:

- Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is the best talk therapy for panic.
- In CBT you slowly and safely face the feelings you fear.
- Exercise for 20 minutes, 3 times a week.
- Cut back on coffee, energy drinks, and soda. Caffeine can trigger attacks.

About your medicine:

- We start with a low dose and raise it slowly.
- It takes several weeks to work.
- Side effects can include headache, nausea, or trouble sleeping.
- Keep taking it for about a year after you feel better. Then we lower it slowly together.
- Do not stop it suddenly. Talk to us first.
- Calming pills like alprazolam or lorazepam can lead to dependence. They are only for short-term use.

Call the clinic if attacks happen more often, you avoid places, or side effects bother you.

If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, call or text 988 any time.

Call 911 if you have chest pain you are not sure is panic, trouble breathing, or fainting.

handouts.title: Grief
handouts.text:
Grief

Grief is the normal pain we feel after a loss. There is no right way to grieve.

What is normal:

- Feelings come in waves. The waves get smaller and farther apart over time.
- You may feel numb, angry, or very sad.
- Crying spells and trouble sleeping are common.
- The hardest part often eases in the first couple of months.
- Milder grief can last a year or longer.

Things that help:

- Talk with family and friends you trust.
- Join a grief support group.
- Talk with clergy, a counselor, or a social worker.
- Avoid using alcohol or drugs to cope.
- If your loved one was in hospice, ask the hospice about grief support. It is offered for up to a year.

Your plan:

- Support: ***
- Counseling: ***
- Next visit: ***

When grief needs more help:

- Sometimes grief stays very strong for a year or more. This is called prolonged grief disorder.
- Special grief therapy works well for it.
- Depression can also start after a loss. It can be treated with counseling and medicine.

Call the clinic if:

- You cannot cope with daily life
- You feel very down most of the day, nearly every day
- You feel worthless or hate yourself
- You are drinking more or using drugs
- Your grief is not getting any easier after many months

If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, call or text 988 any time. In Tulsa County, COPES is 918-744-4800, 24/7.

Call 911 if you are in danger right now.

handouts.title: Eating disorders: a guide for families
handouts.text:
Eating disorders: a guide for families

Eating disorders are serious illnesses. They can harm the heart, bones, and brain. With early treatment, people can fully recover.

Anyone can get an eating disorder. This includes boys, girls, and people at any weight. Someone can look healthy and still be very sick.

Signs to watch for:

- Eating very little, or eating fewer and fewer kinds of food
- Big focus on weight, body shape, or controlling food
- Losing weight, or not gaining as expected while growing
- Exercising too much
- Eating large amounts in secret
- Throwing up after meals, or using laxatives
- Missed periods

Your child's plan:

- Treatment team: ***
- Weight and vital sign checks: ***
- Lab tests: ***
- Next visit: ***

How families can help:

- Family support matters. Family-based treatment works well, especially for teens.
- Keep going to every visit and lab check, even if your child seems better.
- Ask us about a dietitian and a therapist who treat eating disorders.

Call the clinic if your child:

- Keeps losing weight
- Refuses to eat or drink
- Throws up often or uses laxatives
- Seems very sad, anxious, or withdrawn

Go to the ER or call 911 if your child:

- Faints or almost faints
- Has chest pain or a very slow or uneven heartbeat
- Is very weak or feels very cold
- Has a seizure
- Talks about suicide or hurting themselves

If your child has thoughts of suicide, call or text 988 any time.

Free help for families: National Alliance for Eating Disorders, 866-662-1235. ANAD helpline, 888-375-7767.

handouts.title: Meth and stimulants: risks and help
handouts.text:
Meth and stimulants: risks and help

Meth, cocaine, and other uppers speed up your heart and brain. They can cause serious harm. Treatment works, and we can help.

Health risks:

- Heart: high blood pressure, fast or uneven heartbeat, heart failure, heart attack, and stroke
- Mind: paranoia, seeing or hearing things that are not there, depression, and anxiety
- Teeth: cavities, broken teeth, abscesses, grinding, and jaw clenching
- Skin: picking, sores, and skin infections
- Body: overheating, kidney damage, and weight loss from not eating
- Infections: HIV and hepatitis C from shared needles or sex without condoms

Fentanyl danger:

- Fentanyl has been found in meth and cocaine. It can stop your breathing.
- Test every new batch with fentanyl test strips.
- A negative strip does not mean the drug is safe.
- Carry naloxone nasal spray. Teach your friends how to use it.
- Naloxone does not reverse meth. It can reverse fentanyl.
- Use it if someone will not wake up or is not breathing well.
- Do not use alone. Be with someone who has naloxone and can call 911.

Stay safer:

- Drink water and rest in a cool place.
- Eat regular meals.
- Use new needles and supplies every time. Never share.
- Use condoms.
- Brush and floss, and see a dentist.

Get tested:

- HIV, hepatitis C, syphilis, and other sexual infections
- Ask about PrEP. It is medicine that prevents HIV.

Treatment that works:

- Contingency management works best. You earn rewards for drug-free urine tests.
- Counseling, such as CBT, helps too.
- No medicine is FDA-approved for meth yet.
- Some medicines can help, like bupropion with naltrexone. Ask us.

Your plan:

- Treatment: ***
- Medicine: ***
- Next visit: ***

Free, private help any time: SAMHSA National Helpline, 1-800-662-4357.

Call the clinic if you want help cutting back or quitting, or you feel depressed or paranoid.

If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, call or text 988.

Call 911 if someone:

- Has chest pain or trouble breathing
- Has signs of stroke, like a drooping face, weakness on one side, or trouble talking
- Has a seizure
- Is very hot and confused
- Has trouble waking up or slow breathing. Give naloxone too.
- Sees or hears things and may hurt themselves or others

handouts.title: Psoriasis
handouts.text:
Psoriasis

Psoriasis causes thick, red, scaly patches on the skin. You cannot catch it from someone. It can be controlled with care.

Your plan:

- Thick patches on the body: *** 2 times a day for up to *** weeks.
- Face and skin folds: *** 2 times a day.
- Scalp: ***
- Use moisturizer several times a day.

Tips:

- Slowly cut back the steroid when the skin gets better. Do not stop all at once.
- Do not use salicylic acid products with calcipotriene. Salicylic acid stops calcipotriene from working.
- Do not smoke. Limit alcohol.
- Lose weight if you are overweight. This can help your skin.
- Protect your skin from cuts and scrapes. Injured skin can form new patches.

Psoriasis raises the risk of heart disease. Keep up with blood pressure, cholesterol, and sugar checks.

Call the clinic if:

- Your joints are painful, swollen, or stiff.
- Your skin is not better in *** weeks.
- You feel down or hopeless.

handouts.title: Rosacea
handouts.text:
Rosacea

Rosacea causes redness and bumps on the face. It is common and not contagious. It can be controlled.

Your plan:

- Cream or gel: *** on your face *** times a day.
- Pill: ***

Find your triggers:

- Common triggers are sun, heat, stress, alcohol, spicy foods, and hot drinks.
- Keep a journal of what makes your face flare.
- Avoid the triggers you find.

Skin care:

- Use sunscreen every day, SPF 30 or higher, with zinc oxide or titanium dioxide.
- Wear a wide-brimmed hat in the sun.
- Do not use steroid creams on your face. They make rosacea worse.

For dry, gritty, or red eyelids, use warm compresses. Clean your lashes with baby shampoo.

Call the clinic if your face is not better in 3 months. Call right away for eye pain or vision changes.

handouts.title: Seborrheic dermatitis
handouts.text:
Seborrheic dermatitis

This is a common rash with flaky, greasy scale. It shows up on the scalp, eyebrows, and sides of the nose. It is not contagious.

Scalp:

- Use *** shampoo *** times a week.
- Leave it on your scalp for at least 5 minutes before you rinse.
- Once your scalp is clear, keep using it once a week. This helps stop flares.

Face and body:

- Use *** cream 2 times a day.
- Use *** for flares only, for a few days at a time.

Cradle cap in babies:

- Rub mineral oil or petroleum jelly on the scalp to loosen scale.
- Gently brush the scale off with a soft baby brush.
- It usually goes away on its own.

Call the clinic if the rash spreads, oozes, or is not better in 4 weeks.

handouts.title: Ringworm and athlete's foot
handouts.text:
Ringworm (tinea)

Ringworm is a skin infection caused by a fungus. It is not a worm. It spreads by touch and shared items.

Skin, groin, or feet:

- Put *** cream on the rash *** times a day.
- Use it for ***, even if the skin looks better.
- Keep the skin clean and dry.
- Dry well between your toes after bathing.
- Wear wide shoes and clean socks. Do not share towels.

Scalp (in kids):

- Scalp ringworm needs medicine by mouth. Creams do not work.
- Give *** every day for *** weeks.
- If the medicine is griseofulvin, give it with fatty food like whole milk or peanut butter.
- Use *** shampoo 3 times a week. Leave it on 5 to 10 minutes.
- Your child can go back to school once treatment starts.
- For 14 days, do not share combs, brushes, hats, helmets, or pillowcases.
- Check family members for itchy, scaly spots.

Call the clinic if the rash is not better in 2 weeks or keeps spreading. Call for yellow skin, dark urine, or a rash while taking the medicine.

handouts.title: Warts
handouts.text:
Warts

Warts are caused by a virus. Many go away on their own within 1 to 2 years. Treatment can speed this up.

Home treatment with salicylic acid:

- Soak the wart in warm water for 5 minutes.
- Gently file the top with a pumice stone or emery board.
- Put on the salicylic acid. Use liquid once a day or a pad every other day.
- Keep doing this for up to 12 weeks.
- If the skin around it gets sore, stop for a few days. Then start again.
- Do not use it on your face.

After freezing:

- A blister or crust may form. It usually heals in 4 to 7 days.
- Come back in *** weeks for another treatment if needed.

Covering the wart with a bandage helps stop it from spreading.

Call the clinic if the wart bleeds, hurts, grows fast, or changes. Call if it is not better after 3 months.

handouts.title: Scabies
handouts.text:
Scabies

Scabies is an itchy rash caused by tiny mites in the skin. It spreads by close skin contact. It is easy to treat.

How to use the cream:

- Rub it on all skin from the neck to the soles of the feet.
- For babies and young children, also cover the head and neck.
- Wash it off after 8 to 14 hours.
- Do it again in 1 week.

Treat everyone at the same time:

- Everyone in your home needs treatment the same day. This includes people with no itch.
- Tell close contacts from the past 2 months so they can get treated.

Clean your things:

- Wash clothes, towels, and bedding in hot water.
- Dry them on the hot setting.
- Seal things you cannot wash in a plastic bag for at least 3 days.

You can go back to work, school, or child care the day after treatment.

Itching can last 2 to 4 weeks after treatment. This does not mean the treatment failed.

Call the clinic if itching lasts more than 4 weeks or you see new bumps or burrows.

handouts.title: Impetigo
handouts.text:
Impetigo

Impetigo is a skin infection caused by germs. It causes sores that crust over. It spreads easily by touch.

Your plan:

- Ointment: put *** on the sores *** times a day for *** days.
- Pill or liquid: *** for *** days. Finish all of it.

Stop the spread:

- Wash hands often with soap and water.
- Do not share towels, washcloths, or clothes.
- Wash towels and bedding in hot water.
- Clean cuts and scrapes right away.

Your child can go back to school or day care 12 to 24 hours after starting the medicine.

Call the clinic if the sores are not better in 3 to 5 days or keep spreading. Call for fever.

handouts.title: Sun protection and skin self-check
handouts.text:
Sun protection and skin checks

Sun damage adds up over your life. It can cause skin cancer. Protect your skin every day.

Sunscreen:

- Use sunscreen that says broad-spectrum, SPF 30 or higher, and water resistant.
- Use about 1 ounce to cover your body. That is about a full shot glass.
- Put it on 15 minutes before you go outside.
- Put it on again every 2 hours, and after swimming or sweating.
- Use lip balm with SPF 30 or higher.

Other ways to protect your skin:

- Stay in the shade between 10 a.m. and 2 p.m. If your shadow is shorter than you, find shade.
- Wear a wide-brimmed hat, sunglasses, and long sleeves.
- Do not use tanning beds.
- Keep babies under 6 months in the shade and in light, covering clothes.

Check your skin:

- Use a full-length mirror and a hand mirror.
- Look at your scalp, back, the soles of your feet, between your toes, and your nails.

Warning signs in a mole (ABCDE):

- A: Asymmetry. One half does not match the other.
- B: Border is uneven or blurry.
- C: Color varies, with more than one shade.
- D: Diameter is bigger than a pencil eraser.
- E: Evolving. It is changing in size, shape, or color.

Also watch for a spot that looks different from the others.

Call the clinic if you find a new spot, a spot that is changing, or one that itches or bleeds.

handouts.title: Hidradenitis suppurativa
handouts.text:
Hidradenitis suppurativa

This is a long-term skin disease. It causes painful lumps in the armpits, groin, and under the breasts. It is not caused by poor hygiene. It is not contagious.

Your plan:

- Lotion: *** on the bumps 2 times a day.
- Pill: ***
- Shot into a painful lump: ***

Things that help:

- Quit smoking. Smoking makes the disease worse. It also makes the medicine work less well.
- Lose weight if you are overweight. Losing some weight can ease flares.
- Wear loose clothes to cut down rubbing.
- Do not squeeze or cut open the lumps. They usually come back.

This disease can wear you down. Tell us if you feel sad or hopeless. Support groups can help.

Call the clinic if a lump is very painful, spreading, or draining a lot. Go to the ER for fever with a red, hot, spreading area.

handouts.title: Hair loss
handouts.text:
Hair loss

Hair loss has many causes. Most types can be treated or will get better.

Your type of hair loss: ***

Shedding after illness or stress (telogen effluvium):

- Heavy shedding can start 2 to 5 months after an illness, surgery, pregnancy, or big stress.
- It usually stops on its own within 6 months once the cause is gone.

Thinning hair (pattern hair loss):

- Minoxidil foam: put it on the dry scalp *** times a day.
- It takes 6 to 12 months to see results.
- Keep using it. Hair loss comes back when you stop.
- Pill: ***

Round bald patches (alopecia areata):

- This is the immune system attacking the hair roots. Hair often grows back.
- Treatment: ***

Other tips:

- Avoid tight braids, ponytails, and weaves. Pulling can damage hair.
- Do not pull or twist your hair. Tell us if you cannot stop.

Call the clinic if your scalp is red, scaly, or sore. Call if hair loss is fast or leaves smooth, shiny skin.

handouts.title: Knee pain
handouts.text:
Knee pain

Most knee pain gets better with home care and exercise. Your knee problem is: ***

First few days:

- Rest. Avoid things that make the pain worse.
- Ice your knee for up to 15 minutes at a time. Put a towel between the ice and your skin.
- Ice it every hour on the first day, then at least 4 times a day.
- Wrap it with an elastic bandage or sleeve.
- Raise your knee on pillows to bring down swelling.
- Sleep with a pillow under or between your knees.

Pain medicine:

- Ibuprofen or naproxen helps pain and swelling. Take it with food.
- Acetaminophen helps pain but not swelling.
- Ask us first if you have kidney disease, ulcers, or take a blood thinner.
- Your medicine plan: ***

Getting back to activity:

- Do the exercises you were shown every day: ***
- Stretch the front and back of your thigh.
- Bike or swim instead of running until the pain is gone.
- Walk down hills instead of running down them.
- Wear shoes that fit well and have good cushioning.
- If you are overweight, losing weight takes pressure off your knees.

Call the clinic if:

- You still have pain after 3 days of home care
- Your knee buckles, locks, or gives way
- You cannot bend or fully straighten your knee
- You cannot put weight on your knee

Go to the ER or come in the same day if:

- Your knee is red, hot, or very swollen, or you have a fever
- Your knee looks bent out of shape
- Your calf is swollen, painful, numb, or turning blue

handouts.title: Neck pain
handouts.text:
Neck pain

Neck pain is often caused by strained or tight muscles. Sitting bent over a desk for a long time is a common cause.

First few days:

- Use ice for the first 2 to 3 days, then use heat.
- Do not fall asleep with an ice pack or heating pad on.
- Cut back on hard activity for a few days, but do not stay in bed.
- Do not drive if you cannot turn your head easily.

Pain medicine:

- Ibuprofen or naproxen helps pain and swelling. Take it with food.
- Acetaminophen helps pain too.
- Ask us first if you have kidney disease, stomach ulcers, or take a blood thinner.
- Your medicine plan: ***

Getting better:

- Avoid heavy lifting and twisting your neck for about 6 weeks.
- After 2 to 3 weeks, slowly start exercising again.
- Walking, a stationary bike, and swimming are good choices.
- Do the neck stretches and exercises you were shown: ***
- Sleep on a firm mattress with a pillow that supports your neck.

At work and at home:

- Stretch your neck every hour or so.
- Keep your screen and papers at eye level.
- Use a headset if you talk on the phone a lot.
- On long drives, stop and walk about every hour.

Call the clinic if:

- Your pain is not better after 1 week of home care
- You have numbness, tingling, or weakness in your arm or hand
- Your pain wakes you up at night or is worse lying down
- The pain is so bad you cannot get comfortable

Call the clinic right away if:

- You lose control of your bladder or bowels
- You have trouble walking or keeping your balance

Call 911 or go to the ER if:

- You have a fever, a headache, and a neck so stiff you cannot touch your chin to your chest
- You hurt your neck in a fall or injury and cannot move your arm or hand
- You have neck pain with shortness of breath, sweating, nausea, or arm or jaw pain

handouts.title: Living with inflammatory arthritis
handouts.text:
Living with inflammatory arthritis

Your immune system is attacking the lining of your joints. This causes pain, swelling, and stiffness. Starting treatment early helps prevent lasting joint damage.

Your medicines:

- Your arthritis medicine: ***
- These medicines take time. You may feel better in 3 to 6 weeks. The full effect can take 12 weeks.
- Take them even when you feel well. Do not stop them without talking to us.

If you take methotrexate:

- Take it only once a week, on the same day each week. Your day: ***
- Never take it every day. Taking it daily by mistake has caused deaths.
- Take folic acid as directed. It helps prevent side effects.
- Do not drink alcohol. Alcohol and methotrexate together can hurt your liver.
- You need blood tests to check your blood counts, liver, and kidneys. Your next test: ***
- Do not get pregnant while on methotrexate. Use birth control.
- Keep using birth control after your last dose: 6 months for women, 3 months for men.
- Talk with us before you try to have a baby.

If you take hydroxychloroquine:

- Get an eye exam soon after you start.
- After 5 years on the medicine, get an eye exam every year, or sooner if your doctor says.

Stay healthy:

- Stay active. Walking and swimming are good choices.
- Aim for 150 minutes of activity each week, like 30 minutes on 5 days.
- Do muscle strengthening 2 days a week.
- If you smoke, quitting helps your arthritis. For free help, call 1-800-QUIT-NOW.
- Keep a healthy weight.
- Get your vaccines before or soon after starting treatment. Ask us which ones you need.
- Tell any doctor or pharmacist that you take an immune-lowering medicine.

Call the clinic if:

- You have a fever or other signs of infection
- You have a new or worse cough or shortness of breath
- You have mouth sores, nausea, or diarrhea that does not go away
- Your joints flare up and do not settle down
- You think you might be pregnant

Go to the ER if:

- You have trouble breathing
- You have a high fever and feel very sick

handouts.title: Polymyalgia rheumatica
handouts.text:
Polymyalgia rheumatica

Polymyalgia rheumatica, or PMR, causes pain and stiffness in the shoulders, neck, and hips. It is caused by inflammation. A steroid medicine called prednisone treats it well.

Your prednisone:

- Your dose now: *** mg each day. Take it with food.
- Most people feel much better within days of starting. Call us if you are not better in 2 weeks.
- We will lower your dose slowly over many months. Your plan: ***
- Most people need prednisone for 1 to 2 years. Some need it longer.
- Do not stop prednisone suddenly. Your body may not make enough of its own steroid.
- Do not change your dose on your own.

Side effects to watch for:

- Weight gain
- Trouble sleeping
- Mood changes or feeling down
- Higher blood pressure and blood sugar. Get them checked as we advise.
- Weaker bones
- Infections are more likely. Wash your hands often and stay away from sick people.

Protect your bones:

- Get 1,000 to 1,200 mg of calcium each day. Try to get it from food first.
- Take vitamin D as directed: ***
- Stay active. Do the exercises you were shown to keep your muscles strong.
- You may need a bone density test: ***

PMR can come with a serious problem called giant cell arteritis. It affects blood vessels in the head and eyes. Without fast treatment, it can cause lasting vision loss.

Go to the ER right away if you have:

- Blurry vision, double vision, or any loss of vision
- A new headache, often near the temples
- Pain in your jaw when you chew
- A tender scalp

Call the clinic if:

- Your pain and stiffness come back as the dose goes down
- You have a fever or signs of infection
- You feel very tired, weak, or sick to your stomach while lowering or stopping prednisone

handouts.title: After a developmental screen
handouts.text:
After your child's development screen

Today your child did a screen for development or autism. The results show your child may need a closer look.

A screen is not a diagnosis. It tells us who needs more testing. Getting help early makes a big difference.

What happens next:

- We are sending a referral for a full evaluation: ***
- Under age 3: SoonerStart will call you. It is Oklahoma's early intervention program. It is free.
- Age 3 and older: call your school district. Ask for a special education evaluation. It is free.
- We may also send your child for a hearing test. Hearing problems can slow talking.
- You do not have to wait for a diagnosis. Your child can start therapy now.

What you can do at home:

- Talk with your child all day. Name things you see and do.
- Read books together every day.
- Play face to face. Take turns with sounds, toys, and smiles.
- Limit screen time.

Write down your questions and bring them to the next visit.

Call the clinic if:

- No one has called you about the referral within 2 weeks
- Your child loses words or skills they used to have
- You have new worries about how your child plays, talks, or moves

handouts.title: Bedwetting
handouts.text:
Bedwetting

Many children wet the bed. About 15 out of 100 children age 5 still do. It is not your child's fault.

Most children outgrow it. Some stop each year without any treatment.

What to do:

- Never blame, shame, or punish your child.
- Do not let brothers or sisters tease your child.
- Put a plastic cover under the sheet.
- Your child can help change wet sheets. Keep it calm, not a punishment.
- Treat hard stools. Constipation can make bedwetting worse.
- Keep a 2-week chart of wet and dry nights.

Bedwetting alarm:

- The alarm goes off when your child starts to pee.
- Your child wakes up and finishes in the toilet.
- It can take 6 to 16 weeks to work.
- Keep using it until your child is dry 14 nights in a row.

Medicine (desmopressin), if prescribed:

- Your child's dose: *** at bedtime.
- Limit drinks to a few sips starting 1 hour before the dose.
- No more drinks until morning.
- Too much fluid with this medicine can cause a dangerous low salt level.

Call the clinic if your child has:

- Pain, burning, or pink pee
- Wetting during the day, or a very weak stream
- New bedwetting after being dry for 6 months or more
- Headache, vomiting, or confusion while on desmopressin

Go to the ER if your child has a seizure.

handouts.title: Colic
handouts.text:
Colic

Colic is long crying in a healthy baby. It often starts at 2 to 4 weeks. Crying peaks around 6 weeks.

It usually ends by 3 to 4 months. Your baby is not sick, and you did nothing wrong.

Ways to soothe your baby:

- Hold your baby close or walk with your baby in a carrier.
- Rock or sway your baby in your arms.
- Use steady sound, like a fan or white noise.
- Offer a pacifier.
- Lay your baby tummy down across your lap and rub the back. Stay with your baby.
- Swaddle in a thin blanket.

Feeding:

- Do not overfeed. Wait 2 to 2 and a half hours from the start of one feed to the next.
- Breastfeeding: keep going. Ask us before you cut foods from your diet.
- Formula: ask us before you switch formulas.
- Probiotic drops, if we suggested them: ***

Take care of yourself:

- Crying is hard. It is OK to feel tired and frustrated.
- Take turns with another adult. Step away for an hour if you can.
- If you are alone and upset, lay your baby on the back in the crib. Leave the room for a few minutes.
- Never shake a baby. Shaking can cause blindness, brain damage, or death.
- Tell everyone who cares for your baby to never shake the baby.
- Tell us if you feel sad, hopeless, or cannot cope.

Call the clinic if your baby:

- Has a rectal temperature of 100.4 F or higher
- Is vomiting, not feeding well, or has fewer wet diapers
- Cries in a different way, or cannot be calmed at all
- Is very sleepy or hard to wake

Call 911 if your baby is limp, not breathing normally, or turning blue. Call 911 if you feel you might hurt your baby.

handouts.title: Spitting up and reflux in babies
handouts.text:
Spitting up and reflux in babies

Spitting up is normal in babies. If your baby is growing well and happy, it is usually not a problem. Most babies outgrow it by age 1.

Medicine for stomach acid does not help normal spitting up. It also does not help crying in healthy babies.

What helps:

- Do not overfeed. Give smaller feeds more often.
- Burp your baby during and after feeds.
- Hold your baby upright for 15 to 30 minutes after each feed.
- Feed in a calm, quiet place.
- Keep your baby away from tobacco smoke.
- Keep breastfeeding.
- Talk to us before you change formula or your own diet.

Safe sleep:

- Always put your baby to sleep on the back.
- Use a flat, firm crib mattress.
- Do not raise the head of the crib or use wedges.

Our plan for your baby: ***

Call the clinic if your baby:

- Is not gaining weight or is losing weight
- Refuses feeds or arches away during feeds
- Vomits forcefully more than a few times in a day
- Has blood in the stool
- Coughs, chokes, or wheezes with feeds
- Still has reflux after age 1

Go to the ER if your baby vomits blood or green or yellow fluid. Go if your baby is very hard to wake.

handouts.title: Staying strong as you age
handouts.text:
Staying strong as you age
Frailty means your body has less strength and reserve. Illness or a fall can hit harder. The good news: exercise and good food can help.

Move every day:

- Do strength exercises 2 or 3 days a week, with a rest day in between.
- Use bands, ankle weights, water bottles, or your body weight.
- Do 2 or 3 sets of 8 to 12 lifts. The last few lifts should feel hard.
- Do balance exercises at least 3 days a week, like standing on one foot while holding a counter.
- Walk or do other activity you enjoy. Work up to 150 minutes a week if you can.
- Start slow and add a little more each week.
- Your exercise plan: ***
- Free exercise guides: vivifrail.com. Your level: ***

Eat enough protein:

- Eat protein at every meal. Good choices are eggs, fish, chicken, beans, milk, yogurt, and cottage cheese.
- Aim for 25 to 30 grams of protein at each meal.
- Your protein goal: *** grams a day.
- If you are losing weight, add a snack or a nutrition drink between meals.
- Do not go on a weight-loss diet unless we advise it.

Medicines:

- Bring all your pills to each visit, including vitamins and over-the-counter medicines.
- We may stop medicines that are no longer helping you: ***

Prevent falls:

- Clear clutter and loose rugs.
- Use night lights and grab bars.
- Get your eyes and hearing checked.

Tell us about leaking urine, low mood, or memory problems. These can often be treated.

Stay connected with family, friends, and your community. Tell us what matters most to you about your health.

Call the clinic if you:

- Lose weight without trying
- Fall, even if you are not hurt
- Feel weaker, more tired, or more confused than usual
- Need more help at home

Call 911 if you fall and cannot get up.

handouts.title: Hearing loss
handouts.text:
Hearing loss

Hearing loss is common as we get older. Treating it helps you talk with family and friends. It may also lower your risk of memory loss.

Sudden hearing loss is an emergency:

- Hearing loss that comes on over a few days or less is urgent. Call us the same day.
- Treatment works best when started fast, within 2 weeks.

Earwax:

- Earwax is normal and cleans the ear.
- Do not put cotton swabs or other objects in your ears.
- Do not use ear candles.
- If wax blocks your ear, we can remove it.

Hearing aids:

- Over-the-counter hearing aids are for adults 18 and older with mild to moderate hearing loss.
- You can buy them in stores or online without a prescription.
- See a doctor first if you have ear pain, drainage, dizziness, or hearing loss in only one ear.
- If you need more help, an audiologist can test your hearing and fit an aid.
- Your plan: ***

Protect your hearing:

- Turn down the volume on headphones and the TV.
- Wear earplugs or earmuffs around loud noise, like mowers, power tools, or guns.

Call the clinic if you have:

- Hearing loss that gets worse
- Ear pain or fluid from the ear
- Ringing in only one ear
- Dizziness

Call 911 if hearing loss comes with face drooping, weakness, slurred speech, or a severe headache.

handouts.title: Staying healthy when you travel
handouts.text:
Staying healthy when you travel

Plan ahead for a safe trip. Some vaccines and medicines must start weeks before you leave.

Your vaccines today: ***

Malaria medicine, if prescribed:

- Your medicine: ***
- Start it on: ***
- Take it during your trip and keep taking it after you get home until: ***
- Do not stop early. Also prevent mosquito bites.

Upset stomach and diarrhea:

- Mild diarrhea: drink plenty of fluids. You may take loperamide as the package says.
- Do not take loperamide if you have a fever or blood in your stool.
- Severe diarrhea or blood in stool: take your backup antibiotic: ***
- Children and babies get dehydrated fast. Give oral rehydration solution and keep breastfeeding.

Long flights and car rides:

- On trips over 4 hours, get up and walk when you can.
- Flex and point your feet often while seated.
- Pick an aisle seat if you can.
- Wear compression stockings if we told you to: ***

Insurance:

- Check if your health plan covers care in other countries. Medicare does not.
- Think about travel health insurance and medical evacuation insurance.

Animal bites:

- Do not touch dogs, cats, monkeys, or bats.
- If bitten or scratched, wash the wound right away with soap and water. Get medical care the same day.

Call the clinic if you get a fever during your trip or within 1 year after you return. Tell them where you traveled.

Go to the ER or a local hospital for high fever, confusion, or trouble breathing. Go for bloody diarrhea with dehydration.

handouts.title: Tick bites and prevention
handouts.text:
Tick bites and prevention

Ticks can spread germs that cause serious illness. These include ehrlichiosis, Rocky Mountain spotted fever, and tularemia.

How to remove a tick:

- Use fine-tipped tweezers. Grab the tick as close to the skin as you can.
- Pull upward with steady, even pressure. Do not twist or jerk.
- If mouth parts stay in the skin and do not come out easily, leave them alone.
- Clean the bite and your hands with rubbing alcohol or soap and water.
- Put the tick in rubbing alcohol or a sealed bag. Do not crush it with your fingers.
- Do not use nail polish, petroleum jelly, or heat to remove a tick.

To prevent tick bites:

- Use an insect repellent with DEET, picaridin, IR3535, or oil of lemon eucalyptus.
- Do not use oil of lemon eucalyptus on children under 3.
- Treat boots, clothes, and camping gear with 0.5% permethrin.
- Walk in the middle of trails. Avoid tall grass and brush.
- Shower within 2 hours after coming inside.
- Check your whole body for ticks. Look under the arms, in and around the ears and hair, and in the belly button.
- Also check behind the knees, between the legs, and around the waist.
- Dry clothes on high heat for 10 minutes to kill ticks.
- Check your pets and gear too.

If you are being treated:

- Take doxycycline *** exactly as prescribed, even if you feel better.
- Doxycycline is the best medicine for tick illness at any age, including young children.
- Your fever should start to go down in 1 to 2 days.

Call the clinic if you get fever, rash, headache, or body aches in the weeks after a tick bite. Also call if you have a sore with swollen glands near it.

Go to the ER if you have:

- Confusion or very bad sleepiness
- Trouble breathing
- Fever that does not get better after 2 days of doxycycline

handouts.title: Latent TB infection
handouts.text:
Latent TB infection

You have latent TB infection. This means TB germs are sleeping in your body. You cannot spread it to others. Without treatment, about 5 to 10 out of 100 people get sick with TB later.

Your treatment:

- Your medicine is ***.
- Take it *** for *** months.
- Take every dose. Missing doses can make treatment fail.
- Use a pill box, phone alarm, or calendar to help you remember.
- We will see you every month during treatment.

Things to know:

- Rifampin and rifapentine can turn urine, tears, and sweat orange. This is harmless.
- They can stain soft contact lenses.
- They can make birth control pills, patches, rings, and shots work less well. Use condoms during treatment.
- Tell us about all your medicines, including blood thinners and methadone.
- Limit alcohol during treatment. It can hurt your liver.

Stop your TB medicine and call the clinic right away if you have:

- Yellow skin or eyes
- Brown urine, like cola or coffee
- Light-colored stools
- Nausea, vomiting, or belly pain
- Loss of appetite
- Rash or itching
- Fever or flu-like symptoms
- Easy bruising or bleeding
- Tingling in your hands or feet
- Tiredness or weakness that lasts 3 days or more
- Dizziness

Call the clinic if you get a cough that will not go away, fever, night sweats, or weight loss. These can be signs of active TB.

handouts.title: Pink eye
handouts.text:
Pink eye

You have pink eye, also called conjunctivitis. Your pink eye is most likely caused by _a virus / bacteria / allergies.

What to do:

- Use cold compresses and artificial tears to ease redness and dryness.
- Wipe away discharge with a clean wet washcloth or fresh cotton ball. Throw cotton balls away after use.
- Do not touch or rub your eyes.
- If you were given drops or ointment, use them *** for *** days.

Contact lenses:

- Stop wearing contact lenses until your eye doctor says it is OK.
- Throw away disposable lenses and the case you used while your eye was infected.

To keep from spreading it:

- Wash your hands often with soap and water for at least 20 seconds.
- Wash hands before and after you clean your eyes or use eye drops.
- Wash pillowcases, sheets, washcloths, and towels in hot water.
- Do not share towels, pillows, eye drops, makeup, or makeup brushes.
- Do not swim in pools until your eyes are better.

What to expect:

- Pink eye from a virus usually gets better in 1 to 2 weeks. Antibiotics do not help it.
- Pink eye from bacteria usually gets better in 2 to 5 days.
- Pink eye from allergies is not contagious.

School, daycare, and work: Stay home if you have a fever or feel sick. Ask us when it is OK to go back.

Call the clinic if you have:

- Eye pain
- Pain from bright light
- Blurry vision that does not clear when you wipe your eyes
- Very red eyes
- Symptoms that get worse or do not get better
- Pink eye from bacteria that is not better after 24 hours of antibiotics

Call right away if a baby under 1 month old has red eyes or eye discharge.

handouts.title: Mono
handouts.text:
Mono

You have mono, short for infectious mononucleosis. It is caused by a virus. Most people feel better in 2 to 4 weeks. Feeling tired can last longer.

What to do:

- Rest often.
- Drink plenty of fluids.
- Gargle with warm salt water for a sore throat.
- Take acetaminophen *** for fever and throat pain. Do not take more than the label says.
- Do not give aspirin to children or teens.
- Limit or avoid alcohol while you are sick. Mono can affect your liver.
- Antibiotics do not help mono. Do not take amoxicillin or ampicillin unless we tell you to.

Sports and activity:

- Mono can make your spleen swell. A swollen spleen can tear with a hit to the belly.
- Do not play sports for at least 3 weeks after you got sick.
- Start back slowly with light activity that has no contact.
- Ask us before you go back to contact sports.

To keep from spreading it:

- Do not kiss others.
- Do not share drinks, food, forks, spoons, or toothbrushes.

Call the clinic if you have:

- Symptoms that last more than 10 days
