- Belly pain
- Fever above 101.5 F that will not go away
- A very bad sore throat or very swollen tonsils
- Yellow skin or eyes

Call 911 or go to the ER if you have:

- Sudden, sharp, very bad belly pain
- Trouble breathing or swallowing
- A stiff neck or severe weakness

handouts.title: Animal or human bite
handouts.text:
Animal or human bite

Bites can get infected. Cat bites and bites on the hand are the most likely to get infected.

Wound care:

- Keep the wound clean. Wash it gently with soap and water ***.
- If we prescribed an antibiotic, take it *** for *** days. Take every dose.

Tetanus: We _gave you a tetanus shot today / checked your tetanus shot and it is up to date.

Rabies:

- If a healthy dog, cat, or ferret bit you, the animal should be watched for 10 days.
- Call us right away if the animal gets sick, acts strange, or dies.
- Do not let anyone put the animal down during those 10 days unless the health department says to.
- Bites from bats, skunks, raccoons, and foxes need rabies shots unless the animal tests negative.
- If you started rabies shots, get every dose on time. Your next shots are on ***.
- Your local health department can help. Their number is ***.

Your wound check is on ***.

Call the clinic if you have:

- Redness that spreads
- Swelling or pain that gets worse
- Pus or bad smell from the wound
- Fever
- Trouble moving a finger or joint near the bite

Go to the ER if you have fever and feel very sick.

handouts.title: Head lice
handouts.text:
Head lice

Head lice are tiny bugs that live on the scalp. They are most common in preschool and grade school children.

How they spread:

- Lice crawl. They cannot hop or fly.
- Lice spread mostly through head-to-head contact.
- Pets do not get or spread head lice.

Treatment:

- Use medicine only if live lice are seen.
- Use ***. Follow the package directions exactly.
- An adult should put the medicine on, not the child.
- Rinse it off over a sink with warm water, not in the shower or bath.
- Do not use extra medicine or mix different lice products.
- Some medicines need a second treatment on day *** if you still see live lice.
- Comb wet hair with a fine-tooth nit comb every 2 to 3 days for 2 to 3 weeks.

Cleaning:

- Wash clothes, towels, hats, and bedding used in the last 2 days in hot water. Dry on high heat.
- Seal items you cannot wash in a plastic bag for 2 weeks.
- Vacuum the floor and furniture where your child sat or lay.
- Do not use bug sprays or foggers in your home. They are not needed and can be harmful.
- Check everyone in your home. Treat only people who have live lice.

School: Your child does not need to miss school. Your child can go back after the first treatment. Nits left in the hair are not a reason to stay home.

Call the clinic if you still see live lice after 2 treatments.

handouts.title: Pinworm
handouts.text:
Pinworm

Pinworms are tiny worms that live in the gut. They cause itching around the bottom, mostly at night.

Medicine:

- Take *** now. Take a second dose in 2 weeks, on ***.
- The second dose kills worms that hatched from eggs after the first dose.
- If more than 1 person at home has pinworms, treat everyone in the home at the same time.

Stop the spread:

- Shower every morning. Showers are better than baths.
- Put on clean underwear every day.
- Wash hands with soap and warm water after using the toilet and changing diapers.
- Wash hands before eating or making food.
- Keep fingernails short and clean.
- Do not scratch around the bottom. Do not bite your nails.
- Change pajamas, towels, washcloths, and sheets often.
- Wash them in hot water and dry them in a hot dryer. Do not shake them out.
- Do not share washcloths. Children should bathe one at a time.

Call the clinic if the itching does not go away after the second dose, or if it comes back.

handouts.title: Hand, foot, and mouth disease
handouts.text:
Hand, foot, and mouth disease

Your child has hand, foot, and mouth disease. It is caused by a virus. It causes fever, mouth sores, and a rash on the hands and feet. Most children get better in 7 to 10 days.

What to do:

- There is no medicine to cure it. Care at home helps your child feel better.
- Give acetaminophen or ibuprofen for fever and pain. Your child's dose is ***.
- Never give aspirin to children.
- Have your child drink small sips of fluid often. Mouth sores can make drinking hurt.
- Do not use regular mouthwash. It stings.

Stop the spread:

- Wash hands often with soap and water for at least 20 seconds.
- Wash hands well after changing diapers. The virus stays in poop for weeks.
- Do not share cups, forks, spoons, toothbrushes, or towels.
- Clean toys and surfaces that people touch a lot.
- Avoid hugging and kissing others while your child is sick.

Child care and school: Your child can go back when there is no fever and they feel well enough. Your child should also be able to control drooling from mouth sores.

Your child's nails may peel or fall off a few weeks later. They will grow back.

Call the clinic if your child:

- Is not drinking well, or you are worried about dehydration
- Has a fever for more than 3 days
- Is not better after 10 days
- Is younger than 6 months
- Has a weak immune system

Go to the ER if your child has a stiff neck, a very bad headache, or new weakness.

handouts.title: Bell's palsy
handouts.text:
Bell's palsy

Bell's palsy is weakness of the muscles on one side of the face. It comes on fast. It is not a stroke. Most people get better on their own within a few weeks to months.

Your medicine:

- Take prednisone *** as prescribed. Start it right away.
- If we prescribed an antiviral, take *** for *** days.

Protect your eye:

- If your eye does not close all the way, it can dry out and get hurt.
- Use lubricating eye drops during the day ***.
- Use eye gel at night and tape your eyelid closed while you sleep.

What to expect:

- Many people start to improve within 3 weeks.
- It can take weeks or months for full strength to come back.
- Some people have small lasting changes, like a twitch or weak smile.

Call the clinic if you have:

- Eye pain, redness, or vision changes
- Weakness that gets worse
- No improvement after 3 months

Call 911 if you have:

- Weakness or numbness in an arm or leg
- Trouble speaking or seeing
- Weakness on both sides of the face
- A very bad headache
- Trouble walking or bad dizziness

handouts.title: Tremor
handouts.text:
Tremor

A tremor is shaking you cannot control. Your tremor is most likely ***. It is not dangerous, but it can make daily tasks hard.

Things that can help:

- Cut back on caffeine, like coffee, tea, energy drinks, and soda.
- Get enough sleep. Being tired can make shaking worse.
- If stress makes it worse, try relaxation, like slow breathing.
- Use weighted forks and spoons with large handles.
- Wear a heavier watch or bracelet. This can calm hand shaking.
- Fill cups only half full, or use a lid and straw.
- Use slip-on shoes, Velcro, or button hooks.

About alcohol: A small amount of alcohol may calm shaking for a short time. Do not use alcohol to treat your tremor.

Your medicine:

- Take *** as prescribed.
- Do not stop, start, or change any medicine on your own.
- Tell us if you think a medicine is making your shaking worse.

Call the clinic if:

- Your tremor makes daily tasks hard
- You have side effects from your medicine, like dizziness, feeling very tired, or feeling down
- You have new shaking at rest, slow movement, or stiffness

Call 911 if you have sudden weakness, numbness, or trouble speaking.

handouts.title: Painful periods
handouts.text:
Painful periods

Period cramps are common. They come from natural chemicals made in the uterus. Medicine and home care can help a lot.

Pain medicine:

- Take *** by mouth ***.
- Start it the day before your period is due, or at the first sign of pain.
- Keep taking it on a schedule for the first 2 to 3 days of your period.
- Ask us first if you have ulcers, asthma, liver disease, a bleeding problem, or aspirin allergy.

Hormone birth control can also help:

- Pills, the patch, and the ring can ease period pain.
- The implant, the shot, and the hormonal IUD can help too.
- Your plan: ***.

At home:

- Put a heating pad or hot water bottle on your lower belly.
- Never fall asleep with a heating pad on.
- Take a warm bath or shower.
- Exercise most days. Walking, biking, and swimming all help.
- Get enough sleep before and during your period.
- Try yoga, meditation, or other ways to relax.

Acupressure you can try:

- Find the spot on the inside of your lower leg, 4 finger widths above the inner ankle bone.
- Press firmly with your thumb for 6 seconds, then rest 2 seconds. Keep this up for 5 minutes on each leg.
- Skip this spot if you are pregnant.
- It may ease cramps. Use it along with your other treatments.

Call the clinic if:

- Your pain is not better after 3 months of treatment.
- Pain starts more than 5 days before your period or lasts after it ends.
- You have pain at other times of the month.
- You got an IUD more than 3 months ago and still have pain.
- You pass clots or have other new symptoms.

Call right away or go to the ER if you have:

- Fever with pelvic pain
- Bad-smelling discharge
- Sudden, severe pain, especially if your period is late and you have had sex

handouts.title: PMS and PMDD
handouts.text:
PMS and PMDD

PMS is mood and body changes in the days before your period. PMDD is a severe form that affects work, school, or relationships. Treatment can help.

Track your symptoms:

- Each day, write down your symptoms and rate how bad they are.
- Also write down the days of your period.
- Do this for at least 2 months. Bring your notes to your next visit.

What helps:

- Exercise at least 30 minutes most days, not only when you have symptoms.
- Go to bed and wake up at the same times every day.
- Eat whole grains, brown rice, beans, and lentils.
- Eat calcium-rich foods, like yogurt and leafy greens.
- Cut back on fat, salt, sugar, caffeine, and alcohol.
- Eat 6 small meals a day instead of 3 big ones.
- Try deep breathing, meditation, yoga, or massage.
- Taking 1,200 mg of calcium a day can ease mood and body symptoms.

Treatments that can help:

- Antidepressants called SSRIs can help mood symptoms. They often work within a few days.
- Some people take them every day. Others take them only in the days before and early in their period.
- Some birth control pills can also ease symptoms.
- Talk therapy, called CBT, can help with mood symptoms.

Your medicine: ***.

Call the clinic if:

- Side effects from your medicine bother you.
- Your symptoms last all month, not just before your period.
- You are not better after *** months.

Call or text 988, or go to the ER, if you have thoughts of hurting yourself.

handouts.title: Endometriosis
handouts.text:
Endometriosis

Endometriosis is when tissue like the lining of the uterus grows outside the uterus. It can cause painful periods, pain with sex, and pain when you pee or poop. It can also make it harder to get pregnant.

You do not need surgery to start treatment. We can treat you based on your symptoms and exam.

Tests:

- An ultrasound through the vagina is the best first imaging test.
- A normal ultrasound does not rule it out. Small spots may not show up.
- Sometimes an MRI is needed.

Treatment:

- Your medicine: ***.
- Pain medicines like ibuprofen or naproxen can ease pain.
- Birth control pills, the patch, or the ring can ease pain. You can use them to have fewer periods or none.
- Progestin pills, the shot, the implant, or the hormonal IUD can also help.
- Other medicines lower estrogen and shrink the tissue. They can cause hot flashes and bone loss.
- Medicine controls pain for many people, but it does not cure endometriosis.
- Pain often comes back when medicine stops.

Surgery:

- Surgery, called laparoscopy, can confirm endometriosis and remove it.
- It may help if medicine does not work or you want a sure answer.
- Pain can come back after surgery. Taking hormone medicine afterward may help.

Tell us if you want to get pregnant. Some treatments prevent pregnancy while you take them.

Call the clinic if:

- Your pain is not better after *** months of treatment.
- Side effects from your medicine bother you.
- You have been trying to get pregnant without success.

Go to the ER if you have sudden, severe belly pain or pain with fever.

handouts.title: Yeast infection
handouts.text:
Vaginal yeast infection

A yeast infection can cause itching, soreness, discharge, and burning when you pee. It is not a sexually transmitted infection.

Your medicine: ***.

- Fluconazole pill: take 1 pill by mouth one time.
- Vaginal cream or suppository: use it every day for all the days prescribed, even if you feel better.
- Creams and suppositories are oily. They can weaken latex condoms and diaphragms.
- Your partner does not need treatment. A male partner with an itchy rash on the penis can see a doctor.

If you are pregnant:

- Use only a vaginal cream or suppository, for 7 days.
- Do not take the fluconazole pill.

If yeast keeps coming back, 3 or more times in a year:

- We may test to find the type of yeast.
- You may take a fluconazole pill once a week for 6 months.
- If you have diabetes, keeping your blood sugar in range helps.
- Tell us if you take antibiotics often. They can bring on yeast infections.

Do not keep treating yourself with store-bought yeast medicine. Other infections can look like yeast.

Call the clinic if:

- You are not better after treatment.
- It comes back within 2 months.
- You have sores, pelvic pain, fever, or bad-smelling discharge.

Go to the ER if you have bad belly pain with fever.

handouts.title: Abnormal Pap test
handouts.text:
Abnormal Pap test

Your Pap or HPV test showed: ***. Abnormal results are common. Most cell changes are not cancer.

About HPV:

- HPV is a very common virus spread through sex.
- In 9 out of 10 people, HPV goes away on its own within 2 years.
- Some types of HPV can cause cell changes on the cervix.
- Follow-up tests find these changes early, so they can be treated before cancer forms.
- Condoms lower the chance of HPV, but they do not fully protect.

Your next step: ***

What each step means:

- A repeat test looks for HPV or cell changes again.
- A colposcopy is an office exam of the cervix with a magnifying lens. A tiny tissue sample may be taken.
- Treatment removes the abnormal area of the cervix.

What you can do:

- Keep every follow-up visit. This is the most important step.
- If you smoke, quit. Smoking raises the risk of cervical cancer.
- Get the HPV vaccine if you are 26 or younger and have not finished it.
- If you are 27 to 45, ask us if the vaccine is right for you.
- Tell us if you are pregnant. Most follow-up can still be done.

Your next visit: ***.

Call the clinic if:

- You have not heard about your next step within 2 weeks.
- You need to change a follow-up visit.
- You have bleeding after sex or between periods.

handouts.title: Bladder leaks
handouts.text:
Bladder leaks

Leaking urine is common. Simple exercises and habits help many people leak less.

Pelvic floor exercises, called Kegels:

These exercises make the muscles that hold in urine stronger.

- Find the muscles: pretend to stop your pee or hold in gas.
- Keep your belly, thighs, and buttocks relaxed.
- Empty your bladder first. Then sit or lie down.
- Squeeze the muscles and hold for 3 to 5 seconds. Then relax for 3 to 5 seconds.
- Do this 10 times in a row, 3 times a day.
- Over time, try to hold each squeeze longer, up to 10 seconds.
- Do not do them while you pee, except once or twice to find the muscles.
- You should leak less in 4 to 6 weeks. Full benefit can take a few months.
- Keep doing them. Leaks can come back if you stop.

Bladder training, for sudden strong urges:

- Keep a bladder diary for 3 days. Write down what you drink, when you pee, and when you leak.
- Pee on a schedule, every *** hours, even if you do not feel the urge.
- When an urge hits, stand or sit still. Squeeze your pelvic muscles quickly a few times.
- Wait for the urge to pass. Then walk calmly to the bathroom.
- Slowly stretch the time between bathroom trips by 30 to 60 minutes.
- The goal is to go every 3 to 4 hours without leaking.

Healthy habits:

- Drink about 50 to 70 ounces of fluid a day, spread out. Do not cut back too much.
- Drink less in the evening.
- Cut back on coffee, tea, soda, and other fizzy or caffeine drinks.
- Limit alcohol.
- Eat fiber and drink fluids to prevent constipation.
- If you smoke, quit.
- If you are overweight, losing weight can mean fewer leaks.

Your medicine: ***.

Call the clinic if:

- You see blood in your urine.
- It burns when you pee, or you have a fever.
- You feel a bulge in your vagina.
- You only dribble or feel your bladder does not empty.
- Leaks are not better after *** months.

Go to the ER if you cannot pee at all and your belly hurts.

handouts.title: Low testosterone
handouts.text:
Low testosterone

Testosterone is the main male hormone. Low levels can cause symptoms like low sex drive. But these symptoms also have many other causes.

Testing:

- Testosterone levels change during the day, so we check them in the early morning.
- We need 2 low morning tests on different days before treatment.
- We also check other hormones, your blood count, and sometimes PSA, a prostate test.

Before you start treatment:

- Testosterone stops your body from making sperm.
- Do not use it if you want to have a baby soon. Tell us, because there are other options.
- Do not use it if you have prostate or breast cancer.

Your treatment: ***.

If you use testosterone gel:

- Put it on clean, dry skin of your shoulders and upper arms each morning.
- Wash your hands with soap and water right after.
- Let it dry, then cover the skin with a shirt.
- Wait at least 2 hours before you shower or swim.
- Do not let children or women touch the skin where you put the gel. It can cause harmful changes in them.

If you get shots: you will get a shot in the muscle every *** weeks.

Follow-up:

- We will check your testosterone level and blood count after you start, then at least once a year.
- Testosterone can raise your red blood cell count too high. Blood tests check for this.
- If you do not feel better in 3 to 6 months, we will likely stop it.

Call the clinic if:

- A child or woman around you gets new body hair, acne, or other body changes.
- You have trouble peeing.
- Your breasts swell or get tender.

Go to the ER if you have:

- Pain, swelling, warmth, or redness in one leg
- Sudden shortness of breath or chest pain

handouts.title: Hemorrhoids
handouts.text:
Hemorrhoids

Hemorrhoids are swollen veins in and around your bottom. They can itch, hurt, or bleed. Most get better with home care.

What to do:

- Eat more fiber, like fruits, vegetables, beans, and whole grains.
- A fiber supplement like psyllium can help. Take it with a full glass of water.
- Drink plenty of water every day.
- Do not strain. Do not sit on the toilet for a long time.
- Sit in a few inches of warm water for 10 to 15 minutes to ease pain.
- Hydrocortisone cream can ease pain, itching, and swelling. Do not use it more than 2 weeks at a time.
- Witch hazel on a cotton ball can ease itching.
- Wear cotton underwear. Use plain wipes instead of scented toilet paper.

Bleeding from your bottom can have other causes. Tell us about any bleeding.

Call the clinic if:

- Home care does not help after *** weeks.
- You have new bleeding from your bottom.

Go to the ER if:

- You lose a lot of blood.
- You are bleeding and feel dizzy, lightheaded, or faint.

handouts.title: Anal fissure
handouts.text:
Anal fissure

An anal fissure is a small tear in the skin at the opening of your bottom. It can cause sharp pain and a little bleeding with bowel movements. Most heal with home care.

What to do:

- Eat more fiber, like fruits, vegetables, and whole grains.
- Take a fiber supplement like psyllium with a full glass of water.
- Drink more fluids to keep stools soft.
- A stool softener can help prevent hard stools.
- Do not hold in bowel movements. Holding it in makes stool harder.
- Sit in warm water 2 to 3 times a day for 10 to 15 minutes. The water should cover only your hips and bottom.

Medicine:

- Use *** on the area *** times a day for *** weeks.
- Nitroglycerin ointment can cause headaches.
- Do not use nitroglycerin with erection pills like sildenafil or tadalafil.

Keep taking fiber after the tear heals. This helps keep it from coming back.

Call the clinic if:

- Pain or bleeding is not better after *** weeks.
- You get bad headaches from the ointment.

Go to the ER if you lose a lot of blood or feel faint.

handouts.title: Diverticulosis
handouts.text:
Diverticulosis

Diverticulosis means small pouches have formed in the wall of your colon. Most people have no symptoms. Fiber and healthy habits help prevent problems.

What to do:

- Eat more fiber from fruits, vegetables, beans, and whole grains.
- Many adults need about 28 grams of fiber a day. Your goal is *** grams.
- Add fiber slowly over a few weeks. This helps prevent gas and bloating.
- A fiber supplement like psyllium can help you reach your goal.
- You do not need to avoid nuts, seeds, or popcorn.
- Eat less red meat.
- Be active most days, stay at a healthy weight, and do not smoke.
- Ask us before you take pain pills like ibuprofen or naproxen often.

Call the clinic right away if you have any bleeding from your bottom, even a small amount.

Call the clinic the same day if you have:

- Belly pain, most often on the lower left side
- Fever or chills
- Nausea or vomiting

Go to the ER if you have a lot of blood in the toilet or feel faint.

handouts.title: H. pylori treatment
handouts.text:
H. pylori treatment

H. pylori is a germ that lives in the stomach. It can cause ulcers and raise the risk of stomach cancer. Treatment kills the germ.

How to take your medicines:

- Your medicines are: ***.
- Take all of your pills for 14 days, even if you feel better.
- Take the acid pill 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast and dinner.
- Do not drink alcohol while taking metronidazole and for 3 days after. The mix can cause vomiting and flushing.

What to expect:

- Bismuth can turn your stool and tongue dark or black. This is harmless and goes away.
- Mild upset stomach is common.

Test to make sure the germ is gone:

- You need a breath or stool test after treatment.
- Do this test at least 4 weeks after your last antibiotic.
- Stop your acid pill 2 weeks before the test. You may use antacids or famotidine instead.
- Your test date: ***.
- Adults who live with you may need testing too. Ask us.

Call the clinic if you cannot take the pills because of side effects.

Go to the ER if you have:

- Black, sticky, tar-like stools with dizziness
- Vomiting blood
- Severe belly pain

handouts.title: Celiac disease
handouts.text:
Celiac disease

Celiac disease means gluten damages your small intestine. Gluten is a protein in wheat, barley, and rye. The treatment is a gluten-free diet for life.

Foods with gluten:

- Wheat, including durum, semolina, and spelt
- Barley, malt, malt vinegar, and brewer's yeast
- Rye and triticale
- Most beer, ale, and malt drinks

Gluten can hide in:

- Soups, salad dressing, and condiments
- Hot dogs, sausages, candy, and ice cream
- Foods with added flavorings, starches, or thickeners

Safe foods:

- Plain meat, fish, fruits, vegetables, rice, and potatoes
- Corn, quinoa, buckwheat, and flours made from rice, potato, beans, or nuts
- Oats only if labeled gluten-free. Ask us how much is OK.

Tips:

- Read every food label. Look for the words "gluten-free."
- If you are not sure a food is safe, do not eat it.
- Store and make your gluten-free food apart from other food.
- See a dietitian. They can help you shop, cook, and eat out.
- Ask your parents, brothers, sisters, and children to get tested.
- You will need checkups and blood tests on ***.

Call the clinic if your symptoms come back or do not get better on the diet.

handouts.title: Vitamin D
handouts.text:
Vitamin D

Vitamin D helps your body use calcium to keep your bones strong. Your level was low at ***.

How to take it:

- Take vitamin D3 *** IU by mouth ***.
- After *** weeks, take *** IU by mouth each day.
- We will recheck your level on ***.

Foods with vitamin D:

- Fatty fish like salmon, trout, and tuna
- Milk and plant milks with vitamin D added
- Cereals, orange juice, and yogurt with vitamin D added
- Some store mushrooms grown under UV light
- Egg yolks and cheese have small amounts.

Sun and vitamin D:

- Your skin makes vitamin D when it is in direct sun.
- Dark skin, shade, and clouds mean your skin makes less.
- Sun can cause skin cancer. Do not stay in the sun more than a few minutes without sunscreen.

Vitamin D and colds:

- Vitamin D helps your immune system fight germs.
- But vitamin D pills have not been shown to prevent colds.

Too much can harm you:

- Do not take more than your dose unless we tell you.
- Very high doses can raise the calcium in your blood.
- Tell us about any other pills you take that have vitamin D or calcium.

Call the clinic if you have questions about your dose.

handouts.title: Vitamin B12
handouts.text:
Vitamin B12

Vitamin B12 helps make red blood cells and keeps nerves healthy. Your level was low. Low B12 can cause tiredness, numbness, or tingling.

How to take it:

- Take vitamin B12 *** mcg by mouth each day.
- Or get B12 shots on this schedule: ***.
- High-dose pills work as well as shots for most people.
- If the cause cannot be fixed, you will need B12 for life.

Foods with B12:

- Fish, meat, chicken, eggs, milk, and yogurt
- Cereals and nutritional yeast with B12 added
- Plants do not have B12 unless it is added. Vegans need fortified foods or a supplement.

What to expect:

- Blood counts often get better in about 8 weeks.
- Numbness and tingling can take 6 weeks to 3 months to get better.

Some medicines lower B12, like metformin and acid pills. Keep taking them unless we tell you to stop.

Call the clinic if numbness, tingling, or weakness gets worse, or if you have trouble walking.

handouts.title: Kidney stones
handouts.text:
Kidney stones

A kidney stone is a hard piece that forms in the kidney. Most small stones pass on their own in the urine.

While you pass the stone:

- Drink plenty of water.
- Take *** for pain as directed.
- Take tamsulosin *** each day if prescribed. It helps the stone pass.
- Strain your urine to catch the stone. Bring it to us for testing.

To prevent new stones:

- Drink about 85 ounces (2.5 liters) of water each day.
- Water is best. Limit soda.
- Eat less salt and fewer processed and canned foods.
- Do not cut out calcium. Get calcium from food, like 2 to 3 servings of dairy a day.
- Eat less meat. Eat more fruits and vegetables.
- If you have calcium oxalate stones, limit spinach, beets, nuts, and tea.
- Do not take extra vitamin C or calcium pills unless we tell you.

Call the clinic if you have:

- Pain that does not get better with your medicine
- Burning when you pee, or cloudy or bad-smelling urine
- Vomiting

Go to the ER if you have fever or chills with stone pain, or you cannot keep fluids down.

handouts.title: Muscle aches on statins
handouts.text:
Muscle aches on statins

Statins lower cholesterol and help prevent heart attacks and strokes. Some people get muscle aches on them. Serious muscle damage is rare.

What to know:

- Do not stop your statin on your own. Talk with us first.
- Many people with aches on one statin do fine on another one or a lower dose.
- Some people do well taking a statin less often, like every other day.
- Aches can also come from thyroid problems, low vitamin D, hard exercise, or heavy drinking.
- Grapefruit and grapefruit juice can change how some statins work. Ask us before having them.
- If statins do not work for you, other cholesterol medicines can help.

Your plan: ***

Call the clinic if you have muscle pain, cramps, or weakness that does not go away.

Go to the ER if you have:

- Dark, red, or cola-colored urine
- Severe muscle pain or weakness
- Much less urine than normal

handouts.title: High triglycerides
handouts.text:
High triglycerides

Triglycerides are a type of fat in your blood. Yours were ***. Normal is below 150. Very high levels, often over 1,000, can inflame the pancreas.

What to do:

- Cut back on sugar, sweet drinks, sweets, and white bread, rice, and pasta.
- Limit alcohol. If your level is 500 or higher, do not drink any alcohol.
- If your level is very high, you may need a very low-fat diet. A dietitian can help.
- Use healthy fats like olive oil, nuts, and fish instead of butter and fatty meat.
- If you are overweight, losing 5 to 10 percent of your weight helps.
- Be active at least 150 minutes a week. Add strength exercises 2 days a week.
- Do not smoke.
- Take *** as prescribed.

We will recheck your triglycerides on ***.

Call the clinic if you have questions about your diet or medicines.

Go to the ER if you have severe belly pain that spreads to your back, with nausea or vomiting.

handouts.title: Safer drug use
handouts.text:
Safer drug use

If you use drugs, these steps can help keep you alive and healthy. We will not judge you. We are here to help when you are ready.

What naloxone is and how to get it:

- Naloxone is a medicine that can reverse an opioid overdose, including fentanyl.
- The nasal spray is sold over the counter. You do not need a prescription.
- You can buy it at most pharmacies.
- People in Oklahoma can get free naloxone by mail at okimready.org/overdose.
- Free kits near you: ***
- Keep naloxone on you and at home. Show your friends and family where it is.

Signs of an overdose:

- Will not wake up
- Slow, shallow, or no breathing
- Choking, gurgling, or snoring sounds
- Lips or fingernails that turn blue, gray, or pale
- Very small pupils, the black centers of the eyes

How to give naloxone nasal spray:

- Lay the person on their back. Support the neck so the head tilts back.
- Put the tip of the nozzle in one nostril.
- Press the plunger firmly to give the dose.
- Call 911.
- Roll the person onto their side so they do not choke.
- If they do not wake up or breathe better in 2 to 3 minutes, give a second dose.
- Use a new spray in the other nostril for the second dose.
- Stay with the person until help arrives.

Never use alone:

- Use with someone who has naloxone and can call 911.
- Take turns, so one person is always alert.
- If you use alone, call the Never Use Alone line first: 1-800-484-3731.
- That line is private and open 24 hours a day. If you stop answering, they send help to your address.

Test your drugs:

- Fentanyl test strips show if fentanyl is in pills, powder, or drugs you inject.
- They do not show how much fentanyl is there.
- A negative test does not mean the drug is safe. No test is 100 percent right.
- Fentanyl test strips are legal to carry in Oklahoma.
- Xylazine test strips are a separate test. Fentanyl strips do not find xylazine.
- Xylazine strips can show a false positive when the drug has cocaine in it.

Do not mix drugs:

- Opioids mixed with alcohol or other downers can slow or stop your breathing.
- Benzos, or nerve pills like alprazolam and clonazepam, are downers. Do not mix them with opioids.
- Mixing uppers, like meth or cocaine, with opioids is also dangerous.

Start low and go slow:

- Start low after a break, like time in jail, rehab, or detox. Your tolerance drops.
- After a break, an amount you used before can cause an overdose.
- Start low with every new batch. Street drugs have no label, so strength is unknown.
- Use a much smaller amount, and wait before using more.

Needles and supplies:

- Use a new, sterile needle and syringe every time.
- Do not share needles, cookers, cotton, or water. Sharing spreads HIV and hepatitis C.
- Put used needles in a sharps container or a hard plastic bottle with a tight lid.
- Ask us where to get free sterile supplies: ***

Xylazine and wounds:

- Xylazine is an animal sedative. It is often mixed with fentanyl and other drugs.
- Naloxone does not reverse xylazine. Still give naloxone and call 911 for any overdose.
- Xylazine can cause wounds that get infected and worse quickly.
- Wounds that are not treated can lead to losing a limb.
- Get wound care early. Early wounds are easier to treat.

Calling 911 in Oklahoma:

- Oklahoma law protects the person who calls 911 for an overdose from arrest for drug possession.
- It also covers drug supplies, like needles or pipes.
- To be protected, give your name, stay with the person, and help the responders.
- It does not cover very large amounts of drugs.

Treatment when you are ready:

- Buprenorphine and methadone are medicines that treat opioid addiction.
- People who take these medicines are less likely to overdose or die.
- We can start treatment here or refer you: ***
- Free, private help any time: SAMHSA National Helpline, 1-800-662-4357.

We also offer tests for HIV and hepatitis, and vaccines for hepatitis A and B.

Call the clinic if you want help cutting back or stopping, or you have a wound that is not healing.

If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, call or text 988.

Call 911 if someone will not wake up or is not breathing well. Give naloxone too.

handouts.title: Gun safety
handouts.text:
Gun safety

If you have guns at home, safe handling and storage protect you and your family. These tips come from hunter education courses and children's doctors.

The 5 rules of gun safety:

- Treat every gun as if it is loaded, even if you just unloaded it.
- Never point a gun at anything you do not plan to shoot.
- Keep your finger off the trigger until you are ready to shoot.
- Be sure of your target and what is behind it. A bullet can go through or miss.
- Store guns unloaded and locked. Lock the ammunition in a separate place.

Safe storage with children and teens:

- Lock every gun, unloaded, in a gun safe or lock box.
- Lock the ammunition in a different place.
- Keep keys and codes where children cannot get them.
- Never leave a loaded, unlocked gun in the car or anywhere else.
- Do not count on hiding a gun. Many children know where guns are kept.

What to teach your children:

- If you see a gun, do not touch it.
- Leave the area right away.
- Tell an adult.

Teaching alone does not keep children safe. Locked storage is what protects them.

Before your child visits another home:

- Ask, "Is there an unlocked gun in your house?"
- Ask it the same way you ask about pets or allergies.
- If you do not like the answer, invite the children to play at your house instead.

A suicide attempt with a gun is much more likely to end in death. Moving guns out of the home for a while can save a life.

If someone at home is in crisis or thinking about suicide:

- Store all guns outside the home until the crisis passes.
- A trusted friend or relative, a gun shop, a range, or the police may store them. Call first.
- Storage options near you: ***
- If guns must stay home, lock them unloaded, with the ammunition locked separately.
- Call or text 988 for help any time.

Cleaning your gun:

- Point the gun in a safe direction and unload it completely before you clean it.
- Check a second time that it is unloaded.
- Clean in a room with good air flow.
- Wash your hands well after cleaning. Lead from ammunition can get on your hands.

When you shoot:

- Do not drink alcohol or use drugs before or while shooting. They slow your judgment and reflexes.
- Wear eye and ear protection.
- Check that the barrel is clear before shooting.
- Use only the right ammunition for your gun.
- Wash your hands after shooting, before you eat or drink.

Call the clinic if you want to talk about safe storage or someone's safety at home.

Call or text 988 if you or someone else is thinking about suicide.

Call 911 if someone is in danger right now or has been shot.

handouts.title: Staying safe at work
handouts.text:
Staying safe at work

Your job can affect your health. You have the right to a safe workplace, and we can help.

Your rights at work:

- Safety training in a language you understand
- Labels and safety data sheets for chemicals you work with
- Safety equipment the job requires, like gloves, goggles, or a harness
- Safety equipment that fits you. Your employer pays for most required equipment.
- Seeing results of tests done to find hazards at your job
- Reporting an injury or illness, and getting copies of your medical records
- Filing a private complaint with OSHA if your job is unsafe
- Using these rights without being fired, demoted, or punished

What a safety data sheet tells you:

- The dangers of each chemical
- How to handle and store it safely
- What safety equipment to wear
- What to do if it gets on you or you breathe it in

If you get hurt or sick from work:

- Tell your boss right away. Waiting more than 30 days can hurt your claim.
- Get medical care. Tell the doctor or nurse that it happened at work.
- Write down what happened, when, where, and who saw it.
- Ask about workers' compensation. It may pay for your care and some lost pay.
- Workers' compensation help: ***

Tell your doctor about your job:

- What you do and how long you have done it
- Chemicals, dust, fumes, noise, or heat at work
- Heavy lifting or the same motion over and over
- Symptoms that get worse at work or better on days off

Bring safety data sheets to your visit if you can.

Call OSHA at 1-800-321-6742 to report unsafe work or ask about your rights.

Call the clinic if you think your job is making you sick.

Call 911 for a serious injury, trouble breathing, or chest pain.

handouts.title: Chemicals and pesticides at work
handouts.text:
Chemicals and pesticides at work

Many jobs use chemicals that can harm your skin, lungs, and nerves. Simple steps protect you and your family.

Common chemicals at work:

- Solvents in paints, glues, thinners, and degreasers
- Cleaning products, like bleach and ammonia cleaners
- Pesticides on farms, lawns, and in buildings
- Anhydrous ammonia fertilizer on farms

How chemicals get into your body:

- Breathing in fumes, vapors, mists, or dust
- Through your skin, often without you noticing
- Swallowing, from dirty hands, food, or drinks

How to protect yourself:

- Read the label and the safety data sheet before using a chemical.
- Wear the gloves, goggles, or respirator the safety data sheet calls for.
- Work where there is fresh air or fans.
- Never mix cleaning products, especially ones with bleach. Bleach and ammonia make a poison gas.
- Do not eat, drink, or smoke where chemicals are used.
- Wash your hands before you eat, drink, or smoke.
- Stay out of a sprayed field until the wait time on the pesticide label is over.
- Around anhydrous ammonia, keep clean water close by and do not wear contact lenses.

How to keep chemicals out of your home:

- Change your clothes and shoes before you leave work.
- Shower before you go home if you can.
- Keep dirty work clothes away from clean clothes.
- Wash work clothes apart from your family's laundry.
- If you cannot change at work, take off work shoes outside and change as soon as you get home.

If a chemical gets on you:

- Skin: take off soaked clothes and rinse your skin with lots of water.
- Eyes: rinse with clean water for at least 15 minutes. Hold your eyelids open.
- Breathing it in: get to fresh air right away.
- Call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 for advice.

Symptoms that need care:

- Headache, dizziness, or upset stomach at work
- Heavy sweating, blurry vision, or watery eyes after working with pesticides
- Belly cramps or diarrhea after working with pesticides
- Rash, itching, or dry, cracked skin
- Cough, wheezing, or trouble breathing

Call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 any time a chemical gets on you or in you.

Call the clinic if you have symptoms at work, or symptoms that get better on days off.

Call 911 if someone has trouble breathing, a seizure, passes out, or is confused.

handouts.title: Lead at work and home
handouts.text:
Lead at work and home

Lead is a metal that can harm your brain, nerves, kidneys, and blood. No amount of lead is safe. Lead from work can also harm your children.

Jobs and hobbies with lead:

- Construction, demolition, and bridge work
- Fixing, sanding, or painting homes built before 1978
- Making or recycling batteries
- Radiator repair
- Working or shooting at a firing range
- Welding, torch cutting, and soldering
- Casting bullets or fishing weights

How to protect yourself at work:

- Wash your hands before you eat, drink, or smoke.
- Do not eat, drink, or smoke in work areas.
- Wear a clean respirator that fits you.

Lead dust rides home on clothes, shoes, and hair. It can poison your children.

How to keep lead out of your home:

- Change your clothes and shoes before you go home.
- Shower before you go home if you can.
- Keep work items, like toolboxes and lunch coolers, in the trunk of your car.
- Wash work clothes apart from other laundry.

Fixing an older home:

- Paint in homes built before 1978 may have lead.
- Sanding, scraping, or cutting old paint makes lead dust.
- Hire a contractor who is EPA lead-safe certified. Ask to see proof.
- Keep children and pregnant women away from the work area.

Symptoms of lead poisoning:

- Belly pain, upset stomach, or constipation
- Feeling very tired
- Trouble thinking or focusing
- Joint pain
- Mood changes
- Hearing loss

Many people have no symptoms at all. A blood test is the only way to know.

Blood lead testing:

- If you work with lead, ask us for a blood lead test.
- Your employer may have to offer you blood lead tests at work.
- If your level is high, your children and others at home should be tested too.
- Your result: ***
- Your next test: ***

Pregnancy:

- Lead passes to your baby during pregnancy.
- It can harm your baby's brain and nerves. It can also cause miscarriage or stillbirth.
- Tell us if you work with lead and are pregnant or trying to get pregnant.
- We may advise you to stay away from lead work while you are pregnant.

Call the clinic if you have symptoms, work with lead, or want your family tested.

handouts.title: Silica dust
handouts.text:
Silica dust

Silica is a mineral in sand, stone, concrete, and brick. Cutting, drilling, or grinding these makes a fine dust. Breathing it can cause lung disease that lasts for life.

Jobs with silica dust:

- Oil and gas work with fracking sand
- Construction work that cuts, drills, or grinds concrete, brick, or stone
- Making stone countertops, especially engineered stone, also called quartz
- Mining and quarry work
- Sandblasting
- Foundry work

Health risks:

- Silicosis, which scars the lungs. The damage cannot be undone.
- Severe silicosis, and even death, in workers who cut engineered stone countertops
- Lung cancer
- COPD, a long-term lung disease
- Kidney disease
- Tuberculosis, also called TB. Silica raises your risk.

Signs of silicosis:

- Cough
- Shortness of breath
- Feeling very tired
- Chest pain

You can have lung damage with no signs at first. That is why checkups matter.

How to protect your lungs:

- Cut wet. Use water on the blade or tool to keep dust down.
- Use tools with a vacuum or exhaust that pulls dust away where it is made.
- Wear a respirator that fits when dust is still in the air.
- Use at least an N95 respirator around silica dust.
- Get fit tested and trained on your respirator.

Health checkups:

- Ask about regular checkups if you work with silica.
- Checkups may include a chest x-ray, a breathing test, and a TB test.
- Finding silicosis early lets you avoid more dust and slow the damage.

Call the clinic if you have a cough or shortness of breath that does not go away.

Call 911 for severe trouble breathing or chest pain.

handouts.title: Heat illness at work
handouts.text:
Heat illness at work

Working in heat can make you very sick. Heat stroke can kill. Water, rest, shade, and time to adjust keep you safe.

Water, rest, and shade:

- Drink 1 cup (8 ounces) of water every 15 to 20 minutes, even if you are not thirsty.
- Do not drink more than 6 cups (48 ounces) in an hour.
- Avoid alcohol and drinks with a lot of caffeine or sugar.
- Take breaks often in the shade or a cool place.

Get used to the heat slowly:

- New workers should work only 20 percent of a normal day in the heat on day 1.
- Add about 20 percent more each day.
- It takes 1 to 2 weeks for your body to adjust.
- After a week or more away from hot work, build up slowly again.

Watch out for each other:

- Use a buddy system. Check each other for signs of heat illness.
- New workers should not work alone in the heat.
- Anyone with signs of heat illness should stop work and never be left alone.

Things that raise your risk:

- Being new to hot work
- Some medicines and drugs
- Alcohol
- Being overweight or out of shape
- Heavy protective clothing or gear

Ask us if any of your medicines raise your risk.

Signs of heat exhaustion:

- Headache
- Nausea
- Dizziness or weakness
- Heavy sweating
- Feeling hot

What to do for heat exhaustion:

- Move to a cool place and sip water.
- Cool off with cold, wet cloths.
- Go to a clinic or the ER. Call 911 if you cannot get to care.
- Have someone stay with you.

Signs of heat stroke, an emergency:

- Confusion or slurred speech
- Seizures
- Passing out
- Very high body temperature

What to do for heat stroke:

- Call 911 right away.
- Move the person to shade and take off outer clothing.
- Cool them fast with cold water, ice, or cold wet cloths, and fan them.
- Stay with them until help arrives.

Call the clinic if you get heat cramps or heat rash often.

Call 911 for anyone who is confused, has a seizure, or passes out in the heat.

handouts.title: Noise and hearing at work
handouts.text:
Noise and hearing at work

Loud noise at work can damage your hearing for good. This kind of hearing loss can be prevented.

Signs your work is too loud:

- You have to raise your voice to talk to someone 3 feet away.
- You have to shout to be heard at arm's length.
- Your ears ring or hum after work.
- Sounds seem muffled after you leave work.

What your employer must do:

- In most jobs, noise of 85 decibels or more over a workday requires a hearing program.
- The program gives you hearing protection at no cost.
- The program includes a hearing test every year.

How to protect your hearing:

- Wear earplugs or earmuffs every time you are in loud noise.
- Ask to be shown how to put earplugs in the right way.
- Use quieter tools, or move away from noise, when you can.
- Protect your ears off the job too, like when shooting guns.

Hearing damage from noise is permanent. Hearing aids help, but they do not bring back normal hearing.

Hearing tests:

- Get your yearly hearing test at work if you are in a hearing program.
- Ask for copies of your results.
- Ask us for a hearing test if you notice changes. Your plan: ***

Call the clinic if your ears ring or your hearing seems worse.

Call the clinic right away if you suddenly lose hearing in one or both ears. Fast treatment works best.

handouts.title: Using AI chatbots safely
handouts.text:
Using AI chatbots safely

AI chatbots can answer questions fast. They can also be wrong, even when they sound sure. Use them with care.

Why AI health advice can be wrong:

- Chatbots can make up facts and still sound sure.
- Many chatbots are built to agree with you, even when you are wrong.
- Many learn from the internet, not from checked medical sources.
- A chatbot cannot see you, examine you, or diagnose you.

Use AI health advice safely:

- Bring AI answers to your visit and ask us about them.
- Talk with your clinician before you stop or change any medicine.
- Do not use a chatbot in place of your doctor or therapist.

In an emergency or crisis:

- Call 911 for a medical emergency. Do not ask a chatbot first.
- Call or text 988 if you think about suicide or feel in crisis. Help is free, 24 hours a day.
- Do not rely on a chatbot in a crisis. It may not respond safely.

Chats may feel private, but what you type may be saved. Some companies may use chats to build their AI.

Protect your privacy:

- Do not type your full name, birth date, address, or Social Security number.
- Do not share insurance numbers or test results that show your name.
- Check the app's privacy settings. Limit data sharing if you can.
- Ask the company to delete your data if it offers that option.

AI friends and companions:

- Some chatbots act like a friend or partner. They can feel very real.
- A relationship with a chatbot is one-sided, even if it feels real.
- Some teens have formed unhealthy, even dangerous, bonds with chatbots.
- Chatbots can give wrong or harmful advice about feelings, health, or safety.

Tips for teens and parents:

- Keep healthy limits on chatbot friends. Make time for real friends and family.
- Parents, ask your teen which AI apps they use and what they talk about.
- Talk together about how AI works, where it can be wrong, and what not to share.
- Tell a trusted adult if a chatbot says something upsetting or unsafe.

AI can also make fake photos, videos, and voices of real people. They can look and sound real.

Spot and avoid fakes:

- Look closely for odd hands, teeth, eyes, shadows, or movement.
- If a family member calls asking for money, hang up and call them back.
- Make your social media accounts private.
- Share photos and voice clips of yourself only with people you know.

Fake nude images are a crime:

- Sharing a nude or sexual image of a real person without consent can be a federal crime.
- This includes fake images made with AI.
- Threatening to share these images is also a crime.

To get images removed:

- Report the image to the app or website.
- Social media and sharing sites must remove it within 48 hours of a valid request.
- If a site does not remove it, report the site at TakeItDown.ftc.gov.
- For images of you before age 18, use Take It Down at takeitdown.ncmec.org.
- If you were 18 or older and have a copy, StopNCII.org can help block it.

Call the clinic:

- If AI gave you health advice and you are not sure it is right
- Before you stop or change any medicine
- If you or your teen feel lonely, or rely on a chatbot for comfort

Call 911 for an emergency. Call or text 988 for a mental health crisis.

handouts.title: Staying safe online
handouts.text:
Staying safe online

The internet helps you learn and connect with friends. A few habits can keep you and your family safe.

Protect your accounts and devices:

- Use long passwords, at least 16 characters. A phrase of 4 to 7 random words works well.
- Use a different password for every account.
- A password manager can make and save strong passwords for you.
- Turn on two-step login for email, social media, and banking.
- With two-step login, a stolen password alone cannot open your account.
- Keep your apps and phone updated.

Protect your privacy and location:

- Check privacy settings before you use a new app.
- Do not post your address, phone number, birth date, or school name.
- Teens, keep location sharing off unless a parent says it is OK.
- Make your social media accounts private.
- Accept friend requests only from people you know in real life.

Think before you post:

- Pictures you post can be copied, changed, or used to find you.
- Do not post photos that show your home, school, or where you are now.
- Scammers can use AI to turn normal photos into fake nude pictures.

Warning signs someone online is not safe:

- They say they are your age, but something seems off.
- They give lots of compliments and act very interested in your life.
- They offer gifts, gift cards, rides, alcohol, or drugs.
- They talk about sex or ask for pictures.
- They ask for nude photos soon after friending you.
- They want to meet you in person.
- They make you feel uncomfortable, pressured, or afraid.

If you see these signs, stop replying and tell a trusted adult. People online can lie about who they are.

Meeting someone from online:

- Never meet someone from online without telling a parent first.
- If a parent says yes, meet in a public place with the parent there.

Sextortion is when someone threatens to share sexual pictures of you. They demand money or more pictures. The FBI warns it often targets boys ages 14 to 17. Scammers may even make fake pictures with AI.

If someone threatens to share your pictures:

- This is a crime. You are the victim. It is not your fault.
- Do not pay and do not send more pictures. Paying rarely stops it.
- Stop replying. Report and block the account.
- Do not delete your messages or profile. They are evidence.
- Tell a parent or another trusted adult right away.
- Report it to NCMEC at report.cybertip.org or call 1-800-843-5678.
- Report it to the FBI at tips.fbi.gov or call 1-800-CALL-FBI.
- Use Take It Down at takeitdown.ncmec.org to help get pictures removed.

If you are bullied online:

- Do not respond to mean messages.
- Save the messages. Take screenshots.
- Block the person.
- Report it to the app or website.
- Tell a parent, teacher, or other adult.
- Report threats of harm to the police.

Tips for parents:

- Make a family media plan together with the free tool at HealthyChildren.org.
- Use parental controls to limit screen time, downloads, contacts, and purchases.
- Set controls on your Wi-Fi router, phones, tablets, game systems, and apps.
- Know who your child texts and talks to online.
- Watch for changes in your child's behavior that you cannot explain.
- If your child is bullied, do not take away their device. They may stop telling you things.
- Listen and support your child when they tell you about a problem.

Call the clinic if your child seems sad, scared, or withdrawn after time online.
Call or text 988 if you or your teen feel hopeless or think about suicide.
Call 911 if someone is in danger right now.

handouts.title: Avoiding scams
handouts.text:
Avoiding scams

Scammers call, text, and email people every day. Knowing their tricks can protect your money and your identity.

Signs of a scam:

- They pretend to be from a company, bank, or government agency you know.
- They say there is a problem with your account, or that you won a prize.
- They push you to act right now.
- They tell you to pay in a certain way, like a gift card, wire transfer, or crypto.

Gift cards and wire transfers:

- Only scammers ask you to pay with a gift card. No real business or agency will.
- Never pay someone who says you can only pay by wire transfer or crypto.

Scam texts and emails:

- Do not click links in texts or emails you did not expect.
- If a message says your account has a problem, contact the company at a number you know is real.
- Forward scam texts to 7726 (SPAM).
- Forward scam emails to reportphishing@apwg.org.

Scammers can use AI to copy a loved one's voice from a short clip online. Then they call asking for money for an emergency.

If a family member calls asking for money:

- Do not trust the voice. Hang up.
- Call your family member back at a number you know is theirs.
- If you cannot reach them, call another family member or friend.
- Pick a secret family code word ahead of time. Ask for it on calls like this.

Fake pop-ups and tech support calls:

- Real security warnings never ask you to call a phone number.
- Tech companies will not call, email, or text you about a computer problem.
- Scammers ask to get into your computer, then pretend to find viruses.

Medicare scams:

- Medicare will not call you to check your card or your number.
- Medicare will never call to sell you anything.
- Do not give your Medicare number to anyone who calls you.
- Share your Medicare number only with your doctor or people you know should have it.
- Offers of a free brace in exchange for your Medicare number are scams.
- Check your monthly Medicare statement for services you did not get.
- Call 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227) if you think there is Medicare fraud.

How to stop sales calls:

- Sign up for the National Do Not Call Registry at DoNotCall.gov.
- Or call 1-888-382-1222 from the phone number you want to sign up.
- It is free, and your sign-up never expires.
- It can take up to 31 days for sales calls to stop.
- Report unwanted sales calls at DoNotCall.gov.

The Do Not Call Registry does not stop:

- Calls from scammers. They ignore the law.
- Political calls
- Calls from charities
- Calls from debt collectors
- Surveys and calls that only give information
- Calls from companies you recently did business with

If you were scammed:

- Call your bank or card company right away. Ask them to reverse the payment.
- If you paid with a gift card, call the number on the card. Keep the card and receipt.
- Change your passwords and turn on two-step login.
- If you gave out your Social Security number, go to IdentityTheft.gov.
- Report the scam at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.
- For free help, call the AARP Fraud Watch Network Helpline at 877-908-3360.
- The helpline is open weekdays, 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. Central time.

Call the clinic if you are not sure a call or bill from us is real.
Call the clinic if a scam leaves you feeling scared, stressed, or unable to sleep.

handouts.title: Elder abuse: know the signs and get help
handouts.text:
Elder abuse: know the signs and get help

Elder abuse is when an older adult is harmed on purpose or neglected. It can happen to anyone. It is never the person's fault.

Who can cause harm:

- A family member, friend, or caregiver
- Staff in a nursing home or assisted living
- Strangers who reach out by phone, mail, email, or the internet

It is often a caregiver or someone the person trusts.

Types of abuse:

- Physical: hitting, kicking, pushing, or other force that hurts the person.
- Emotional: insults, threats, put-downs, or keeping the person away from family and friends.
- Sexual: any sexual contact that is forced, tricked, or unwanted.
- Neglect: a caregiver does not provide food, water, clothing, hygiene, or needed medical care.
- Self-neglect: a person cannot or does not meet their own needs, like food, bathing, medicine, or a clean home.
- Financial: someone steals or misuses the person's money, property, or benefits. Scams by strangers count too.

Warning signs:

- Bruises, cuts, burns, or sores that no one can explain
- Weight loss or signs of not drinking enough
- Missing glasses, walker, or medicines
- Poor hygiene or medical needs that are not cared for
- Torn, stained, or bloody underwear, or a new sexually transmitted infection
- New fear or worry, or changes in sleep or behavior
- Pulling away from friends, family, or usual activities
- Unpaid bills, sudden changes in spending, or signatures that look faked

How to get help:

- Call 911 if someone is in danger right now.
- Call Oklahoma Adult Protective Services at 1-800-522-3511. You can also report online at okhotline.org.
- Call or text the Eldercare Locator at 1-800-677-1116 to find help near you.
- Call the National Elder Fraud Hotline at 1-833-372-8311 for scams against someone 60 or older. It is open on weekdays.
- For problems in a nursing home or assisted living, call the long-term care ombudsman at 1-800-211-2116.
- Tell your doctor or nurse. We can help you make a report.

You do not have to give your name when you report.

Oklahoma law:

In Oklahoma, anyone who thinks a vulnerable adult is being abused, neglected, or exploited must report it. Report as soon as you know. You need a reason to believe it, not proof.

Call the clinic if you have questions or want help making a report.

Call 911 if you or someone else is in danger right now.

handouts.title: Caring for the caregiver
handouts.text:
Caring for the caregiver

Caring for someone you love is important work. It can also be hard on your body and mind. Taking care of yourself is not selfish.

Signs of caregiver stress:

- Feeling so worn out that daily tasks seem too hard
- Trouble sleeping because of worry
- Feeling angry, irritable, or short with the person you care for
- Pulling away from friends and things you used to enjoy
- Worry about the future
- Feeling sad, anxious, or lonely
- Trouble focusing, or forgetting appointments
- New health problems of your own

Many caregivers feel this way. It does not mean you are failing. Tell your doctor if you notice these signs.

Take care of your own health:

- Try to sleep at least 7 hours a night.
- Eat regular meals with lots of fruits and vegetables.
- Move your body. Even a 20-minute walk 3 times a week helps.
- Keep your own doctor visits and checkups.
- Take your own medicines as prescribed.
- Tell your doctor that you are a caregiver.
- Try slow deep breathing or meditation to relax.

Asking for help is a sign of strength. Do not wait until you are overwhelmed.

Ways to get help from others:

- Make a list of tasks others can do, like meals, rides, or errands.
- Ask family or friends to take a set block of time each week.
- Use a shared calendar so helpers can sign up.
- Say yes when people offer to help.

Take a break with respite care:

Respite care gives you a short break while someone else cares for your loved one. Even a few hours a week can help.

- A friend, relative, volunteer, or paid aide can help at home.
- Adult day centers offer activities, and often meals and rides.
- Some care communities offer short overnight stays.

Where to find support:

- Join a support group, in person or online.
- Alzheimer's Association Helpline: call 1-800-272-3900, 24 hours a day, 7 days a week.
- Eldercare Locator: call or text 1-800-677-1116 to find local services.
- Family Caregiver Alliance: caregiver.org has tips and resources for family caregivers.
- VA Caregiver Support Line, for caregivers of veterans: call 1-855-260-3274.

Plan ahead:

- Talk early about wishes, while your loved one can still take part.
- Durable power of attorney: names someone to handle money if your loved one cannot.
- Health care power of attorney: names someone to make medical decisions.
- Living will: says what care your loved one wants if they cannot speak for themselves.
- Give copies to family, the doctor, and the lawyer.
- Laws vary by state. A lawyer can help.

If your loved one has dementia, keep them safe:

- Wandering: use door alarms and keep a recent photo ready.
- If they go missing, search nearby first. Call 911 if they are not found in 15 minutes.
- Driving: watch for getting lost, hitting curbs, or missing traffic signs. Ask the doctor about stopping.
- Car keys: keep them out of reach once your loved one stops driving.
- Guns: remove them from the home, or keep them in a locked cabinet.
- Medicines: keep them locked up. Use a pill box to track each dose.
- Falls: remove throw rugs, cords, and clutter.

Call the clinic if you:

- Feel sad, hopeless, or overwhelmed most days
- Cannot sleep or eat well
- Feel you cannot keep caring for your loved one
- Need help finding respite or support

Call or text 988 any time if you feel you might hurt yourself. It is free and open 24/7.

If you ever feel you might hurt your loved one, call 988 or the clinic right away. You are not alone.

Call 911 if anyone is in danger right now.

handouts.title: Molluscum
handouts.text:
Molluscum

Molluscum is a common skin virus. It causes small, smooth bumps with a dimple in the middle. The bumps are harmless. They usually go away on their own in 6 to 12 months, sometimes longer.

What to do:

- Do not pick, scratch, or squeeze the bumps.
- Cover bumps with clothing or a bandage.
- Wash hands often.
- Do not share towels or clothes.

School and swimming:

- Your child can go to school or daycare.
- Your child can swim if there are no open sores.

Your treatment plan: ***

If you use the gel at home:

- Mix equal amounts from the two tubes.
- Spread a thin layer on each bump once a day.
- Do not put it on normal skin.
- Use it for up to 12 weeks.

If we put blister medicine on the bumps in clinic:

- Do not cover the treated bumps with a bandage.
- Wash it off with soap and water 24 hours later.
- Wash it off sooner if there is a bad blister or bad pain.
- Keep it away from the eyes and mouth.
- Stay away from fire and smoking until it is washed off.

If the medicine gets in the eyes, rinse with water for 15 minutes and get care right away.

Call the clinic if:

- A bump gets red, swollen, painful, or drains pus
- The treated skin has a large blister or bad pain
- The bumps are on the genitals

handouts.title: Genital herpes
handouts.text:
Genital herpes

Genital herpes is a common virus spread by sex. It causes painful sores or blisters. There is no cure, but medicine helps sores heal faster and come back less.

Your medicine: ***

How to use medicine:

- For an outbreak, start medicine within 1 day of the first sore or tingling.
- Keep medicine at home so you can start right away.
- Daily medicine can prevent many outbreaks.
- Daily medicine also lowers the chance of passing herpes to a partner.

Protect your partners:

- Tell your partners before sex.
- Do not have sex when you have sores or tingling.
- Condoms lower the risk but do not remove it.
- Herpes can spread even when you have no sores.
- Your partner can get a blood test for herpes.

If you are pregnant:

- Tell your pregnancy care team you have herpes.
- Daily medicine is advised starting at 36 weeks.
- Tell the hospital if you have sores or tingling when labor starts.

Call the clinic if:

- Sores are not healed after 10 days of medicine
- You have many outbreaks
- You become pregnant

Go to the ER if you have a bad headache with a stiff neck, or confusion.

handouts.title: Fifth disease
handouts.text:
Fifth disease

Fifth disease is caused by a virus. It often starts with bright red cheeks. A lacy rash on the body may follow. Adults may get sore joints instead.

Is it contagious?

- It spreads by coughs and sneezes before the rash shows.
- Once the rash appears, your child cannot spread it.
- Your child can go to school or daycare.

What to do:

- Rest and drink plenty of fluids.
- For fever or sore joints, use acetaminophen or ibuprofen as directed on the label.
- Wash hands often.
- Do not share cups or food.

If you are pregnant:

- Call your doctor if you were around someone with fifth disease.
- A blood test can show if you are already protected.
- Most babies are fine, but some need extra checks.

Call the clinic right away if:

- Your child has sickle cell disease or another blood disorder
- Your child looks pale, very tired, or weak
- You have a weak immune system and feel sick

Call the clinic if your child seems very sick or will not drink.

handouts.title: Roseola
handouts.text:
Roseola

Roseola is a common virus in babies and toddlers. It causes a high fever for 3 to 5 days. A pink rash shows up as the fever goes away. The rash is not itchy and fades in 1 to 4 days.

What to do:

- Give plenty of fluids, even if your child is not hungry.
- For fever, give acetaminophen. Ibuprofen is OK if your child is 6 months or older.
- Your child's dose: ***
- Your child can go back to daycare after 24 hours with no fever.
- The rash does not need treatment.

About fever seizures:

- High fever can cause a seizure in some young children.
- These seizures are scary, but they do not cause brain damage.
- Fever medicine helps comfort but does not prevent seizures.

If your child has a seizure:

- Lay your child on the floor or bed, away from hard or sharp things.
- Turn your child's head to the side.
- Do not put anything in the mouth.
- Time the seizure.

Call 911 if a seizure lasts more than 5 minutes.

Call the clinic after any seizure.

Call the clinic right away if your child:

- Is very sleepy or hard to wake
- Is not drinking well or has fewer wet diapers
- Has a rash with blisters or sores, or sores on the lips or in the mouth

handouts.title: Flu
handouts.text:
Flu (influenza)

Flu is caused by a virus. It often starts suddenly with fever, cough, sore throat, body aches, and tiredness. Antibiotics do not treat flu.

Flu medicine like Tamiflu (oseltamivir) helps only a little:

- It shortens the flu by less than 1 day for most adults, and about 1 day for healthy children.
- It has not been shown to keep healthy adults out of the hospital.
- About 1 in 20 people who take it throw up because of it. Some feel sick to their stomach.
- If you are healthy, taking it is your choice. It matters more for people at high risk.

Your medicine:

- Take *** by mouth *** for *** days.
- It works best when started within 2 days of the first symptoms.
- Take it with food if it upsets your stomach.

What helps at home:

- Rest and drink plenty of fluids.
- Use acetaminophen or ibuprofen for fever or aches as directed on the label. For children, use the dose based on weight.
- Do not give aspirin to anyone under 19 years old.
- Cover coughs and sneezes. Wash your hands often.

When you can go back to work or school:

- Stay home until you have had no fever for 24 hours without fever medicine.
- Your symptoms should also be getting better overall.
- For the next 5 days, wear a mask around others and wash your hands often.
- If fever comes back, stay home again.

Protect your family:

- Flu is most dangerous for babies, adults 65 and older, pregnant women, and people with long-term illness.
- Call us if someone at high risk in your home was exposed. Medicine can help if started within 2 days.
- Everyone 6 months and older should get a flu shot every year.

Call the clinic if:

- Fever or cough gets better, then comes back or gets worse
- You are not better after 3 to 5 days of medicine
- A long-term illness, like asthma or diabetes, gets worse
- You throw up your medicine
- Your child acts confused or behaves strangely

Call 911 or go to the ER if you or your child has:

- Trouble breathing or fast breathing
- Ribs pulling in with each breath
- Pain or pressure in the chest or belly that does not go away
- Blue lips or face
- Confusion, trouble waking up, or a seizure
- No urine in 8 hours, a dry mouth, or no tears when crying
- A baby under 12 weeks old with any fever
- Fever over 104 F that does not come down with medicine

handouts.title: Measles
handouts.text:
Measles

Measles is a serious illness caused by a virus. It spreads very easily through the air. It can stay in a room for 2 hours after a sick person leaves.

Signs of measles:

- High fever, which can go above 104 F
- Cough, runny nose, and red, watery eyes
- A rash that starts on the face and spreads down the body
- Signs start 7 to 14 days after being near someone with measles

If you were exposed to measles:

- Call the clinic before you come in. Do not walk into a clinic, urgent care, or ER without calling first.
- We will check your vaccine record to see if you are protected.
- The MMR vaccine within 3 days of exposure may prevent measles or make it milder.
- A shot of antibodies within 6 days can help babies, pregnant women, and people with weak immune systems.
- Watch for fever, cough, red eyes, or rash for 21 days.
- If you are not protected, stay away from schools, child care, and hospitals for up to 21 days.

If you have measles:

- Stay home until the 5th day after the rash starts. Your doctor or the health department will tell you when.
- Stay away from other people in your home as much as you can.
- The health department will call you. Please help them find people who were near you.
- Rest and drink plenty of fluids.
- Your child may need vitamin A: *** IU by mouth today and tomorrow.

How the MMR vaccine protects you:

- One dose of MMR is 93% effective against measles. Two doses are 97% effective.
- Children get MMR at 12 to 15 months and again at 4 to 6 years.
- Babies 6 to 11 months old need a dose before travel to another country.
- Adults need at least 1 dose. Some adults need 2.
- Pregnant women should not get MMR. Get it before or after pregnancy.

Call the clinic if:

- You think you or your child has measles. Call before you come in.
- You have ear pain or diarrhea that will not stop

Go to the ER if you have any of these. Have someone call the ER first:

- Trouble breathing
- Chest pain when breathing or coughing
- Signs of dehydration, like no urine in 8 hours
- Fever or headache that will not go away
- Confusion
- Blue color around the mouth

handouts.title: Mumps
handouts.text:
Mumps

Mumps is caused by a virus. It causes puffy cheeks and a sore, swollen jaw. It can also cause fever, headache, tiredness, and poor appetite. Most people get better within 2 weeks.

How mumps spreads:

- Through spit, coughs, sneezes, and talking
- By sharing cups or drinks
- From a few days before the swelling starts until 5 days after

Protect others:

- Stay home from school and work for 5 days after the swelling starts.
- Skip social events during this time.
- Do not share cups or drinks.

What helps:

- Put ice or a heat pack on the swollen area.
- Take acetaminophen for pain as directed on the label. For children, use the dose based on weight.
- Drink extra fluids.
- Eat soft foods that are easy to chew.
- Gargle with warm salt water.
- Do not give aspirin to anyone under 19 years old.

Vaccine:

- Two doses of the MMR vaccine give the best protection.
- During an outbreak, the health department may advise a third dose.

Call the clinic if:

- A testicle hurts, swells, or has a lump
- Red eyes
- Sleepiness that will not go away
- Vomiting or belly pain that will not go away
- A bad headache
- Trouble hearing

Call 911 if:

- A seizure happens

handouts.title: Whooping cough
handouts.text:
Whooping cough (pertussis)

Whooping cough is a lung infection caused by bacteria. It causes bad coughing fits that can last for weeks. It is most dangerous for babies under 1 year old.

Signs of whooping cough:

- First, a runny nose, mild fever, and mild cough for 1 to 2 weeks
- Then, coughing fits that can last up to 10 weeks
- A high-pitched whoop when breathing in after a coughing fit
- Throwing up or feeling worn out after a coughing fit
- Babies may not cough. They may stop breathing or turn blue.

Your medicine:

- Take *** by mouth *** for *** days.
- Antibiotics help stop the spread to others.
- The cough may last for weeks, even after the medicine.

Protect others:

- Stay home from school, child care, and work until you have taken antibiotics for 5 days.
- People in your home may need antibiotics too, even if they feel fine.
- Stay away from babies and pregnant women until you finish 5 days of antibiotics.

Vaccines that prevent whooping cough:

- Babies and young children get DTaP shots.
- Preteens get a Tdap shot at 11 to 12 years old.
- Pregnant women get Tdap in every pregnancy, between weeks 27 and 36. This helps protect the newborn.
- Adults who never had Tdap need 1 dose.

Call the clinic if:

- Coughing fits get worse or happen more often
- You cannot keep food or fluids down after coughing
- A baby under 1 month old throws up forcefully after feeds

Call 911 or go to the ER if:

- A baby stops breathing, even for a few seconds
- Lips or face turn blue or gray
- You or your child has trouble breathing
- A seizure happens

handouts.title: Chickenpox
handouts.text:
Chickenpox

Chickenpox is caused by a virus. It causes an itchy rash of blisters that turn into scabs. It takes about 1 week for all the blisters to scab over.

What helps the itch:

- Put calamine lotion on itchy spots.
- Take a cool bath with baking soda or colloidal oatmeal.
- Keep fingernails short. Try not to scratch.
- If you scratch a blister, wash your hands with soap for 20 seconds.

Fever medicine:

- Use acetaminophen for fever. Follow the label, or use the dose based on weight for children.
- Do not give aspirin. In children it can cause Reye syndrome, which harms the liver and brain.
- Try not to give ibuprofen. It has been linked to serious skin infections.

Your medicine, if prescribed:

- Take *** by mouth *** times a day for 5 days.
- Start it as soon as you can. It works best in the first 24 hours of the rash.

When you can go back to school or work:

- Stay home until all blisters have crusted over.
- Had the vaccine and spots do not crust? Stay home until no new spots appear for 24 hours.
- Until then, stay away from pregnant women, newborns, and people with weak immune systems.

Protect your family:

- People who never had chickenpox or the vaccine can catch it.
- The chickenpox vaccine within 3 to 5 days after exposure can help prevent illness.
- Call us if someone in your home is pregnant, a newborn, or has a weak immune system.

Call the clinic if:

- The sick person is under 1 year old, over 12, pregnant, or has a weak immune system
- Fever lasts more than 4 days or goes above 102 F
- Skin becomes very red, warm, or sore, or leaks pus
- Vomiting happens often
- A bad cough starts

Go to the ER if there is:

- Trouble breathing
- Trouble waking up or confusion
- Trouble walking
- A stiff neck
- Bad belly pain
- A rash with bleeding or bruising

handouts.title: Shingles
handouts.text:
Shingles

Shingles is a painful rash caused by the chickenpox virus waking up. It is often a band of blisters on one side of the body. Blisters scab over in 7 to 10 days. The rash clears in 2 to 4 weeks.

Can I spread it?

- Shingles itself does not spread from person to person.
- Your blisters can give chickenpox to people who never had chickenpox or the vaccine.
- You cannot spread it before blisters appear or after the rash scabs over.

Protect others until the rash scabs over:

- Keep the rash covered.
- Do not touch or scratch the rash.
- Wash your hands often.
- Stay away from pregnant women who never had chickenpox or the vaccine.
- Stay away from babies born early or small, and people with weak immune systems.

Your medicine:

- Take *** by mouth *** for *** days.
- It works best when started as soon as the rash appears.

Pain and itch relief:

- Take *** for pain as directed.
- Put cool, wet cloths on the rash.
- Calamine lotion or an oatmeal bath may ease itching.

After you get better:

- Get the shingles vaccine once the rash is gone. It is for adults 50 and older or with weak immune systems.
- It is 2 shots, given 2 to 6 months apart. It helps keep shingles from coming back.

Call the clinic if:

- Pain is not controlled
- Pain lasts after the rash heals
- The rash becomes red, warm, swollen, or leaks pus
- You have a weak immune system

Go to the ER today if:

- The rash is on your forehead, near your eye, or on the tip of your nose
- You have eye pain, a red eye, or vision changes. Shingles in the eye can cause blindness.
- You feel confused

handouts.title: Bladder or kidney infection in children
handouts.text:
Bladder or kidney infection in children

Your child has a urinary tract infection, or UTI. Germs got into the bladder or kidneys. Antibiotics treat it.

Give the medicine:

- Give the antibiotic *** as directed for *** days.
- Give it until it is gone, even if your child feels better.
- Try not to miss any doses.
- For pain or fever, you can give acetaminophen *** or ibuprofen ***.
- Give extra fluids, like water.

What to expect:

- Fever is usually gone within 48 hours.
- Pain and burning are often much better within 48 hours.
- We will check the urine culture in 1 to 3 days. We may change the antibiotic.

Tests your child may need:

- Fever with this UTI and under age 5: we will order an ultrasound of the kidneys and bladder.
- Some children need an X-ray of the bladder, called a VCUG. This is only if the ultrasound shows a problem or the infection comes back.
- Follow-up visit: ***

Help prevent another UTI:

- Treat constipation. Offer fruits, vegetables, beans, and water every day.
- Have your child pee as soon as they feel the urge. Do not wait.
- Give your child enough time to fully empty the bladder.
- Wipe from front to back after poops.
- Avoid bubble baths and scented soaps.
