- Choose cotton underwear and loose clothes.
- Tell us if your child has hard or painful poops.

Call the clinic if:

- Fever lasts more than 48 hours after starting the antibiotic
- Symptoms come back after the antibiotic is done
- Your child gets a new fever with no clear cause
- Your child starts wetting again after being dry
- Your child has back or side pain

Go to the ER if your child:

- Vomits and cannot keep the antibiotic down
- Looks or acts very sick
- Cannot pee or passes only a few drops
- Has a very dry mouth or pees much less than usual
- Is under 2 months old with a fever of 100.4 F or higher

Call 911 if your child is not moving or too weak to stand.

handouts.title: Pneumonia
handouts.text:
Pneumonia

Pneumonia is an infection in the lungs. It can cause cough, fever, and trouble breathing. Most people get better at home.

Take your medicine:

- Take every dose of the antibiotic ***. Do not miss any doses.
- Finish it all, even if you feel better.
- Do not use cough or cold medicine unless we say it is OK.
- Do not give a child cough medicine with codeine or dextromethorphan.

Fever and pain:

- Adults: take acetaminophen *** or ibuprofen *** as we told you.
- Children: give acetaminophen *** or ibuprofen *** based on weight.
- Do not give aspirin to a child.

Rest and fluids:

- Get plenty of rest. Take naps if you sleep poorly at night.
- Adults: drink 6 to 10 cups of fluid a day, unless we told you to limit fluids.
- Babies under 1 year: give breast milk or formula. Offer small amounts more often.
- Older children: offer small drinks often.
- Do not drink alcohol.

Help your lungs heal:

- Coughing helps clear your lungs.
- Take a few deep breaths 2 to 3 times every hour.
- If you smoke, now is the time to quit. Call 1-877-448-7848 for free help.
- Do not let anyone smoke in your home or car.

What to expect:

- You should start to feel better within 2 to 3 days of starting the antibiotic.
- The cough slowly gets better over 1 to 2 weeks. In children it can last several weeks.
- You may feel tired for about a month.

Vaccines that help prevent pneumonia:

- Flu shot every year for everyone 6 months and older.
- Pneumonia shot for all children under 5 and adults 50 and older. Some younger people with health problems need it too.
- RSV shot for adults 75 and older, and adults 50 to 74 at higher risk.
- Ask us if you need a COVID shot.

Call the clinic if:

- You or your child are not better after 2 to 3 days of antibiotics
- The fever goes away and then comes back
- You cough up dark mucus or blood
- You have chest pain when you take a deep breath

Go to the ER or call 911 if:

- Breathing gets harder or faster, or you cannot get a deep breath
- Lips, skin, or fingertips turn blue or gray
- You are very sleepy or confused
- You have a very dry mouth or pee much less than usual
- A child breathes faster than 50 to 60 breaths a minute when not crying
- A child's chest muscles pull in with each breath, or the nostrils flare
- A child will not eat or drink, or is limp or floppy

handouts.title: Home care for your child's cold
handouts.text:
Home care for your child's cold

Colds are caused by viruses. Antibiotics do not help. The tips below can help your child feel better while the cold runs its course.

Nose care:

- Put a few salt water (saline) drops in each nostril.
- For babies, wait about 10 seconds. Then gently suck out the mucus with a bulb syringe.
- Do this when a stuffy nose makes it hard to drink or sleep.

Drinks and food:

- Give plenty of fluids. Babies need breast milk or formula. Older kids can also have water.
- For older kids, warm drinks or soup, like chicken soup, can soothe a sore throat.
- Warm drinks may also help loosen mucus for a short time.
- Make sure drinks and soup are warm, not hot.
- Honey can help a cough in children 1 year and older. Never give honey to a baby under 1.
- How much honey: ages 1 to 5, half a teaspoon. Ages 6 to 11, 1 teaspoon. Age 12 and up, 2 teaspoons.

Moist air:

- Run a clean cool-mist humidifier in your child's room.
- Or sit together in a steamy bathroom with a hot shower running. Keep your child away from the hot water.
- Do not have your child breathe steam from a bowl or pot of hot water. Children get bad burns this way.
- Hot steam vaporizers can also burn small hands. Choose cool mist.

Sleep and rest:

- Let your child rest as much as they need.
- Put babies to sleep on their back for every nap and at night, even with a cold.
- Use a firm, flat crib mattress with a fitted sheet only.
- Do not use pillows, blankets, wedges, or anything that props up or tilts your baby.
- If your baby falls asleep in a car seat or swing, move them to their crib on their back.

Medicine:

- For fever or pain, you may give acetaminophen ***.
- Ibuprofen *** is only for babies 6 months and older.
- Use the dose for your child's weight. Ask us before giving any medicine to a baby under 2.
- Ask us before giving any cough or cold medicine to a child under 6.

Gentle hands-on comfort care

Many parents like to use gentle touch to comfort a sick child. It can help your child relax and may help loosen mucus. It has not been shown to make a cold go away faster.

Back patting for an older child with a wet cough:

- Have your child sit and lean forward over a pillow, or lie on their tummy across your lap.
- Keep a thin shirt on your child.
- Cup your hand, like you are holding water.
- Gently pat the upper back over the ribs. You should hear a hollow sound, not a slap.
- Pat each side for up to 2 minutes.
- Do not pat the spine, the lower ribs, or the belly.
- Then have your child take a deep breath and cough.

Face and sinus strokes:

- Use clean hands and very light pressure, just enough to move the skin.
- Stroke from the top of the nose out across the cheeks toward the ears.
- Stroke along the eyebrows from the middle out to the sides.
- Stay away from the eyes.

Neck strokes:

- Lay your flat fingers on the side of your child's neck.
- With light strokes, gently move the skin down toward the collarbone.
- Repeat 10 to 15 times on each side.

Keep it safe:

- Use light pressure only. Touch should never hurt or leave red marks.
- Stop if your child cries, vomits, or seems uncomfortable.
- Never squeeze or press hard on a baby's chest.
- Wait at least 1 hour after a meal or feeding.
- Skip any area that is sore, red, or swollen.

Call the clinic if:

- Fever lasts more than 3 days
- Your child has ear pain or fluid draining from the ear
- Cold symptoms last more than 10 days, or get better and then worse
- Your child has fewer wet diapers, a dry mouth, or fewer tears when crying

Call 911 or go to the ER if your child:

- Is breathing very fast or working hard to breathe
- Has skin pulling in between the ribs, grunting, or flaring nostrils
- Has blue or gray lips, skin, or nails
- Is very tired, limp, or floppy
- Is under 3 months old with a fever of 100.4 F or higher

handouts.title: Healthy eating, the Mexican way
handouts.text:
Healthy eating, the Mexican way

Traditional Mexican food is healthy. In one study, a traditional Mexican diet helped the body use insulin better than a typical American diet. In the US, many families eat fewer corn tortillas and more sweets, chips, pizza, and fries. Keep your traditions and cut back on the American extras.

Keep eating:

- Beans, like pinto and black beans
- Corn tortillas
- Nopales, squash, tomatoes, chiles, onions, and other vegetables
- Salsa made with tomato, chile, and onion
- Fresh fruit like oranges, guava, mango, and papaya
- Avocado
- Homemade soups and stews, like pozole
- Fish and chicken

Watch out for:

- Soda, juice, sports drinks, and other sweet drinks
- Aguas frescas with a lot of added sugar
- Fast food, pizza, and French fries
- Chips, pan dulce, cookies, and other sweets
- Processed meat like hot dogs, bacon, and deli meat
- Fried foods and refried beans made with lard
- Flour tortillas
- Lots of cheese and sour cream

Simple swaps:

- Pick corn tortillas over flour tortillas.
- Eat whole beans, or cook beans with a little vegetable oil instead of lard.
- Bake tostadas in the oven instead of frying them.
- Use salsa for flavor instead of cheese sauce.
- Try plain yogurt in place of sour cream.
- Make agua fresca with fruit and water and little or no sugar.
- Fill half your plate with vegetables.
- Drink water with meals.

For children, the best drinks are water and plain milk. Do not give juice before age 1. Whole fruit is better than juice. Skip soda, sports drinks, and fruit drinks.

My goal: ***

Call the clinic if you want help planning meals or want to see a dietitian.

handouts.title: Healthy eating, the Korean way
handouts.text:
Healthy eating, the Korean way

Traditional Korean meals are healthy. Rice, soup, kimchi, and many vegetable side dishes make a balanced meal. Korean Americans eat more fast food and fewer vegetables than people in Korea. Keep your traditions and cut back on the American extras.

Keep eating:

- Banchan, especially namul and other vegetable side dishes
- Kimchi and other fermented vegetables
- Tofu and beans
- Fish
- Seaweed, like gim
- Rice made with mixed grains or beans, like japgokbap
- Foods that are boiled, blanched, or fermented instead of fried

Watch out for:

- Salt. Kimchi, soups, stews, ramyeon, and soy sauce add the most salt to Korean meals.
- Large bowls of white rice
- Soda, juice, and sweet drinks
- Fast food and eating out often
- Chips, cookies, and other packaged snacks
- Processed meat like ham, bacon, and hot dogs

Simple swaps:

- Eat the vegetables in soup and leave some of the broth.
- Use a smaller soup bowl.
- Taste your food first, then add a little soy sauce or salt if needed.
- Make kimchi and banchan with less salt.
- Have ramyeon less often.
- When you eat out, ask for less salty food.
- Mix grains or beans into your rice.
- Make vegetable banchan the biggest part of your meal.
- Drink water instead of soda or juice.

For children, the best drinks are water and plain milk. Do not give juice before age 1. Whole fruit is better than juice. Skip soda, sports drinks, and fruit drinks.

My goal: ***

Call the clinic if you want help planning meals or want to see a dietitian.

handouts.title: Healthy eating, the Afghan way
handouts.text:
Healthy eating, the Afghan way

Many Afghan foods are very healthy. Dal, beans, yogurt, fresh herbs, and vegetables are good for your whole family. The problems are too much oil and sugar, and new American foods like soda and fast food.

Keep eating:

- Dal, chickpeas, and kidney beans
- Plain yogurt, as a side dish or sauce
- Fresh mint and cilantro
- Vegetables like spinach, eggplant, okra, cauliflower, carrots, and peas
- Salad with tomato, cucumber, and onion
- Shorwa and ash with lots of vegetables
- Whole wheat bread and bulgur
- Fresh fruit like oranges, apricots, peaches, and figs
- A small handful of nuts
- Black or green tea without sugar

Watch out for:

- Lots of oil in rice and stews
- Deep-fried foods
- Sugar in tea
- Big servings of bread and rice at the same meal
- Sweets, cakes, cookies, and many dates or dried fruits
- Soda, juice, and fast food
- Chips and chocolate bars
- Lots of salt in cooking and at the table
- More meat and fewer vegetables than you ate before

Simple swaps:

- Use less oil when you cook rice, korma, and other dishes.
- Choose grilled kebab more often than fried foods.
- Drink tea with less sugar, or none at all.
- Serve vegetables first, then meat or beans, and rice last.
- Use your fist to measure your rice.
- If you eat bread and rice together, take half the rice.
- Eat 2 or 3 dates, not a handful.
- Fill half your plate with salad and vegetables.
- Drink water, plain tea, or doogh instead of soda.

For children, the best drinks are water and plain milk. Do not give juice before age 1. Whole fruit is better than juice. Skip soda, sports drinks, and fruit drinks.

My goal: ***

Call the clinic if you want help planning meals or want to see a dietitian.

handouts.title: Healthy eating, the Zomi way
handouts.text:
Healthy eating, the Zomi way

Traditional Zomi and Chin meals are healthy. Rice, many vegetables, and soups with chili make a good meal. Back home, most families ate lots of vegetables and only a little meat. In the US, many families eat fewer vegetables, more meat, and bigger servings.

Keep eating:

- Lots of vegetables, like mustard greens, pumpkin leaves, bamboo shoots, eggplant, gourds, and beans
- Boiled vegetables and vegetable soups
- Chili for flavor
- Fish and chicken
- Fruit like papaya, mango, and banana
- Plain green tea without sugar

Watch out for:

- Big plates of white rice
- Lots of salt, fish sauce, and fish paste
- Lots of cooking oil and fried foods
- Soda, juice, fruit drinks, and sweet milk tea
- Fast food, chips, cookies, and candy
- Eating more meat and fewer vegetables than you did back home

Simple swaps:

- Fill half your plate with vegetables, the way you ate back home.
- Take a smaller scoop of rice.
- Add less salt and fish sauce. Taste your food first.
- Make sabuti with less salt and less fat.
- Boil vegetables or stir-fry with a little oil instead of deep-frying.
- Buy fresh greens at Asian grocery stores.
- Cook at home more often than you buy fast food.
- Drink water or plain tea instead of soda or juice.

For children, the best drinks are water and plain milk. Do not give soda or fruit drinks to babies or young children. Do not give juice before age 1.

My goal: ***

Call the clinic if you want help planning meals or want to see a dietitian.

handouts.title: Clean-out plan for your child's constipation
handouts.text:
Clean-out plan for your child's constipation

Your child's bowel is packed with hard stool. A clean-out flushes it out with medicine. Then a smaller daily dose keeps stools soft.

Before you start:

- Plan the clean-out for a weekend or days at home.
- Your child needs to stay close to a toilet.
- Polyethylene glycol (PEG) is a powder. One capful is 17 grams.
- Mix PEG in a clear drink, like water, juice, or a sports drink. Do not mix it with milk.
- Stop any daily constipation medicine during the clean-out.

Clean-out plan:

- Day 1: PEG *** capfuls in *** ounces of drink, given ***.
- Day 2: ***
- Day 3: ***
- Laxative tablet or liquid: ***, given ***.
- Other: ***

Drinks and food:

- Give extra drinks between doses, like water, clear juice, broth, or an electrolyte drink.
- Food during the clean-out: ***

What to expect:

- PEG can start working in 30 minutes to 3 hours.
- Your child will have many loose or watery stools.
- Belly cramps are common. A warm bath may help.
- It is working when stools are watery with no solid pieces. They often look clear or yellow.
- If your child feels sick or throws up, stop the drink for 30 minutes. Then start again.

Daily dose after the clean-out:

- Start the day after the clean-out, unless we told you otherwise.
- Daily dose: PEG *** capfuls in *** ounces of drink, once a day.
- Goal: 1 or 2 soft stools every day, soft like mashed potatoes or pudding.
- If stools are watery, give a little less.
- If stools are hard or your child skips days, give a little more.
- Keep giving it for at least 2 months, even when your child is better.
- Stopping too soon often brings it back. We will lower the dose slowly together.

Toilet time:

- Have your child sit on the toilet for 5 minutes after meals.
- Use a footstool so knees are higher than hips.
- Praise trying. Never punish accidents.

Foods that help after the clean-out:

- Offer fruit 3 or more times a day, like prunes, pears, peaches, apricots, or figs.
- Offer whole grains, like oatmeal, brown rice, or whole wheat bread.
- Give enough water to stay well hydrated.

Call the clinic if your child:

- Throws up more than once or cannot drink the medicine
- Has no watery stools by the end of the clean-out
- Has blood in the stool
- Gets hard stools or belly pain again on the daily dose

Go to the ER if your child has:

- Severe belly pain
- A swollen belly with vomiting, or green vomit
- Signs of dehydration: little or no pee, very dark pee, dizziness, or being very sleepy or confused

handouts.title: Clean-out plan for constipation
handouts.text:
Clean-out plan for constipation

Your bowel is packed with hard stool. A clean-out flushes it out with medicine. Then a smaller daily dose keeps stools soft.

Before you start:

- Plan the clean-out for days you can stay home, close to a toilet.
- Polyethylene glycol (PEG) is a powder. One capful is 17 grams.
- Mix PEG in water or another clear drink.
- Do not take fiber powders or pills until the clean-out is done.

Clean-out plan:

- Day 1: PEG *** capfuls in *** ounces of water, finished over *** hours.
- Day 2: ***
- Day 3: ***
- Enema or suppository: ***
- Other: ***

Drinks:

- Drink extra fluid during the clean-out, about 4 more cups a day.
- Water, clear broth, and electrolyte drinks are good choices.

What to expect:

- You will have many loose or watery stools.
- Belly cramps and bloating are common.
- It is working when stools are watery with no solid pieces.
- Most clean-outs work in 1 to 3 days.

Daily dose after the clean-out:

- Daily dose: PEG *** capfuls in 8 ounces of drink, once a day.
- Goal: a soft stool that is easy to pass, most days.
- If stools are watery, take a little less.
- If stools are hard or you skip days, take a little more.
- Keep taking it for *** months, even when you feel better.
- Add fiber slowly after the clean-out, like fruit, vegetables, beans, and whole grains.
- Foods that help: 2 green kiwis or about 10 prunes a day.
- Sit on the toilet at the same time each day, like after breakfast. Put your feet on a small stool.

Call the clinic if you:

- Throw up or cannot finish the medicine
- Have no watery stools by the end of the clean-out
- See blood in your stool
- Get hard stools again on the daily dose

Go to the ER if you have:

- Severe belly pain
- A swollen belly with vomiting, or you cannot pass gas
- Signs of dehydration: little or no pee, very dark pee, dizziness, or confusion

handouts.title: Constipation from opioid pain medicine
handouts.text:
Constipation from opioid pain medicine

Opioid pain medicine slows your bowels. Hard stools are very common. Your body does not get used to this side effect.

What to do:

- Take your laxative every day while you take the opioid. Do not wait until you are stuck.
- Your laxative: ***
- Polyethylene glycol: 17 grams mixed in 8 ounces of drink, once a day.
- Senna 8.6 mg: 1 to 2 tablets at bedtime.
- A stool softener pill alone is not enough. Use one of the medicines above.
- Fiber pills do not help this kind of constipation.
- Drink fluids and move your body every day.
- Go to the bathroom as soon as you feel the urge.

If you are still hard after a week, tell us. We may add a second laxative. We may also add a medicine that blocks the opioid in your gut.

If we start a gut-blocking medicine:

- Your medicine: ***
- Stop your other daily laxatives when you start it, unless we say otherwise.
- You may use them again if you still have trouble after 3 days.
- Stop it if you stop your opioid.
- Belly cramps and loose stools can happen. Stay close to a bathroom after the first doses.

Call the clinic if you have no stool in *** days, or blood in your stool.

Go to the ER if you have bad belly pain, vomiting, a swollen belly, or cannot pass gas.

handouts.title: Constipation and straining in babies
handouts.text:
Constipation and straining in babies

Babies often grunt, strain, and turn red when they poop. This is normal if the poop comes out soft.

Breastfed babies older than 1 month may poop only every 4 to 7 days. This can be normal if the poop is soft and does not hurt.

Formula-fed babies often poop less often than breastfed babies. Their poop is often firmer.

Straining with soft poop (dyschezia):

- Some babies under 9 months strain and cry for 10 minutes or more before a soft poop.
- This is normal. The muscles are still learning to work together.
- It gets better on its own. Your baby does not need medicine for it.
- Do not put a thermometer, cotton swab, or finger in your baby's bottom.

What helps hard poop:

- Over 1 month old: give 100% pear or apple juice each day.
- Give 1 ounce per month of age each day. Do not give more than 4 ounces a day.
- Over 3 months old: prune juice can be used.
- Eating baby food: offer pureed prunes, pears, peaches, plums, peas, or beans 2 times a day.
- Hold your baby's knees to the chest. Gently press on the lower belly.
- Stop after a few minutes if no poop comes out.
- Medicine, only if we prescribe it: ***

Do not give mineral oil, enemas, or laxatives unless we tell you to.

Call the clinic if your baby:

- Is under 1 month old, breastfed, and pooping less often
- Is under 2 months old and seems constipated
- Has blood in the poop
- Has a swollen belly, or vomits 2 or more times
- Is not feeding well or not gaining weight
- Has a weak suck or seems floppy

Go to the ER if your baby vomits green fluid or looks very sick.

handouts.title: Soiling (encopresis)
handouts.text:
Soiling (encopresis)

Soiling means poop leaks into your child's underwear. It almost always comes from constipation.

Hard poop gets stuck and stretches the bowel. Soft poop then leaks around it. The stretched bowel does not feel it well.

Your child is not doing this on purpose. It is not laziness or bad behavior.

Step 1, clean out (if needed): ***

Step 2, daily medicine:

- Polyethylene glycol, mixed in 4 to 8 ounces of drink.
- Your child's dose: *** capfuls or *** grams, once a day.
- Goal: a soft poop every day and no leaks.
- If poop is watery, use less. If it is still hard, use more.
- Keep giving it every day, even after the leaks stop.
- Many children need it for 6 to 12 months.
- Do not stop it on your own. We will lower it slowly.

Step 3, toilet sits:

- Have your child sit on the toilet for *** minutes after meals.
- Use a footstool so your child can squat a little.
- Use a sticker chart. Give a sticker for every sit, even if no poop comes out.

Step 4, stay positive:

- Never blame, shame, or punish your child for accidents.
- Pack spare underwear and wipes for school.
- Accidents and setbacks are common, especially early on.

Foods that help:

- Offer fruit 3 or more times a day, like prunes, pears, peaches, apricots, or figs.
- Offer whole grains, like oatmeal, brown rice, or whole wheat bread.
- Give enough water to stay well hydrated.

Constipation comes back in about half of children. If hard poop or leaks come back, restart the plan and call us.

Call the clinic if:

- Leaks or hard poop come back
- Your child has not pooped in *** days on medicine
- Your child has belly pain or blood in the poop
- Your child is sad, worried, or teased about accidents

Go to the ER if your child has a swollen belly with vomiting, green vomit, or severe belly pain.

handouts.title: Skin tear care at home
handouts.text:
Skin tear care at home

A skin tear happens when thin, fragile skin is rubbed, bumped, or pulled. Most heal in about 4 weeks with gentle care.

Your dressing:

- Leave the dressing on until ***.
- There is an arrow drawn on the dressing. Always take it off in the direction of the arrow.
- Peel it off slowly. This keeps the skin flap from lifting.
- Do not use tape, plastic film, or bandages with strong glue on your skin.
- Keep the wound covered and moist. Do not let it dry out.

Next dressing change: ***

Protect your skin:

- Put lotion or cream on your arms and legs twice a day. Use one without perfume.
- Pat skin dry after bathing. Do not rub.
- Use warm water, not hot, and a gentle soap-free cleanser.
- Wear long sleeves, long pants, or shin guards.
- Pad bed rails, wheelchair arms, and sharp furniture edges.
- Keep fingernails short and remove rings when you help with care.
- Clear clutter and use good lighting to prevent falls.

For caregivers:

- Do not grab arms or legs with your fingertips.
- Use a lift sheet or support under the body when you help them move.

Tetanus shot: ***

Call the clinic if:

- Redness, warmth, or swelling is spreading
- There is pus or a bad smell
- Pain is getting worse
- The skin flap turns dark or black
- Blood or a lump builds up under the flap
- The tear is not getting better after 2 weeks

Go to the ER if bleeding does not stop after 10 minutes of firm pressure.

handouts.title: Scrapes and small cuts in children
handouts.text:
Scrapes and small cuts

Most small cuts and scrapes heal in less than a week. Good cleaning helps prevent infection.

Stop the bleeding:

- Press firmly with a clean cloth or gauze for 10 minutes.
- Do not lift it to peek. Peeking often makes bleeding start again.

Clean it:

- Wash your hands first.
- Wash the wound with soap and water for 5 minutes.
- Gently scrub out any dirt with a washcloth.
- Do not use hydrogen peroxide, rubbing alcohol, or iodine. They can irritate the skin.

Cover it:

- Put on a thin layer of petroleum jelly from a tube (AAD) or antibiotic ointment (AAP).
- Cover it with a clean bandage.
- Change the bandage every day, or sooner if it gets wet or dirty.
- Keep the area out of the sun while it heals. Sun on a healing cut can make the scar worse.

For pain, you may give acetaminophen ***. Ibuprofen *** is only for babies 6 months and older. Use the dose for your child's weight.

Your child may need stitches if:

- The cut is split open or gaping
- The cut is longer than half an inch
- A cut on the face is longer than a quarter inch
- You can see fat or muscle in the cut

Stitches work best when done soon. Come in right away, within 6 hours if you can.

Tetanus shot:

- A dirty cut needs a tetanus shot if the last one was over 5 years ago.
- A clean cut needs one if the last shot was over 10 years ago.

Your child's tetanus shot is ***.

Call the clinic if:

- Your child is under 1 year old
- Dirt is still in the wound after 15 minutes of scrubbing
- The scrape is very deep or covers a large area
- The cut came from an animal or human bite
- Your child stepped on a nail
- There is spreading redness, a red streak, pus, warmth, or fever
- The wound is not healed after 10 days

Go to the ER if bleeding does not stop after 10 minutes of firm pressure.

Call 911 if:

- Blood is spurting out or soaks through the bandages
- Bleeding is heavy and does not stop with pressure

handouts.title: Bruises and hematomas
handouts.text:
Bruises and hematomas

A bruise happens when small blood vessels break and leak blood under the skin. A big bruise can form a pool of blood under the skin. This is called a hematoma.

What to expect:

- A bruise often starts red or blue. It turns green, then yellow, as it heals.
- Gravity can pull the bruise lower. A bruise on the leg may spread to the ankle or foot.
- Most bruises go away in 2 to 4 weeks. Bruises on the legs take longer.

First 2 days:

- Rest the area. Do not overwork the bruised muscles.
- Ice it for 10 to 20 minutes at a time. Put a thin cloth between the ice and your skin.
- Raise it above the level of your heart on pillows as much as you can.
- If we gave you a wrap, wear it as shown. Loosen it if your fingers or toes tingle, turn cold, or turn pale.

After 2 days:

- Use a warm, wet washcloth for 10 minutes, 3 times a day.

Pain medicine:

- Use acetaminophen for pain. Do not take more than the label says.
- On a blood thinner? Do not take ibuprofen, naproxen, or aspirin unless your doctor says it is OK.
- Do not stop your blood thinner unless your doctor tells you to. Your plan: ***

Call the clinic right away if:

- The bruise or swelling keeps getting bigger
- Pain is getting worse
- The skin over a hematoma turns dark or dusky, or forms blisters
- You see red streaks, pus, or have a fever
- Your leg has new pain, swelling, or redness in the calf, thigh, or groin
- You get bruises without any injury
- You take a blood thinner and you fall or hit your head
- You take a blood thinner and see pink or brown urine, black stools, or bad nosebleeds

Go to the ER if:

- The bruised area feels very tight and tense, with very bad pain
- It hurts a lot more when you move or stretch the area
- The area is numb, tingling, cold, or pale
- You vomit blood or something that looks like coffee grounds

Call 911 if you hit your head and are confused, very sleepy, or pass out.

handouts.title: Tendon pain
handouts.text:
Tendon pain

A tendon joins a muscle to a bone. Tendon pain often starts after a new activity or doing more than usual. Most people get better with the right exercise.

Your sore tendon: ***

Keep moving, but do less:

- Do not stop all activity. Cut back on what hurts most.
- Swap hard activities for easier ones, like biking or swimming.
- Go back to full activity slowly.

Use pain as your guide:

- Some pain during exercise is OK.
- Keep pain at 5 out of 10 or lower during and right after exercise.
- Pain should be back to normal by the next morning.
- If pain is worse the next morning, do less the next day.

Your exercise plan:

- Exercise: ***
- How many and how often: ***
- Most tendon exercise plans last about 12 weeks.

Outer elbow (tennis elbow):

- Rest your forearm on a table, palm down, with your hand over the edge.
- Hold a 1 to 2 pound weight, like a soup can.
- Slowly raise and lower your hand 8 to 12 times.
- Wear your forearm strap during activity if you were given one.

Back of the heel (Achilles):

- Stand with the front half of your feet on a stair. Hold the rail.
- Rise up on your toes. Then slowly lower your heels below the step.
- Do 3 sets of 15, twice a day.
- Skip this one if your pain is where the tendon meets the heel bone.
- Heel lifts in your shoes can ease the strain.

Front of the knee below the kneecap:

- Lean your back against a wall. Bend your knees partway, like sitting on a tall stool.
- Hold for 45 seconds. Rest up to 2 minutes.
- Do this 5 times.

Outer hip:

- Sit with a belt around your thighs. Push your knees out against the belt.
- Hold for 30 seconds. Do this 4 times, 3 rounds.
- Do not cross your legs or sit in low chairs.
- Do not stand with your weight hanging on one hip.
- Sleep on your back, or on your good side with a pillow between your knees.

Thumb side of the wrist:

- Wear your thumb splint as directed, most of all at night.
- Avoid side-to-side wrist motions that hurt.

Ice and pain medicine:

- Ice the sore spot for up to 20 minutes at a time.
- Put a cloth between the ice and your skin.
- Rub diclofenac gel on the sore spot 4 times a day.
- Measure the gel with the dosing card. Your dose: *** grams.
- Ibuprofen or naproxen pills can help for 1 to 2 weeks. Take them with food.
- Ask us first if you have heart disease, high blood pressure, kidney disease, or stomach ulcers.

What to avoid:

- Do not go back to full-speed sports or heavy work until the pain settles.
- Do not over-stretch a sore tendon.
- Tell any doctor who gives you an antibiotic that you have tendon pain.
- Antibiotics like ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin can harm tendons.

How long it takes:

- Tendons heal slowly. Most people get better over weeks to months.
- Full healing can take more than 6 months.

Call the clinic if:

- Your pain is not better after *** weeks of your exercises
- Your pain gets worse even when you do less
- You get tendon pain while taking an antibiotic like ciprofloxacin or levofloxacin
- You have numbness or tingling in your hand or foot

Go to the ER or come in the same day if:

- You hear or feel a sudden pop, then have trouble walking or standing on your toes
- A new bulge shows up in your upper arm after a pop
- The area is red, hot, and swollen, and you have a fever

handouts.title: Low sexual desire or arousal
handouts.text:
Low sexual desire or arousal

Many women have times when they are not interested in sex. Interest changes with age, health, stress and relationships. It is only a problem if it bothers you.

Desire can come after you start:

- For many women, desire does not come out of the blue.
- It often grows after touch and closeness begin.
- This is normal. It is called responsive desire.

What can help:

- Plan time for closeness when you are not rushed or tired.
- Get enough sleep and find ways to lower stress.
- Tell your partner what feels good and what does not.
- Be active and limit alcohol.

Touch practice (sensate focus):

- Set aside 30 to 40 minutes when you both feel relaxed.
- Take turns. One person touches and the other just notices how it feels.
- Touch for at least 15 minutes. Skip breasts and genitals at first. No sex at this step.
- Speak up if anything feels uncomfortable.
- Do this a few times. When you both feel ready, add breasts and genitals, still without sex.
- Go at your own pace. There is no test to pass.

For dryness or pain with sex:

- Use a lubricant each time you have sex.
- Water-based and silicone-based lubricants are safe with condoms.
- Oil-based products, like coconut oil, can break latex condoms.
- A vaginal moisturizer is different. Use it 2 to 3 times a week, even on days without sex.
- Test a new product on a small patch of skin for 24 hours first.
- If a product burns or itches, try a silicone-based one.

Medicines we talked about:

- ***
- How to take it: ***

Call the clinic if:

- Sex hurts, or you have bleeding after menopause.
- You feel down most days or lose interest in things you enjoy.
- A medicine side effect bothers you.
- You feel unsafe with a partner, or someone forces you to have sex.

Call 911 if you are in danger now or you faint.

handouts.title: Premature ejaculation
handouts.text:
Premature ejaculation

Coming too fast during sex is common. Practice, medicine, or both can help. Many men do best with both.

Things to try:

- Masturbate 1 to 2 hours before sex.
- Use a thicker condom to lower feeling.
- Try having your partner on top, so they can pull away when you are close.

Stop-start and squeeze practice:

- Practice alone first. Stimulate yourself until you are close to coming.
- Stop. For the squeeze method, squeeze the head of the penis for 10 to 20 seconds.
- Wait about 30 seconds, then start again. Repeat several times.
- When you feel more in control, try it with your partner.
- It takes lots of practice, so be patient.

Your medicine: ***

- Daily pill: it may start to help in 1 to 2 weeks.
- Numbing cream: put it on the head of the penis 20 minutes before sex.
- Use a condom with the cream so your partner does not get numb.
- Side effects can include upset stomach, tiredness, and lower sex drive.

Call the clinic if:

- Side effects bother you.
- You also have trouble getting or keeping an erection.
- You want to have a baby and take a daily pill.

Call 988 or 911 if you have thoughts of hurting yourself.

handouts.title: Erection problems and low sex drive
handouts.text:
Erection problems and low sex drive

These problems are common and can be treated. Erection problems can be an early sign of heart or blood vessel disease. That is why we check your heart health too.

Common causes:

- Diabetes, high blood pressure, heart disease, and hardened arteries
- Low testosterone or other hormone problems
- Some medicines, like antidepressants and some blood pressure pills
- Smoking, alcohol, and drugs
- Stress, worry, depression, or problems in your relationship
- Sleep apnea, which can lower testosterone

Do not stop a medicine on your own. Ask us first.

What you can do:

- Stop smoking and avoid street drugs.
- Have no more than 2 drinks a day.
- Be active most days and eat well.
- Keep a healthy weight.
- Get enough sleep. Tell us if you snore loudly or are sleepy in the day.
- If you have diabetes, keep your blood sugar under control.

Erection pills (sildenafil, tadalafil):

- They help blood flow to the penis. They work only when you are sexually aroused.
- Sildenafil: take it 30 minutes to 4 hours before sex. A heavy, fatty meal can slow it down.
- Tadalafil can be taken with or without food. Some men take a small dose every day.
- Take no more than 1 dose a day.
- Try it several times at the right dose before you decide it does not work.
- Common side effects are headache, flushing, stuffy nose, upset stomach, and back or muscle pain.
- Never take it with nitrates, like nitroglycerin, or with poppers. Your blood pressure can drop too low.
- If you need emergency care for chest pain, tell them you took an erection pill and when.

Your plan: ***

Testosterone:

- Low testosterone can lower sex drive. We check it with 2 early morning blood tests.
- Treatment is only for men with symptoms and 2 low tests.
- Testosterone stops your body from making sperm. Tell us if you want to have a baby.
- Your result and plan: ***

Call the clinic if:

- The pills do not work after several tries.
- Side effects bother you.
- You have trouble peeing, or you feel down most days.

Go to the ER if:

- An erection lasts more than 4 hours.
- You suddenly lose vision or hearing.

Call 911 if you have chest pain.

handouts.title: Helping your child gain weight
handouts.text:
Helping your child gain weight

Your child is not gaining weight as fast as expected. Most often, a child just needs more calories. Most children catch up with changes at home.

Our plan:

- Calorie goal: *** calories a day.
- Next weight check: ***
- Write down everything your child eats and drinks for 3 days. Bring it to your next visit.

Feeding your baby:

- Feed your baby *** ounces every *** hours.
- If you breastfeed, keep going. After feeds, give *** ounces of pumped milk or formula.
- Do not give juice before age 1.
- Do not put cereal in the bottle unless we tell you.

Mixing higher-calorie formula:

- Make *** calorie formula.
- Measure *** ounces of water first. Then add *** level scoops of powder.
- Use only the scoop from that can. Do not pack the powder.
- Mix it exactly as we told you. Never change the recipe on your own.
- Too much water means fewer calories. Very watery formula can cause seizures.
- Too much powder can make your baby dehydrated.
- Keep mixed formula in the fridge. Throw it out after 24 hours.
- Throw away formula left in the bottle after a feeding.

Extra calories, 6 to 12 months:

- Add 1 teaspoon of oil or melted butter to each 4 ounces of baby food.
- Offer whole milk yogurt, cheese, and mashed avocado.
- Mix infant cereal with breast milk or formula. Feed it with a spoon.
- Thin a little peanut butter into baby food or yogurt.
- Ask us first if your baby has bad eczema or an egg allergy.

Extra calories, 1 year and older:

- Add butter, cheese, sauces, or cream to foods. Use about 1 teaspoon per 4 ounces of food.
- Give whole milk until age 2.
- Avoid choking foods like whole nuts, popcorn, whole grapes, and raw vegetables.

Mealtimes for toddlers:

- Serve 3 meals and 3 snacks at set times each day.
- You choose what, when, and where your child eats.
- Your child chooses how much to eat, or whether to eat.
- Do not pressure your child to eat.
- Offer only water between meals and snacks. No grazing or sipping all day.
- Milk: no more than 16 to 24 ounces a day. Too much milk fills your child up.
- Juice: no more than 4 ounces a day for ages 1 to 3.

Weight checks:

- Weigh your child at the clinic only. Home weights go up and down from day to day.
- Weight checks: ***

Call the clinic if your child:

- Vomits often or after most feeds
- Has fewer wet diapers than usual
- Has a dry mouth or fewer tears
- Refuses to eat or drink
- Is more sleepy or plays less than usual

Call us if you cannot get enough formula or food. We can connect you with WIC and other help.

Go to the ER if your child is very sleepy, hard to wake, or has a sunken soft spot.

handouts.title: Thyroiditis
handouts.text:
Thyroiditis

Your thyroid gland is inflamed. It is leaking extra thyroid hormone into your blood. This usually gets better on its own.

What to expect:

- First, too much hormone for about 3 to 6 weeks. You may feel shaky, hot, or have a fast heartbeat.
- Next, your thyroid may run low for a few months. You may feel tired, cold, or constipated.
- Most people are back to normal within a year.

Your medicines:

- For pain: *** by mouth ***. Take it with food.
- For a fast heartbeat or shaking: *** by mouth ***. We will stop it when your levels are normal.
- Steroid if pain is severe: prednisone *** mg by mouth every morning. Do not stop it suddenly.
- Thyroid hormone if your levels run low: levothyroxine *** mcg every morning.

Blood tests:

- We will check your thyroid every *** weeks until it is normal.
- Stop biotin (hair, skin, nail vitamins) 2 days before each blood test.

After a pregnancy:

- This can happen again after a future pregnancy.
- Get a thyroid blood test once a year. Your thyroid can stay low later in life.
- Tell your doctor about this if you plan another pregnancy.

Call the clinic if your neck pain gets worse or comes back when the steroid dose goes down.

Call the clinic if you feel very tired, cold, low, or depressed.

Go to the ER if you:

- Have a high fever and a red, swollen neck
- Have trouble swallowing or breathing

Call 911 if you have chest pain or fainting.

handouts.title: Thyroid nodule
handouts.text:
Thyroid nodule

A thyroid nodule is a lump in your thyroid gland, in the front of your neck. Nodules are very common. Most are not cancer.

What we found:

- Size: *** cm.
- Ultrasound result: ***.
- Biopsy result: ***.

What happens next:

- Next ultrasound: ***.
- Biopsy: ***.
- Visit with a specialist: ***.

About the biopsy:

- A thin needle takes a few cells from the nodule. We use ultrasound to guide it.
- Some results are unclear. We may repeat the biopsy or send a special test.

Good to know:

- We do not use thyroid pills to shrink nodules. The benefit is small and the risks are higher.
- If your nodule is stable on ultrasound for 5 years, you may stop scans.
- Two harmless biopsies of the same nodule usually means no more scans for it.

Call the clinic if:

- The lump gets bigger quickly
- You find a new lump in your neck
- You have trouble swallowing or a feeling of pressure in your neck

Go to the ER if you have trouble breathing.

handouts.title: After a heart attack
handouts.text:
After a heart attack

A heart attack happens when blood flow to part of your heart is blocked. Medicines and healthy habits lower your chance of another one.

Your medicines and why:

- Aspirin ***: keeps blood clots from forming.
- *** (blood thinner pill): keeps your stent open and stops clots. Take it until ***.
- *** (statin): lowers cholesterol to help prevent another heart attack.
- *** (beta-blocker): protects your heart and slows your heart rate.
- *** (ACE inhibitor or ARB): lowers blood pressure and protects your heart.
- Nitroglycerin under the tongue: for chest pain.
- Other: ***

Never stop your blood thinner pills unless your heart doctor says it is OK. Stopping too soon can cause a clot and another heart attack.

- If another doctor or dentist asks you to stop, call your heart doctor first.
- Do not take ibuprofen or naproxen. Ask before any new medicine or supplement.
- Take only low-dose aspirin, 81 mg, unless we tell you otherwise.

How to use nitroglycerin:

- Sit down. Put 1 tablet under your tongue and let it melt. Do not chew or swallow it.
- Wait 5 minutes. If the pain is not better, is worse, or comes back, call 911.
- Do not take more than 3 tablets in 15 minutes.
- Do not use it within 24 hours of sildenafil or vardenafil, or 48 hours of tadalafil.
- Keep the tablets in their glass bottle with the cap on tight.

Cardiac rehab:

- Cardiac rehab is a supervised exercise and teaching program.
- It lowers your chance of another heart attack and of going back to the hospital.
- Most programs are 36 visits over 12 weeks. Your program: ***

Activity:

- Take it easy for the first 4 to 6 weeks. Do not lift heavy things.
- Walking is good. You should be able to talk while you walk. If you cannot, slow down.
- Work: most people are off work at least 1 week. Your return date: ***
- Driving: your start date is ***. Do not drive while you still have heart symptoms.
- Sex: if light activity causes no symptoms, most people can have sex 1 week after a heart attack.
- Ask us first about sex. After bypass surgery, wait 6 to 8 weeks.
- No alcohol for at least 2 weeks. Then ask us how much is safe.

Food:

- Eat vegetables, fruit, beans, nuts, whole grains, and lean protein like fish or chicken.
- Limit salt, bacon, hot dogs, white bread, white rice, and sugary drinks.

Smoking:

- If you smoke, quitting is the best thing you can do for your heart.
- Stay away from secondhand smoke. We can help with medicine. Free help: call 1-800-QUIT-NOW.

Mood:

Feeling sad, worried, or tired is common after a heart attack. For most people it gets better in 2 to 3 weeks. Tell us if it does not. Depression can be treated.

Call the clinic if:

- Your chest pain comes more often, lasts longer, or happens at rest.
- Nitroglycerin does not work as well as before.
- You have bleeding that lasts a long time, pink or red urine, or black stools.
- You have bruises with no known cause.

Call 911 if you have:

- Chest pain, pressure, or squeezing that lasts more than a few minutes or goes away and comes back
- Pain in your arms, back, neck, jaw, or upper belly
- Trouble breathing, a cold sweat, nausea, or sudden dizziness
- Vomit that is bloody or looks like coffee grounds

Do not drive yourself to the hospital. An ambulance is the safest way to get there.

handouts.title: Chest pain, when to call 911
handouts.text:
Chest pain: when to call 911

Today your tests did not show a heart attack. Chest pain can still be a warning sign, so know what to watch for.

Your next step: ***

Call 911 right away if you have:

- Chest pain, pressure, squeezing, or fullness that lasts more than a few minutes
- Chest pain that goes away and comes back
- Pain in one or both arms, your back, shoulders, neck, jaw, or upper belly
- Shortness of breath at rest or with a little activity
- A cold sweat, nausea, vomiting, or sudden dizziness

Older adults and people with diabetes may have mild signs or none. Women more often feel very tired. Older adults more often feel short of breath.

Call 911 even if you are not sure it is a heart attack. Every minute matters.

- Do not drive yourself or let someone else drive you.
- An ambulance crew can start treatment on the way.

Call the clinic if:

- Chest pain comes back with activity and goes away with rest.
- You have questions about your tests or your follow-up.

handouts.title: Fluid behind the eardrum
handouts.text:
Fluid behind the eardrum

Your child has fluid behind the eardrum. This is not an ear infection. It often follows a cold or an ear infection. It usually goes away on its own within 3 months.

What to know:

- Antibiotics do not help this fluid.
- Allergy medicines, decongestants, and steroids do not help either.
- The fluid can make sounds muffled for a while.
- We will check your child's ears again in *** months.

Help your child hear and learn:

- Get your child's attention before you talk.
- Get within 3 feet of your child.
- Turn off the TV or music in the background.
- Face your child and speak clearly. Point to pictures to help.
- Read with your child every day. Talk about the pictures.
- At school, ask for a seat near the front of the class.

Hearing test:

- If the fluid lasts 3 months or more, your child needs a hearing test.
- If the fluid lasts and causes hearing problems, ear tubes may help.

Call the clinic if your child:

- Has ear pain or fever
- Does not seem to hear you
- Seems behind with talking
- Has new problems with balance, school, or behavior
- Has fluid draining from the ear

handouts.title: Drainage from ear tubes
handouts.text:
Drainage from ear tubes

Drainage from an ear tube is common. It usually means an ear infection. Ear drops treat it. Most children do not need antibiotics by mouth.

How to give the drops:

- Warm the bottle in your hand for 1 to 2 minutes. Cold drops can cause dizziness.
- Lay your child down with the draining ear facing up.
- Put in *** drops.
- Push in on the small flap in front of the ear 4 or 5 times. This pumps the drops through the tube.
- Keep your child lying this way for *** minutes.
- Give the drops *** times a day for *** days.
- Then do the other ear if needed.

Water:

- Most children with tubes do not need earplugs.
- Most can swim and bathe as usual.

Tube checkups:

- Your child needs ear checks until the tube falls out.
- Next ear check: ***

Call the clinic if:

- Drainage is not better after 7 days of drops
- Drainage comes back 2 or more times in 6 months
- Your child has a fever or is getting worse

Go to the ER if your child:

- Has swelling or redness behind the ear
- Has an ear that sticks out more than before
- Has a stiff neck or a weak face
- Is very sleepy

handouts.title: Earwax
handouts.text:
Earwax

Earwax is normal. It cleans and protects your ears. Sometimes it builds up and blocks the ear. This can cause muffled hearing or a full feeling.

To soften wax at home:

- Put *** drops in the blocked ear twice a day for up to *** days.
- Plain water, salt water (saline), or store-bought earwax drops all work. No kind works best.
- Hold the bottle in your hand for a few minutes first, so the drops are near body temperature.
- Tilt your head so the ear faces up. Keep the drops in for a few minutes.

To rinse wax out, only if we said it is OK:

- Use a soft rubber bulb syringe and body-temperature water.
- Cold water can make you dizzy.
- Gently squirt water toward the side of the ear canal.
- Tip your head to let the water drain out.
- Do not use a jet water device to clean your ears.

Do not:

- Put cotton swabs, bobby pins, or other objects in your ear.
- Use ear candles. They do not work and can cause harm.

Do not use drops or rinse your ears if you have:

- A hole in your eardrum or ear tubes
- Had ear surgery
- Ear pain, drainage, or bleeding
- Diabetes or a weak immune system, unless we said it is OK

If you wear hearing aids, have your ears checked every 3 to 6 months.

Call the clinic if:

- Your ear is still blocked after *** days
- You have ear pain, drainage, fever, or dizziness
- Your hearing is still low after the wax is gone

Call us the same day if you have sudden hearing loss.

handouts.title: Blocked ear tubes
handouts.text:
Blocked ear tubes

The Eustachian tube connects your middle ear to the back of your nose. It lets air in so the pressure stays even. Colds, allergies, flying, or diving can block it.

Your ear may feel full, pop, hurt, or sound muffled.

What helps:

- Swallow, yawn, chew gum, or suck on hard candy.
- Breathe in. Then gently breathe out while you hold your nose closed and your mouth shut.
- Treat allergies or sinus problems if you have them: ***
- Steroid nose sprays help allergies. They have not been shown to fix blocked ear tubes alone.

Flying:

- Try not to fly with a cold or bad allergies.
- Stay awake while the plane comes down. Swallow, yawn, or chew gum.
- For babies and young children, nurse, give a bottle, or give sips of a drink during landing.
- Adults: we may suggest a decongestant pill 30 minutes before the flight: ***

Diving:

- Go down and come up slowly.
- Do not dive with a stuffy nose from a cold or allergies.

Call the clinic if:

- Ear pain after flying or diving does not ease after a few hours
- You have ear drainage, bleeding, fever, or bad ear pain
- Your ear still feels blocked after *** weeks

Call us the same day if you have sudden hearing loss.

handouts.title: Ringing in the ears
handouts.text:
Ringing in the ears

Tinnitus means hearing a sound that others cannot hear. It may ring, buzz, or hum. It often comes with hearing loss. For many people it gets better or bothers them less over time.

What helps:

- Background sound, like a fan, soft music, or a sound app with rain or waves. This can help at bedtime.
- Hearing aids, if you have hearing loss. They can make the ringing less noticeable.
- A type of counseling called cognitive behavioral therapy, or CBT. It has the best proof of helping.
- Good sleep, and treating stress, worry, or low mood.

What does not help:

- No medicine cures tinnitus.
- Vitamins, herbs, and supplements like ginkgo have not been shown to work.

Protect your ears:

- Avoid loud noise. Use earplugs or earmuffs at concerts, at work, or with loud tools.
- Tell us about all your medicines. Some can cause ringing.
- Do not stop a medicine without asking us.

Your plan: ***

Call the clinic if:

- The ringing is in only one ear
- You hear a pulsing sound, like your heartbeat
- You have hearing loss, dizziness, ear pain, or drainage
- The ringing makes you feel very sad or hopeless

Call us the same day if you have sudden hearing loss.

Call 911 if you have new weakness, numbness, a drooping face, or trouble speaking. Call 988 if you have thoughts of hurting yourself.

handouts.title: Swimmer's ear
handouts.text:
Swimmer's ear

Swimmer's ear is an infection of the ear canal. Ear drops treat it. Most people feel better in 2 to 3 days.

Your drops: *** drops in the *** ear, *** times a day for *** days.

How to put in ear drops:

- If you can, have someone else put the drops in.
- Warm the bottle in your hand for 1 to 2 minutes. Cold drops can make you dizzy.
- Lie down with the sore ear facing up.
- Put in enough drops to fill the ear canal.
- Gently push in and out on the small flap in front of the ear a few times.
- Stay lying down for 3 to 5 minutes. Use a timer.
- Wipe off any extra drops.

If you have a wick, a small sponge in the ear:

- It helps the drops get in. Put the drops right on it.
- It may fall out on its own. This is a good sign.
- Do not pull it out yourself unless we tell you to.

While your ear heals:

- Use the drops for at least 7 days, even if you feel better sooner.
- Keep water out. Before a shower, put in a cotton ball coated with petroleum jelly.
- Ask us before you swim.
- Do not scratch or put anything in your ear, not even cotton swabs.
- Pain medicine: ***
- If you can taste the drops, tell us. You may have a hole in your eardrum.

To prevent swimmer's ear:

- Wear well-fitting earplugs when you swim.
- After swimming or bathing, tilt your head to let water drain out.
- Dry your ears with a hair dryer on the lowest setting.
- Do not scratch your ear canal or put objects in it.

Call the clinic if:

- You are not better in 2 to 3 days
- You still have symptoms after 7 days of drops
- Redness or swelling spreads to your outer ear, face, or neck
- The drops hurt or you get a rash

Do you have diabetes or a weak immune system? Go to the ER if you get a fever or a weak face.

handouts.title: Home strength and balance program
handouts.text:
Strength and balance at home

These exercises make your legs stronger and help prevent falls. They are based on the Otago and Vivifrail programs for older adults.

Your Vivifrail level, A, B, C, or D: ***
Your ankle weight: *** pounds

When to exercise:

- Strength: 3 days a week, with a rest day in between, like Monday, Wednesday, and Friday.
- Balance: at least 3 days a week. Every day is fine.
- Walking: start with 5 to 10 minutes. Add a few minutes each week, up to 30 minutes.

How hard:

- Use an ankle weight or water bottle you can lift 8 to 10 times before your muscles tire.
- Most people over 80 start with 2 to 4 pound ankle weights.
- Rest 1 to 2 minutes between sets.
- Breathe out as you lift. Breathe in as you lower.

Strength exercises:

1. Sit to stand. Sit in a sturdy chair with your feet flat. Stand up without using your hands if you can. Stand up quickly, then sit down slowly.

2. Heel raises. Stand behind a counter and hold on. Rise up on your toes as high as you can. Hold for 3 seconds, then lower slowly.

3. Knee straightening. Sit in a chair with your ankle weight on. Straighten one knee until your leg is out straight. Lower slowly. Do both legs.

4. Side leg lift. Stand and hold the counter. Keep your back straight and toes forward. Lift one leg out to the side, then lower slowly. Do both legs.

5. Back knee bend. Stand and hold the counter. Bend one knee to bring your foot up behind you. Lower slowly. Do both legs.

6. Arm curls. Sit with a water bottle in each hand. Bend your elbows to bring the bottles up to your shoulders. Lower slowly.

Balance exercises:

7. Heel to toe walk. Hold the counter. Walk 10 steps, putting your heel right in front of your other toes. Rest, then repeat.

8. One leg stand. Hold the counter. Stand on one leg and count to 10. Switch legs. Work up to 30 seconds.

Hold on at first. Let go only when you feel steady, and only with someone nearby.

How to build up:

- Weeks 1 and 2: 2 sets of 10.
- Weeks 3 and 4: 2 sets of 12 to 15.
- Weeks 5 and 6: 3 sets of 12.
- Week 7: use a heavier weight and start again at 2 sets of 10.
- The program is 12 weeks. Keep going after that, or the gains fade.

Free guides with pictures: vivifrail.com

Stay safe:

- Use a sturdy chair and counter.
- If you have arthritis, move only as far as you can without pain.
- Stop and call the clinic if you feel dizzy, short of breath, or have chest pain.
- Call the clinic if muscle pain does not go away, or if you fall.

Call 911 if chest pain does not go away with rest.

handouts.title: Protein for older adults
handouts.text:
Protein for strong muscles

As we age, muscles need more protein to stay strong. Eat protein at every meal, and keep doing your exercises.

Your goal: *** grams of protein a day. That is about *** grams at each meal.

Most older adults need 25 to 30 grams of protein at each meal.

Protein in common foods:

- 1 large egg: 6 grams
- 1 cup of milk: 8 grams
- 6 ounces of plain Greek yogurt: about 16 grams
- Half a cup of cottage cheese: about 12 grams
- 3 ounces of canned tuna, drained: about 22 grams
- 3 ounces of cooked chicken breast: about 26 grams
- Half a cup of cooked beans: about 8 grams
- Half a cup of cooked lentils: about 9 grams
- 2 tablespoons of peanut butter: about 7 grams

A day that meets the goal:

- Breakfast: 2 eggs, 1 cup of milk, and half a cup of cottage cheese, about 32 grams.
- Lunch: tuna sandwich with 3 ounces of tuna and 1 cup of milk, about 30 grams.
- Supper: 3 ounces of chicken and half a cup of beans, about 34 grams.

Low-cost choices:

- Eggs, milk, canned tuna, peanut butter, and dried or canned beans and lentils.
- Store-brand yogurt and cottage cheese.
- Ask us about home-delivered meals or food help: ***

If chewing is hard, try eggs, yogurt, cottage cheese, beans, and soft fish.

Nutrition drinks, only if we suggest them:

- Drink *** bottles a day between meals, not in place of a meal.
- Pick one with at least *** grams of protein per bottle.
- Keep going for at least 1 month. We will check your weight.

Cautions:

- If you have kidney disease, ask us before eating more protein. Some people with weak kidneys need less.
- Drink enough fluids unless we told you to limit them.
- Women need at least 7 cups a day. Men need at least 8 and a half cups.
- Beans, lentils, fruits, and vegetables add fiber and help prevent constipation.

Call the clinic if you:

- Keep losing weight without trying
- Have constipation that does not get better
- Have trouble chewing or swallowing
- Eat less than half your meals for more than a week

handouts.title: Tantrums
handouts.text:
Tantrums

Tantrums are a normal part of growing up. They happen most between ages 1 and 3. Most children have fewer tantrums as they learn to talk.

Why tantrums happen:

- Your child wants to do things on their own but cannot yet.
- Your child does not have the words to say how they feel.
- Being tired, hungry, or sick makes tantrums more likely.
- Not getting what they want is a common trigger.

How to prevent tantrums:

- Keep regular times for meals, naps, and bed.
- If your child no longer naps, plan 15 to 20 minutes of quiet rest each day.
- Bring a healthy snack when you go out.
- Give small choices, like "red cup or blue cup?" Do not offer a choice when there is none.
- Praise good behavior often. Catch your child being good.
- Pick your battles. Focus on safety, not small things like which shoes to wear.
- Plan ahead for hard times, like errands or long waits. Tell your child what you expect.
- Keep off-limits things out of sight and reach.

During a tantrum:

- Stay calm. Take a slow breath before you respond.
- Keep your child safe. Move them away from danger, like a street.
- If your child is safe, ignore the tantrum. Do not argue or explain.
- Try to distract a young child with a new toy, a new room, or a song.
- Away from home, move to a quiet spot, like the car.
- Do not give in. Giving in teaches your child that tantrums work.
- If your child hits, kicks, bites, or throws things, act right away. Use a time-out or take away a privilege.

After a tantrum:

- Wait until you and your child are both calm.
- Praise your child for calming down. Offer a hug if they want one.
- Name the feeling: "You were mad when we left the park."
- If your child is old enough, talk about better ways to show anger.
- Do not give your child what the tantrum was about.

Take care of yourself:

- Tantrums are not a sign of bad parenting.
- Take breaks. Let another adult take over when you feel upset.

Call the clinic if:

- Tantrums get worse or happen often after age 5
- Tantrums often last more than 25 minutes
- Your child has more than 5 tantrums a day for several days in a row
- Your child cannot calm down after tantrums
- Your child hurts themselves, hurts others, or breaks things
- Your child holds their breath and faints
- Your child also has nightmares, new toilet accidents, headaches, stomachaches, worry, or clinginess
- Your child refuses to eat or sleep
- You often feel angry or out of control, or you fear you might hurt your child

Call 911 if your child is hurt or in danger.

handouts.title: How to use time-out
handouts.text:
How to use time-out

Time-out is a short break from your attention after a problem behavior. It is for young children, about ages 2 to 5. It works best when your child gets lots of praise and attention at other times.

When to use time-out:

- Unsafe or hurtful behavior, like hitting, biting, pushing, or throwing things
- Not following a direction after a warning

When not to use time-out:

- For whining. Ignore whining instead.
- When your child is very upset or scared. Stay close and help them calm down.

Pick the spot:

- Choose a safe, boring spot, like a sturdy chair at the end of a hallway.
- Keep it away from toys, TV, windows, and people.
- If you use a room, keep the light on and stay nearby. Never use a closet.

Step by step:

- Give one calm warning. Say it, do not ask it: "If you hit again, you will go to time-out."
- Wait about 5 seconds. If your child stops, praise them.
- If the behavior happens again, say calmly: "You hit. Time-out."
- Walk your child to the spot. Do not lecture, scold, or argue.
- Set a timer for 1 minute for each year of age. A 3-year-old gets 3 minutes.
- Most young children need only 2 to 5 minutes.
- During time-out, do not talk to, look at, or touch your child.
- Ignore yelling, crying, and promises to be good.

If your child gets up:

- Put your child back without talking. Start the timer over.
- You may need to do this many times at first. It gets easier.
- If your child keeps leaving, warn that they will lose a privilege, like bike time today. Then follow through.

Ending time-out:

- Your child should be quiet for the last 5 seconds before getting up.
- Then repeat the direction your child did not follow, like "Pick up the blocks."
- If your child still says no, go back to time-out.
- Praise the next good thing your child does. Start fresh.

Tips:

- Use time-out every time for the same behavior.
- All caregivers should do time-out the same way.
- Never warn of a time-out and then not follow through.
- If two children fight, put both in time-out in separate spots.
- Children 3 and older can learn to take a break and come back when calm.
- For school-age children, taking away a privilege is another choice.

Special time:

Special time is a short play time each day where your child leads. It builds warmth and cooperation.

- Play together for 5 to 15 minutes every day. Start with 5 minutes if that is easier.
- Do it at the same time each day. Put your phone away.
- Let your child pick the toy or game. Follow their lead.
- Choose blocks, crayons, or other toys that build. Skip screens and toys that play on their own.
- Praise what you like: "You are sharing so nicely."
- Describe what your child is doing, and copy their play.
- Avoid questions, commands, and criticism during this time.
- Ignore small misbehavior. If your child does something unsafe, stop play and use time-out.
- Keep special time every day, even on hard days. It is not a reward to earn.

Call the clinic if behavior is not getting better, or if you feel angry or out of control. Call 911 if a child is hurt or in danger.

handouts.title: Helping your child's behavior
handouts.text:
Helping your child's behavior

Many children have hard behavior at times. The 4 tools below help most children behave better. They work best when every caregiver uses them every day.

Our plan:

- Behaviors to work on first: ***
- Referral: ***
- Next visit: ***

Tool 1, special time:

- Play with your child for 5 to 15 minutes every day. Let your child lead.
- Praise, describe, and copy their play. Skip questions, commands, and criticism.
- Keep special time every day, even on hard days.

Tool 2, praise:

- Catch your child being good. Praise right away.
- Say exactly what you liked: "Thank you for putting your shoes away."
- A smile, a thumbs up, or a high-five also counts.

Tool 3, ignore small stuff:

- Ignore whining, pouting, or interrupting if no one is in danger. Do not look, talk, or touch.
- The behavior often gets worse at first. Stay calm and do not give in.
- As soon as the behavior stops, praise what your child is doing well.
- Never ignore hurting others, unsafe acts, or breaking things. Stop it right away.

Tool 4, clear directions and steady consequences:

- Get close, make eye contact, and use your child's name.
- Give one direction at a time. Say it, do not ask it.
- Say what to do, not what to stop: "Walk, please" instead of "Don't run."
- Use a calm, firm voice. Offer a choice of two when you can.
- If your child does not listen, repeat the direction once and warn of a consequence.
- Follow through every time with time-out or loss of a privilege.
- Give consequences right away. Young children learn best this way.
- Praise your child when they listen.

Behavior chart:

- Pick 1 or 2 behaviors. Say what you want, like "Gets dressed by 7:30."
- Our target behaviors: ***
- Choose a reward your child really wants. It does not need to cost money.
- Our rewards: ***
- Make a simple chart with pictures. Put it where your child can see it.
- Give a sticker or mark right after the behavior. Say what your child did well.
- Never take away a sticker or reward your child already earned.
- When the behavior becomes a habit, pick a new one or slowly stop the chart.

Parenting programs:

Parent training programs teach these tools step by step, with a coach. They are a top first treatment for behavior problems.

- Programs include Parent-Child Interaction Therapy (PCIT), Triple P, and The Incredible Years.
- Most programs take 8 to 16 sessions.
- Our referral: ***

Home safety:

- If you have guns at home, store them unloaded and locked.
- Lock up the ammunition in a separate place.

Take care of yourself:

- Parenting a child with hard behavior is stressful. You are not alone.
- When you feel angry, take a break first. Breathe deeply and count to 10.
- Take breaks. Let another adult take over when you need it.
- Tell us if you feel sad, hopeless, or very stressed most days. We can help.
- For help with food, housing, or bills, call 211.
- If you or your child are in crisis, call or text 988 any time.

Call the clinic if:

- Behavior gets worse, or is not better by your next visit
- Your child often hurts others, hurts themselves, or breaks things
- Problems at school or daycare get worse
- You feel you might lose control or hurt your child

Call 988 or go to the ER if your child talks about suicide or hurting someone. Call 911 if anyone is hurt or in danger.
